content.text: EON Reality is a Singapore based augmented and virtual reality company, and it is best known to Lab MGM through its role as the industry partner behind NTU's Centre for Augmented and Virtual Reality, or CAVR. During a December 2022 collaboration trip to Singapore, Lab MGM's delegation met EON Reality in that capacity, as CAVR's partner, rather than through a direct prior relationship between MGM and the company.
A meeting, and a plan to pursue an MoU

FILKOM's account of the trip describes the meeting with EON Reality as covering the state of AR, VR, and XR technology and its use in fields such as healthcare and education. Coming out of that conversation, the parties are reported to have agreed to pursue a memorandum of understanding aimed at developing an AR and VR centre of excellence at Universitas Brawijaya.

props.caption: A virtual reality headset in use, illustrating the kind of technology discussed at the meeting. Image: Digits.co.uk Images, CC BY 2.0.

content.text: It is worth being precise about what that agreement was. FILKOM's own language is that the parties agreed to pursue an MoU, which describes an intention rather than a completed contract. FILKOM's account does not report that a final memorandum was signed, and this account does not treat the proposed AR and VR centre of excellence as an established fact. Readers should take it as a plan that was discussed and agreed to be pursued, not as a finished partnership.

Even framed cautiously, the meeting mattered for Lab MGM. EON Reality's work sits close to the AR and VR research the lab already pursues, and the discussion gave FILKOM a concrete reference point, a centre of excellence built with an established AR and VR technology provider, to weigh against its own ambitions in the same space.

It also illustrates how far a single trip can carry a research group. Lab MGM did not arrive in Singapore with an existing tie to EON Reality; the introduction happened because EON Reality is CAVR's strategic partner, and CAVR was already on the itinerary. That kind of second-degree connection can be productive, but it is also a reason to be careful about the language used to describe it. An agreement to pursue an MoU is a starting point for negotiation, not a partnership already in place.
It records a meeting and a stated intention, which is the accurate description of where things stood as of the visit.
Source: https://filkom.ub.ac.id/2022/12/22/inisiasi-kerjasama-dan-perbaikan-kurikulum-filkom-ub-kunjungi-cavr-ntu-dan-fxmedia-singapura/

article.title: Two Blibli Designers Spoke at Lab MGM's Interaction Design Series
article.subtitle: Lab MGM invited Blibli's Vivy Junita and Dara Adhelia, in separate 2022 sessions, to speak about UX strategy and emotional design.

content.text: Across its 2022 Webinar Series on Interaction Design, a guest lecture program built around FILKOM alumni working in industry, Lab MGM at Fakultas Ilmu Komputer, Universitas Brawijaya invited two different guest speakers from Blibli, an Indonesian e-commerce platform, into two separate sessions held months apart.

The first was Vivy Junita, a Product Manager at Blibli and a 2016 graduate of FILKOM's Informatics Engineering program, who joined the series' second session on March 11, 2022. Speaking alongside Verrel Radiman, then a UX Researcher at Mekari, Junita told the roughly 90 attending students that user experience extends beyond visual design into company strategy, playing a role in business outcomes through product innovation.
A Second Session on Emotional Design

Blibli returned for the series' third session on May 20, 2022, represented by Dara Adhelia, a UI Designer at Blibli and a 2016 graduate of FILKOM's Information Systems program. Adhelia spoke alongside Fathin Naufal Hawi of Mister Aladin on emotional design, telling around 70 student participants that emotion is a form of feeling that shapes how people experience a product, and that attractive design can create the positive response that keeps users engaged.

props.caption: A person shopping online from a laptop. Image: Bogdan Hoyaux, CC BY 4.0.

content.text: Both appearances were individual guest lecture invitations. Junita and Adhelia shared their own professional experience as FILKOM alumnae, the same way any invited speaker would, rather than acting on behalf of any agreement between Blibli and Lab MGM.

props.caption: Jakarta's business district. Image: Shubhi Rofiddinsa, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: Having two people from the same company speak months apart, on different themes, gave FILKOM students two distinct views of UX work inside a large online retail platform, one centered on strategy, the other on the emotional detail of everyday interface design. The two sessions sat inside a wider four part series that also brought in speakers from Tokopedia, tiket.com, and Mister Aladin over the course of the year, each invited individually rather than through any lasting arrangement with their employer.

Source: https://filkom.ub.ac.id/2022/05/23/mengetahui-minat-masyarakat-dan-konsumen-melalui-emotional-design/, https://filkom.ub.ac.id/2022/10/07/sertifikat-webinar-series-on-interaction-design/, and https://filkom.ub.ac.id/2022/03/18/mendefinisikan-dampak-strategi-ux-dari-perspektif-dunia-industri/

article.title: BINUS Researchers Join MGM's Look at the Future of Shopping
article.subtitle: Researchers from BINUS University's School of Computer Science coauthored a shopping technology study with MGM and ITS, a research coauthorship rather than an institutional partnership.

content.text: Retail technology research brought together three institutions in 2020: BINUS University's School of Computer Science, MGM at Universitas Brawijaya, and Institut Teknologi Sepuluh Nopember.

The resulting paper, "A literature review: Feasibility Study of technology to improve shopping experience," was presented at the 2020 International Conference on Computer Science and Computational Intelligence and later published in Procedia Computer Science, volume 179, in 2021. Its authors are Heraldo Y. Purwantono, Alexander A. S. Gunawan, and Widodo Budiharto from BINUS's School of Computer Science, together with MGM's Herman Tolle and Muhammad Attamimi of ITS.
Weighing three retail technologies

The paper examined three technologies aimed at changing how people shop: smart shopping trolleys that track items as they are placed in the cart, virtual reality shopping that lets a customer browse a store from home, and Just Walk Out style checkout free stores where sensors handle billing automatically. Rather than building a new system, the authors ran a feasibility study across each idea, weighing market viability, technical requirements, cost, regulation, and risk using a jobs to be done framework, to judge which of these emerging retail concepts were closest to practical, everyday use.

props.caption: Image: Gandy Peejay, CC BY-SA 4.0. BINUS University's Alam Sutera campus in Tangerang, Indonesia.

content.text: It is worth being precise about what this paper represents. It is a piece of coauthored research between individual researchers at BINUS's School of Computer Science, MGM, and ITS, not a signed cooperation agreement between BINUS University and Universitas Brawijaya. BINUS is a private university with several campuses across the Jakarta metropolitan area, known for its computer science and information technology programs, and this study is one point of contact between its researchers and MGM's own interest in human computer interaction.

props.caption: Image: Taman Renyah, CC BY 3.0. BINUS University's Anggrek campus in Jakarta.

content.text: For MGM, the paper is a useful example of how research on everyday technology, in this case the future of grocery shopping, can quietly connect researchers across three different Indonesian institutions long before any formal partnership is discussed.
Source: https://scholar.its.ac.id/en/publications/a-literature-review-feasibility-study-of-technology-to-improve-sh/ and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877050921000351

article.title: A Phone That Listens While You Learn to Speak
article.subtitle: Treating the microphone as an input changes what a language app can ask of a learner, and what it must get right.

content.text: Learning to speak a language alone is awkward. There is nobody to answer, and nobody to tell you that your pronunciation drifted three sentences ago. A microphone changes that arrangement, because the phone can play both roles.

props.caption: Self study asks the learner to be their own critic. Photo: Rexdanato, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What speaking input changes

Reading and writing give immediate feedback on the screen. Speaking gives none unless the app listens, so learners quietly avoid it and spend their practice time on the skills that already respond. Adding a microphone rebalances the app toward the skill that needs the most repetition.
Repeating a phrase becomes a two way exchange instead of a silent exercise.
A learner can compare their own attempt against a native model.
Speaking practice moves into the spare minutes of a commute, not only into class.

props.caption: Course materials for a first year Japanese class. Image: Yoko Sato, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The engineering questions it opens

The authors framed the work as a feasibility study, which is an honest description of how much remains. Speech recognition has to run well on a mid range Android phone, in a noisy room, for a learner who is still making mistakes. That is a harder speech problem than dictating for someone who is already fluent.

Then comes the feedback loop. Recognising words is not the same as judging pronunciation, and a learner told they are wrong without being told why will simply switch the feature off. The usability result in the paper, 81.0, says the shell works. The hard part is what happens inside it.

props.caption: Headphones that turn a phone into a listening lab. Photo: Akb48akb, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Where the idea points

The direction reaches past Japanese. Any skill a phone can hear, whether it is a language, a musical instrument or a physiotherapy routine, can become an interactive drill once the device is allowed to listen. What this paper shows is that the interaction design, not the feature list, is what makes that work.

Source: Brata, K. C., & Brata, A. H. (2018). An Idea of Interactive Japanese Language M-Learning Application to Support Listening and Speaking Exercise. 2018 International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Students Who Rebuild a Given Map Learn More Online
article.subtitle: A comparison of two ways to map a reading text together found a clear advantage for the guided approach.

content.text: When classes moved online, the hardest part was not delivering the material. It was keeping the discussion alive. Group work that once happened naturally around a table had to be rebuilt inside a browser window, and the tools had to carry the interaction that a room used to provide.

props.caption: Students link up across two countries. Photo: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Concept maps moved online

A concept map turns a text into nodes and labelled links, so students can see how the ideas fit together. Doing that in pairs adds another layer, because partners must agree on what connects to what. The authors built an online system where two students work on the same map at the same time, in real time.

props.caption: Nodes and labelled links turn a reading into a structure. Photo: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Two ways to map together
The experiment compared two collaborative strategies with graduate students working in pairs. Everyone read the same material and took the same tests, so only the mapping method differed.
Collaborative Kit-Building gave each pair a ready made set of nodes and links taken from a teacher's map, and the pair rebuilt the map together.
Collaborative Scratch Mapping let each pair build an open ended map from nothing but the text.

props.caption: Partners negotiate every link over a video call. Photo: Project Kei, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the comparison showed

Comprehension improved in both groups, which is expected from any serious study session. The interesting part is the gap between them. On the test taken after the mapping activity, the Kit-Build pairs scored significantly higher than the open ended pairs.

The authors also asked about how the pairs managed their own collaboration, using a shared metacognition questionnaire. Here the Kit-Build method again came out ahead, with students reporting that they could monitor and manage their joint work more easily than with open ended mapping.

The conclusion is direct. For distance learning, the authors recommend Kit-Build concept map as the collaborative strategy, because the supplied components remove the uncertainty of where to start while leaving the reasoning to the students.

Source: Pinandito, A., et al. (2021). Efficient Online Collaborative Learning Through Concept Mapping with Kit-Build Concept Map. 6th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Eye Exercises in Mobile VR Show Small but Consistent Results
article.subtitle: A five week diary study put a century old relaxation technique inside a smartphone headset and watched what happened to myopia.

content.text: Myopia is one of the most common vision problems in the world, and it keeps growing. The paper opens with a projection that shortsightedness will affect 52 percent of the global population by 2050, with rates of 70 to 80 percent among young adults in parts of Europe and East Asia.

props.caption: Reading a Snellen chart during a vision check. Photo: Beendy234, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: An old idea for a growing problem

Glasses, contact lenses and corrective surgery help people see, but they are expensive and do not address the underlying cause. The Bates method, developed by the New York ophthalmologist William Horatio Bates, takes a different route. Its core claim is that the eye reaches its best acuity when it is fully relaxed, and it offers concrete routines such as palming, shifting, sunning and blinking.

props.caption: A labelled diagram of the human eye. Photo: Chris Sullivan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Putting the method inside a headset

The authors built an Android application that runs on a phone slotted into a mobile headset. Their first job was deciding which parts of the method a headset can actually deliver. Some techniques survived the move, and some clearly did not.
Head swing was supported by driving a pointer with the gyroscope so it moves across all three axes.
Optical swing was supported by animating an object the eyes track while the head stays still.
Palming, sunning and colour day were dropped, because you cannot massage your eyes, summon sunlight, or wear a headset for a full day.
The five week diary

Fourteen participants took part, seven men and seven women aged 21 to 42, all with myopia and some wearing glasses. They were asked to run the routine twice a day, morning and evening, and to keep a retrospective diary for 30 days.

props.caption: A headset holds the phone that runs the routine. Photo: Bert Niehaus, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: After five weeks there was no significant difference in myopia levels between participants. The average change was still encouraging: a reduction of 0.13 diopter, with a small standard deviation, which suggests the measurement was at least consistent.

Participants also reported eye fatigue during long headset sessions, and described the guided routine as simpler, faster and more enjoyable than their usual habits. The authors present this as a preliminary feasibility result rather than proof that the method works.
Source: Brata, K. C., et al. (2023). Virtual reality eye exercises application based on bates method: a preliminary study. Indonesian Journal of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Why Japanese Learning Apps Skip Speaking
article.subtitle: Vocabulary and reading drills are everywhere. A conference paper argues the microphone is the missing input.

content.text: Open almost any Japanese learning app and you will find flashcards, stroke order diagrams and reading drills. What you will rarely find is an app that asks you to open your mouth and speak.

props.caption: A classroom in a Japanese high school. Photo: frwl, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The gap the authors noticed

Japanese is one of the most popular foreign languages in Indonesian higher education, and also one of the hardest to learn. A wave of mobile learning apps grew up around that demand. The authors observe that the popular ones train the same three skills: vocabulary, writing and reading.

Speaking gets left out. That is an odd omission, because conversation is usually the reason someone starts a language in the first place, and it is the part a classroom has the least time to rehearse. An app that never listens to the learner cannot correct pronunciation or build the reflexes that speaking needs.
What the paper proposes

The proposal is speaking input treated as a first class interaction. Instead of tapping an answer or dragging a character, the learner says it out loud. The application is meant to deliver listening and speaking practice in a form that feels natural on a phone, using the microphone that every device already carries.

props.caption: Studio microphones on a rack. Photo: Justin De La Ornellas, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Feasibility first
This is not a report on a finished product. Its stated objective is narrower and more useful: to investigate whether the speaking method can support mobile learning at all.

props.caption: Chart of the sounds an app must teach. Image: International Phonetic Association, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The evaluation concluded that the overall functionality is feasible for future implementation, with a usability score of 81.0. The authors present that as an invitation to keep building rather than as a final verdict.
What the idea leaves open

A feasibility score answers one question and raises several. Pronunciation feedback needs speech recognition good enough to be useful on an ordinary phone. Practice also needs a shape, because repeating a phrase alone grows dull quickly. The interaction has to hold attention for weeks, not minutes, before it can replace the drills learners already accept.

Source: Brata, K. C., & Brata, A. H. (2018). An Idea of Interactive Japanese Language M-Learning Application to Support Listening and Speaking Exercise. 2018 International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: GLSL Unggul atas WebGL pada Augmented Reality Berbasis Web
article.subtitle: Sebuah eksperimen membandingkan dua cara menggambar objek virtual di peramban, dan pemenangnya cukup jelas.

content.text: Augmented reality tidak lagi harus berupa aplikasi yang dipasang di ponsel. Peramban modern sudah mampu menampilkan objek virtual di atas gambar kamera, dan tantangan utamanya adalah menjaga tampilan itu tetap mulus sambil terus memproses video dari dunia nyata.
Penelitian ini membandingkan dua cara menggambar objek tersebut. Tim peneliti menulis shader sendiri, menggabungkannya dengan beberapa pustaka web, lalu melihat mana yang memberi kinerja lebih baik.
WebGL, GLSL, dan pustaka pendukung

WebGL adalah standar untuk merender grafik 3D di antarmuka web. GLSL adalah bahasa skrip yang mengatur bagaimana hasil render itu ditampilkan. Three.js berperan sebagai perangkat JavaScript untuk membuat grafik 3D interaktif, sedangkan AR.js menangani sisi augmented reality.

props.caption: Tahapan pemrosesan shader di WebGL. Diagram: Scriptor universalis, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Pendekatan yang dipakai adalah shader mentah. Alih alih mengandalkan lapisan bawaan, peneliti menulis instruksi langsung untuk kartu grafis. Jalur ini lebih panjang, tetapi memberi kendali penuh atas setiap piksel yang digambar.
Cara perbandingan dilakukan

Kedua pendekatan dijalankan pada skenario augmented reality berbasis web yang sama. Shader yang sudah diimplementasikan digabungkan dengan Three.js dan AR.js, lalu diamati bagaimana masing masing menampilkan objek virtual di layar.

props.caption: Perbandingan teknologi grafis web. Diagram: Scriptor universalis, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Hasilnya
GLSL menang. Shader GLSL memberi kinerja yang lebih baik saat menampilkan objek virtual di augmented reality berbasis web dibandingkan jalur WebGL yang diuji pada studi ini.

Bagi pengembang web, temuan ini masuk akal. WebGL menyembunyikan banyak detail perangkat keras supaya mudah dipakai. Ketika detail itu dibuka lewat shader sendiri, kendali atas proses penggambaran menjadi lebih besar, dan hasilnya lebih ringan.
Augmented reality berbasis web penting karena tidak memerlukan instalasi. Pengguna cukup membuka tautan. Karena itu, setiap frame yang bisa dihemat berdampak langsung pada kenyamanan pemakaian.

props.caption: The graphics hardware that executes every shader call. Photo: C. Spille, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Kesimpulannya, cara menggambar objek tidak kalah penting dari model 3D atau kamera yang dipakai. Pilihan pada tingkat shader ikut menentukan seberapa nyaman sebuah pengalaman AR di peramban.

Sumber: Hamzaturrazak, M., et al. (2024). Analisis Kinerja Augmented Reality Hypertext Markup Language Dengan Pemanfaatan Web Graphics Library Dan OpenGL Shading Language Untuk Pengembangan 3D. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: Why outdoor AR authoring keeps breaking on the desktop
article.subtitle: Separating the place where you build AR content from the place where it appears is the root of most alignment errors.

content.text: There is a quiet assumption built into most outdoor augmented reality workflows. It says that the place where you create content and the place where that content appears can be separated, as long as you write down the coordinates carefully enough.

That assumption is where the trouble starts. A developer stands on a footpath with a phone, notes a latitude and longitude, walks back to a desk, opens Unity with an AR SDK, and builds a virtual sign. Weeks later the sign hovers half a metre to the left of where it belongs, or floats above the shopfront instead of beside the door.

props.caption: A mapping survey vehicle, source of the imagery that anchors outdoor AR. Photo: Hannes Grobe, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: The desktop gap, in plain terms

Desktop tools work from fixed or prerecorded environmental data. They cannot see that the tree grew, that a delivery van now parks there, or that the pavement was repainted last spring. Every one of those changes shifts the visual features the tracking system relies on, so the content drifts. The team behind a 2025 study in Electronics names this as the central limitation of the mainstream approach.

Their answer was to move authoring into the moment and the location. Stand at the point of interest, create the object, store it, and let the localization happen live. The reasoning is straightforward: if the anchor is captured under the same conditions the user will encounter, far less has to be corrected later.

props.caption: A phone running a map navigation app. The handset becomes the authoring device. Photo: Santeri Viinamaki, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: What this changes for developers
Novices no longer need SDK knowledge before they can contribute content. The barrier moves from programming to walking.
Field edits become cheap. A misplaced marker is fixed on the spot instead of in a build cycle.
Teams can hand authoring to people who know the site, not just the tooling.

props.caption: Street View imagery acts as a shared reference layer for outdoor localization. Photo: Jove, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: None of this makes desktop tooling obsolete. Complex 3D assets still belong on a workstation. But the placement step, which is where accuracy is won or lost, now has a credible alternative that fits in a pocket.

Source: Brata, K.C., Funabiki, N., Panduman, Y.Y.F., et al. (2025). A Proposal of In Situ Authoring Tool with Visual-Inertial Sensor Fusion for Outdoor Location-Based Augmented Reality. Electronics. DOI:
10.3390/electronics14020342

article.title: The Hard Part of Recommending Food Is Asking Better Questions
article.subtitle: A recommendation is only as good as the preferences it was given. An Android system turned that into a series of small choices.

content.text: Two people can stand in front of the same row of food stalls and disagree completely. One weighs price above everything. The other will walk twenty minutes for a better bowl. Neither is wrong, and no single rating captures both.

That is the design problem behind culinary recommendation systems. Collecting data about restaurants is straightforward. Learning what a particular person actually values is the part that decides whether the recommendation feels useful or random.
Why pairwise beats a rating scale

A Universitas Brawijaya team built an Android application around the Analytical Hierarchy Process, and the interesting choice is how it asks. Rather than requesting a score out of ten for price, it asks which of two criteria matters more and by how much.

props.caption: A warung offers the same decision with fewer labels. Credit: Veriyanta Kusuma, CC BY-SA 3.0.

content.text: Comparisons are easier to answer honestly, and they carry more information than a flat rating. They also give the method something to check. A contradictory set of answers gets flagged as inconsistent, which is a signal that the questions need revisiting rather than that the user is being difficult.
What carries over to any recommender
Preference collection is the interface. Where you ask the weighing question decides how good the answer is, so it is not a settings screen bolted on at the end.
Put the tool where the decision happens. A recommendation is useful on a street corner, which is the argument for building it as a mobile application.
Measure against people, not just logic. The real bar is whether the top recommendation matches what a knowledgeable person would choose.

props.caption: Ranking options needs weights first, and weights are personal. Credit: Coach lai, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: The follow-up work from the same group makes the difficulty plain. When AHP and hybrid versions were compared for mobile culinary recommendation, agreement with expert choices stayed modest, with the fuzzy variant doing best. Structured questioning helps, but taste resists being reduced to numbers.

Source: Aryo Pinandito, Chandrawati Putri Wulandari and Ratih Kartika Dewi (2015). Culinary Recommendation Systems Using Analytical Hierarchy Process on Google Android Platform. International Conference on Engineering and Information Technology (ICEIT).

article.title: What Students Think of Extended Kit Build Mapping
article.subtitle: A study turns to the Technology Acceptance Model to find out whether learners actually want to use the method.

content.text: A learning tool can be effective on paper and still sit unused. Whether students adopt it depends on something harder to measure: what they think of it after using it.

Extension concept mapping connects an existing concept map to a new knowledge structure. Learners review what they already mapped, find missing relationships and add new components. The Kit Build version asks students to recompose a map from components provided by a teacher.

props.caption: A concept map linking ideas into a knowledge structure. Image: Komila Olimova, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How the study was framed

Earlier work had already suggested that the Extended Kit Build design supports student achievement. What had not been evaluated was how students felt about it. The team used the Technology Acceptance Model as their lens.
That model breaks acceptance into three constructs.
Perceived ease of use, or how much effort the tool appears to demand.
Perceived usefulness, or whether the tool appears to help learning.
Behavioural intention, or whether the student plans to keep using it.

props.caption: A hand drawn map of connected ideas. Photo: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the study found

The results were positive across the board. Learners perceived the Extended Kit Build approach as easy to use and as a useful learning tool, and they reported a high intention to use it in the future.

props.caption: Learners at work in a classroom. Photo: Esthee2010, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: For anyone building learning software, the framing is the useful part. Achievement scores tell you whether a method works. Perception tells you whether it will survive contact with real classrooms, where a tool that feels awkward gets abandoned quietly.
Source: Prasetya et al. (2021). The Effect of Extended Kit-Build Concept Mapping on Students' Perceptions. 2021 7th International Conference on Education and Technology. DOI:

article.title: What a Ten Day Delay Shows About Concept Mapping
article.subtitle: Students understood more after mapping together, and they understood less again days later. Retention is the part worth planning for.

content.text: A test handed out right after a lesson measures the lesson. A test handed out ten days later measures the learner. The gap between those two numbers is where most teaching actually happens.

The 2020 study of online collaborative Kit Build concept mapping was arranged to expose that gap. Forty international graduate students worked in pairs, each partner on a separate computer in a separate room, and the researchers measured understanding three times rather than once.
The two measurements

The first result was the encouraging one. Compared with the pre-test, pairs that mapped together improved significantly on the immediate post-test, and a Wilcoxon paired test placed the effect at a strong level of significance. The sessions worked.

props.caption: Students at work on study material. Photo: Esthee2010, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The second result was the useful one. When the same students were tested again ten days later, their understanding had declined significantly. The gain was real, and it was not permanent.
What to do with that
Treat the immediate post-test as a progress signal, never as evidence that the material has been learned.
Put a review session on the calendar before the ten day mark, while the structure is still partly there.
Keep the map as a revision artefact rather than a final deliverable, because a saved map is a cheap thing to revisit.

props.caption: A mind map grouping related subjects. Photo: Useamuse, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: There is a quiet advantage in the collaborative format here. A map built by two people belongs to both of them, so revisiting it is a shared task rather than a solitary one, and the pair can pick up the argument where they left it.

props.caption: Reviewing material after the first session. Photo: Heidy Garcia, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The honest reading of the study is that collaborative concept mapping is effective at the moment of use, and that this is exactly as much as it claims. A method that lifts understanding today and fades by next week is still worth using, as long as nobody mistakes the first measurement for the last one.
Source: Pinandito, Hayashi and Hirashima (2020). Online Collaborative Kit-Build Concept Map. Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2020).

article.title: What a Systematic Review Says About Running Remote Work
article.subtitle: The eleven productivity factors add up to a checklist for teams that work from anywhere.

content.text: Most arguments about remote work are settled with anecdotes. Someone is more productive at home, someone else is not, and the discussion goes nowhere. A systematic review published in 2024 offers something better: a structured list of the factors research links to productivity away from the office.

props.caption: A business running from home. Image: Jaggery, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The review screened literature in three passes and repeated each pass to check consistency, using Cohen's Kappa to measure how well the rounds agreed. Seventeen studies made the cut. Eleven factors emerged from them.
Sorting the factors into three groups
Read as a list, the eleven factors look like a random collection. Read as three groups, they turn into something a manager can act on.
Conditions you provide: adequate technology and a work environment that supports concentration.
Benefits the arrangement creates: time efficiency, cost efficiency and geographical flexibility.
People factors you can only influence, not control: psychology, health, personality, salary, gender and communication.

props.caption: Location flexibility is one of the named factors. Image: CruiseAmerica, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The first group is the most straightforward. A reliable laptop, a stable connection and a room where interruptions are rare do more for output than most policy documents. When productivity falls, check the hardware and the setup first.

The third group is where remote work gets hard. Communication sits in the same list as health and personality, which is a reminder that a distributed team is not a process diagram. It is a set of people whose circumstances differ, and the review treats that variety as a finding rather than a complication.

It is worth being precise about what this work claims. It summarises existing studies rather than running a new experiment, so it describes the state of the evidence, not a proven formula. The authors' goal was a needs analysis as a first step towards modelling better Work From Anywhere processes.
For anyone deciding how their team should work, the takeaway is modest but real. Before changing a policy, check which of the eleven factors is failing.
Source: Fauziyah et al. (2024). Factors Influencing Employee Productivity in Work From Anywhere: A Systematic Literature Review (SLR). Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: WebGL Is Fine Until the Model Gets Big
article.subtitle: A rendering benchmark for web based augmented reality found the two candidate approaches split only at high polygon counts.

content.text: Rendering a 3D object in a browser is no longer remarkable. Rendering a heavy one, on a phone, inside an augmented reality view, is a different problem.

A 2023 study from Brawijaya University put two rendering approaches side by side in an HTML based AR application, built on the AR.js library, which brings augmented reality to the web without extra plugins.
What was compared

The two candidates were WebGL running raw shaders, and the OpenGL Shading Language, GLSL. Both reach the same hardware on the device. What differs is how much work the application has to do to drive it.

The study tested them across polygon counts that step up by orders of magnitude, from a couple of thousand triangles to several million. That range is what makes the result useful, because the answer changes partway through.

props.caption: A ray traced 3D render showing different materials. Image: Adamgmz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Where the split shows up

Low poly and medium poly models rendered fine on both approaches. There was no practical reason to prefer one over the other at that scale, which covers a lot of everyday AR content: product markers, simple overlays, small animated figures.

High polygon models separated them. WebGL performance dropped significantly, while GLSL rendered the same objects at a level comparable to native library rendering. For heavy geometry, the choice stopped being a preference and became a requirement.

props.caption: An augmented reality game running on a phone screen. Image: Mimzy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The authors recommend GLSL shaders for 3D objects on the web. The recommendation is narrow by design. It is about the rendering path, at the polygon counts they measured, not a claim about every web graphics task.

The useful habit is the one their method models: test at the scale you actually intend to ship. A model that renders perfectly at two thousand polygons tells you nothing about what happens at four million.

Source: Hamzaturrazak et al. (2023). Performance Analysis of 3D Rendering Method on Web-Based Augmented Reality Application Using WebGL and OpenGL Shading Language. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: How Light Changes Augmented Reality on Outdoor Streets
article.subtitle: Tests at five locations found that dim conditions stretch anchor errors past nine meters.

content.text: When an augmented reality object lands in the wrong place, users notice immediately. A sign that floats three meters from its doorway, or a label that drifts down the street, breaks the illusion faster than a slow frame rate. Getting the anchor point right is the whole game in location based augmented reality.

props.caption: Location based AR places digital objects onto real streets. Image: Mimzy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: There are two common ways to place that anchor. The first fuses GPS and inertial sensors, which is quick to build but rarely precise enough outdoors. The second reads the camera image instead, using Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping, or VSLAM. A team had already paired VSLAM with Google Street View imagery so that the system matches what the camera sees against street level reference photos. What nobody had measured carefully was how ambient light changes the result.
The experiment

The team ran 100 trials across five points of interest around Okayama University in Japan, using Android devices and the ARCore engine. Trials were sorted into four lighting groups: daylight, day overcast, day rainy, and low light. Each group held 25 datasets, so the comparison rested on equal footing.

props.caption: Tests ran at five Okayama University locations. Image: tatushin, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the numbers show

Light intensity and accuracy move together. The analysis found a significant correlation below the 0.05 threshold, and illuminance explained roughly 42 percent of the variation in distance error. In bright conditions the anchor error hovered under a meter. In the low light group, errors ran past nine meters, which is the difference between a useful overlay and a confusing one.

Using confidence interval estimation, the team put a number on the practical floor: at least 434 lux is needed for feasible and consistent accuracy. Rain added a second problem, because wet surfaces change the visual references the tracker relies on, which pushed horizontal tracking time and accuracy around.

The takeaway is not that vision based AR fails. It is that the approach has a measurable operating range, and developers can design around it with adaptive strategies instead of discovering the limits during a demo. The team points toward dynamic light adaptation algorithms as the next step.

Source: Komang Candra Brata et al. (2024). Performance Investigations of VSLAM and Google Street View Integration in Outdoor Location-Based Augmented Reality under Various Lighting Conditions. Electronics. DOI:
10.3390/electronics13152930

article.title: Why Outdoor AR Fails at Dusk and What to Do About It
article.subtitle: A field study puts a number on the light level that vision based tracking needs to stay reliable.

content.text: Teams building outdoor augmented reality usually test in the middle of a bright day, then ship. The app works in the demo and behaves strangely at six in the evening. A study of vision based tracking explains why, and it gives developers a threshold they can actually work with.

props.caption: Street View imagery supplies reference photos for matching. Image: Jove, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The 434 lux line

The research team measured anchor accuracy across four natural lighting groups and used confidence interval estimation to find the lower bound. Their answer is 434 lux. Above it, anchor placement stayed feasible and consistent. Below it, the numbers degraded quickly, with the low light group producing distance errors beyond nine meters.

For developers, the useful part is not the exact figure but the shape of the curve. Illuminance explained about 42 percent of the variance in distance error, and that relationship was statistically significant. Brightness is not a background detail. It is a variable in your accuracy budget.

props.caption: Tracking depends on what the camera can see. Image: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Practical lessons from the field
Design a fallback for low light instead of letting the anchor drift
Treat rainy surfaces as a separate case, since reflections change feature matching
Read the device light sensor and adapt the experience to the conditions on site

The rainy condition deserves its own note. Wet pavement alters the visual scene enough to shift horizontal tracking time as well as accuracy, which means a system tuned in the dry season may behave differently in the wet one. Testing across the calendar is as important as testing across the clock.

The authors close by pointing to dynamic light adaptation, where the system adjusts its own strategy as conditions change. Until that ships, knowing where the floor sits is enough to keep an outdoor AR experience honest about what it can promise.

Source: Komang Candra Brata et al. (2024). Performance Investigations of VSLAM and Google Street View Integration in Outdoor Location-Based Augmented Reality under Various Lighting Conditions. Electronics. DOI:
10.3390/electronics13152930

article.title: How Visual SLAM and Street View Pull Outdoor AR Anchors Into Place
article.subtitle: A team cut the average anchor error from about 7 metres to under 1 metre.

content.text: Outdoor location based augmented reality puts digital labels on real places. Point a phone at a building and a floating card explains what it is. The hard part is getting that card to sit on the right spot. Most Android apps lean on GPS and a compass, and both drift. Labels land metres away from the door they should mark.

A team from Okayama University and Universitas Brawijaya tested a way to close the gap. They added visual SLAM and cloud based matching against Google Street View on top of the usual sensor fusion. The prototype runs as a native Android app through ARCore.
How the prototype works

Visual SLAM tracks features across the camera feed and maps the surroundings as the user walks. When the tracker loses its grip, during a quick turn or on featureless pavement, the app sends a frame to a cloud service. That service matches it against Street View panoramas and pulls the device pose back to a known coordinate. GPS and inertial data keep the result steady between matches.

props.caption: Street View cars collect the reference panoramas. Credit: 姒姓賢寧, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The evaluation used 10 points of interest around the Universitas Brawijaya campus in Malang. Each was measured several times and compared with the true coordinate using the Haversine distance.
What the team found
Overall mean error fell from 7.328 metres with the conventional approach to 0.796 metres with the proposal.
Overall root mean square error dropped from 7.379 metres to 0.806 metres.
Resource use rose: average CPU load from 13 percent to 29 percent, and memory from 152 MB to 294 MB.

props.caption: AR content placed through a phone camera. Credit: Fmalka, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The catch

The method needs Street View coverage. Where Google has not driven, the matching step has nothing to work with and the app falls back to sensor fusion alone. The extra accuracy is not free either: more threads stay busy and more memory is held, which matters on budget devices.
Next comes testing under different lighting conditions, and folding the approach into a full outdoor navigation build rather than a point of interest prototype.
Source: Brata et al. (2024). An enhancement of outdoor location-based augmented reality anchor precision through VSLAM and Google Street View. Sensors, 24(4), 1161. DOI:

article.title: Picking Between Video and a 360 Tour for Campus Outreach
article.subtitle: The medium decides who controls the camera, and that decides what information people actually get.

content.text: Anyone who markets a place faces the same problem. A crew walks a route, an editor cuts it, and the viewer sees what the crew saw. That is a good fit for a story and a poor fit for a question.

A study from Universitas Brawijaya compared a YouTube video and a WebVR tour of the same faculty building in Surabaya, produced by the same team. The WebVR format left users with more control over what they looked at, and with more detail in hand at the end.
What changes when the viewer holds the camera

A video has a running order. That is its strength: a presenter can walk a visitor from the gate to the lab to the canteen in ninety seconds, with no effort from the viewer. The cost is that every question the presenter did not think of goes unanswered, and the viewer cannot go back to check.

props.caption: Exploring a virtual space. Credit: InclusiveGameLab, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A 360 degree scene inverts that. Nothing is scripted, so a curious visitor can linger on the equipment in a laboratory or check how wide a corridor really is. For a prospective student weighing a move to another city, that freedom is the point.
What a WebVR build asks for
A dual lens camera to capture photo spheres on site.
Stitching software to turn those spheres into seamless panoramas, PTGui in this case.
A coverage plan before shooting. The team grouped the faculty into four areas and placed two to five spots in each.

props.caption: A university library in Surabaya. Credit: Institut Teknologi Sepuluh Nopember, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: Where video still wins

Video remains cheaper, faster and easier to distribute. It also works without a strong browser and a decent connection, which still matters on the phones many students carry. The practical answer is rarely one or the other. Put the guided story in a video, and put the questions it cannot answer in a 360 tour beside it.

Source: Pratama et al. (2023). Improving Information Delivery Effectiveness and Efficiency Using WebVR Technology. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology, 657-663. DOI:

article.title: Why Define a Transit API Before Building the App
article.subtitle: A design proposal from Malang shows how much of a transport app is settled by its data contract.

content.text: Riders see an app. Developers see the contract underneath it, and that contract quietly decides which features are even possible. A 2017 proposal for local public transport in Malang is interesting less for its interface and more for the questions it forces a city to answer before code is written.
Begin with the rider's questions
The proposed interface reads like a list of things a passenger would ask at a terminal. Map each question to a shape of data and the design work is mostly done.
Which vehicle serves this trip, and what will it cost and take? These are read operations with parameters.
Can I call or book one? This is a write operation, which brings its own problems around identity and confirmation.
What modes exist, and what is each one actually like? These need list and detail resources.

props.caption: A street in the Celaket area of Malang. Image: Evan Pasha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Quality belongs in the schema

The proposal attaches six indices to every mode: comfortability, security, safety, privacy, availability, and accessibility. Putting those in the payload rather than in prose is a design decision with consequences. Values on a shared scale can be sorted, filtered, and compared across modes, while the same information buried in a description cannot.
It also raises the harder question of where those numbers come from. An index is only as good as the operator willing to maintain it.

props.caption: A motorcyclist crossing the Suhat bridge in Malang. Image: Evan Pasha, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: What the proposal leaves open

The authors describe a draft, and the paper reports no deployed service and no measured result. Questions about authentication, rate limits, and how vehicle positions stay current are not settled here. The transport data itself still has to come from the operator.
Even so, the approach is worth copying. Write the contract first, and every rider app built afterward becomes a client rather than a rewrite.

Source: Agi Putra Kharisma and Aryo Pinandito (2017). Design of REST API for Local Public Transportation Information Services in Malang City. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Target Search Decomposition and the Art of a Lighter Reading Task
article.subtitle: The design choice behind a cheaper concept map exercise, and what it asks of teachers.

content.text: Ask a student to rebuild a concept map from a box of loose parts and working memory gets a real workout. Every node and phrase floats free until the learner finds its partner. That search is not the learning, and it is where class time disappears.

props.caption: A concept map built from linked nodes. Image: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The design idea behind the study comes straight from cognitive load theory, which suggests partial completion as a way to shrink the problem space. If learners can reach a workable solution faster, they spend their limited attention on the relationships that matter rather than on hunting for pieces.
Two ways to build a kit

Full decomposition cuts every connection between a link and its concepts. Target Search Decomposition keeps the link welded to its source concept and cuts only the far end. The learner still has to work out which concept completes each proposition, but the search is roughly halved.
The expert map stays hidden either way, so students cannot copy the answer.
The same concepts and links are used, only the starting layout differs.

props.caption: A concept map of water patterns on Earth. Image: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What changed in the classroom

Across 74 usable responses, the partial version asked less of learners in every way the team measured. It felt easier, took less time, and needed fewer dragging actions to complete. Comprehension scores did not suffer, and the flow state learners reported was at least as good.
Shorter tasks mean more room in one lesson for review or discussion.
Saved mental effort can be redirected to the concepts students find hardest.

The authors are careful about what this does not settle. Because part of each proposition is handed over, the task is easier by design, and that could shade how learners judge their own understanding. The study also applied one uniform level of decomposition throughout. A threshold worth aiming for may exist, and finding it is left to future work.

For anyone designing a mapping activity, the lesson is to treat difficulty as a dial rather than a switch. Handing over one anchor per link keeps the reasoning intact while cutting the busywork, and that is usually the trade a full class period can afford.

Source: Nawras Khudhur et al. (2024). Investigating the Efficacy of Partial Decomposition in Kit-Build Concept Maps for Reducing Cognitive Load and Enhancing Reading Comprehension. IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems. DOI:

article.title: What Suggestions Really Add to a Mapping Tool
article.subtitle: Helpful features can make software more engaging without making it faster.

content.text: Adding help to an editor feels like an obvious win. Suggestions appear, the user picks one, and the work goes faster. A 2019 evaluation of a concept map authoring tool complicates that assumption in a useful way.

props.caption: A concept map of water patterns. Image: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The tool helps students build Kit Build maps, where concepts and linking phrases arrive as separate pieces. One version added suggestions: keywords and candidate propositions drawn from the reading being studied.
Two qualities, measured apart

The evaluation used the short User Experience Questionnaire, which keeps pragmatic and hedonic quality on separate scales. Pragmatic covers the practical side, such as whether a tool feels efficient and predictable. Hedonic covers whether it feels stimulating.
A tool can be pleasant and still be clumsy.
A tool can be efficient and still feel dull.

props.caption: Ideas linked around one topic. Image: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the split revealed

Both versions scored positively overall. The supported version scored higher on the hedonic side, which fits the intuition that suggestions make the activity feel more alive and less like filling in blanks.

Pragmatically it was not consistently ahead. Suggestions introduce choices, and choices cost attention. In the middle of a thought about two concepts, a list of candidate phrases may help or may interrupt.

For anyone designing a learning tool, the lesson is to test the two halves separately. A better hedonic score is a real gain, since students who enjoy the activity stay with it, but it does not excuse a slower workflow.
The open question is timing. Suggestions offered at the moment of a decision can be valuable, while the same suggestions parked on screen as a constant panel may only add noise.

Source: Pinandito et al. (2019). User Experience Evaluation on Computer-Supported Concept Map Authoring Tool of Kit-Build Concept Map Framework. 2019 International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology (SIET). DOI:

article.title: What Students Thought of the Kit-Build Concept Map Tool
article.subtitle: A study on English reading comprehension measured adoption, not learning gain, and found two factors that tipped the decision.

content.text: A learning tool can work exactly as designed and still fail, because students decide for themselves whether to keep using it. Measuring that decision is the purpose of the Technology Acceptance Model.

A study from Brawijaya University applied the model to a Kit-Build concept map authoring tool built to support English reading comprehension. In the Kit-Build approach, students do not draw a map from a blank page. They rebuild one from a supplied set of components, which keeps the activity focused on the relationships between ideas.
How the study was set up

Seventy three third year undergraduates took part. Each had a minimum TOEFL score of 450 and was comfortable with web applications, so basic unfamiliarity with the tool was not a barrier. They read English texts, built concept maps, then answered a questionnaire.

The questionnaire used a seven point scale. Fifteen items covered the four core TAM variables: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude towards using, and behavioral intention. Eleven more items covered three external variables the authors added: compatibility, habit, and enjoyment.

props.caption: Students reading a text in class. Image: chia ying Yang, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What came back
Most of the results lined up with the original TAM. That is useful on its own, because it suggests the model holds for this kind of tool and this group of students.

Two of the added variables stood out. Compatibility and enjoyment both showed a significant effect on whether students adopted the tool. Compatibility is about fit, meaning whether the tool matches how students already study. Enjoyment is about the experience of using it.

props.caption: A concept map tracing one topic across linked ideas. Image: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The practical reading is that a study tool competes with everything else a student already does. If it asks them to change their habits, or if using it feels like a chore, the acceptance numbers will show it.
The authors do not claim the tool improves reading comprehension. They measured whether students accept it, which is the earlier question. A tool that nobody adopts cannot help anyone learn.

Source: Pinandito et al. (2021). Students' Acceptance towards Kit-Build Concept Map Authoring Tool in Supporting Learning of English Reading Comprehension. Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Why semi automatic beats fully automatic for lesson content
article.subtitle: The accuracy numbers from a concept map tool show why a suggestion engine should aim for recall, not precision.

content.text: There is a pattern that shows up whenever automation meets teaching material. The tool produces something plausible in seconds, and the teacher still rewrites it from scratch. The output is not wrong. It is simply not theirs.

The Kit-Build concept map project ran straight into this. Fully automatic map generation had already been tried. The maps covered the reading text but missed the point: which ideas the teacher wanted to emphasise, what the students were ready to handle, and how the topic fit the lesson plan.

props.caption: A concept map in German. Structure carries a teacher's intent, not just content. Image: Hk kng, public domain.

content.text: The design choice that made it work

The team kept a human in the loop at the level where judgement actually lives. The system handles the tedious part, scanning a text for candidate concepts and relationships. The teacher handles the meaningful part, deciding which pieces belong in the map and how they connect.
Suggestions arrive one sentence at a time, so the teacher stays oriented in the text.
Any suggested keyword can be swapped for another before it goes onto the canvas.
Propositions can be written by hand whenever the suggestions miss the point.

That split explains the accuracy results. Keyword recall was high at 0.953, meaning the system rarely missed something a teacher wanted. Precision was low at 0.405, meaning it offered plenty that the teacher did not want. For a suggestion engine, that is the right trade.
Recall matters more than precision when a person reviews every item anyway. Missing a concept costs the teacher a manual entry. Offering an extra one costs a glance.

props.caption: A clustered concept map. Which clusters belong stays the teacher's call. Image: National Cancer Institute, PD.

content.text: Where this generalises

The lesson reaches past concept maps. Any tool that drafts content for a professional, whether lesson plans, code scaffolding, or report outlines, faces the same question about where to stop. Systems that stop too early create cleanup work. Systems that stop too late create a different kind of cleanup work.

The conclusion the authors draw is narrower than a product claim, and more useful for it. The tool was perceived as helpful for refining a concept map in detail, not for producing one from nothing. Knowing exactly which job a tool does well is worth more than a broad pitch.

Source: Pinandito, A., Prasetya, D.D., Hayashi, Y., et al. (2021). Semi-Automatic Concept Map Generation Approach of Web-Based Kit-Build Concept Map Authoring Tool. International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies. DOI:

article.title: Making a Map Search Faster by Simplifying the Path First
article.subtitle: Cutting redundant points from a route made one map algorithm almost 88 times quicker.

content.text: Map applications answer more questions than directions. A travel app also wants to know what sits near the road you are about to take, so it can suggest a restaurant, a fuel station, or a landmark. On an Android map, that surrounding area search is handled by an algorithm called RouteBoxer, and it has a scaling problem.

props.caption: Map apps need the shape of a route, not every point. Image: Santeri Viinamäki, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How RouteBoxer works

RouteBoxer receives a list of geographic points that describe a path, plus a distance to search away from it. It lays a grid of rectangles over the area that covers the whole path, then walks along the path and marks every rectangle the route passes near. The result is a set of boxes the app can query for nearby places.
The cost scales with the number of points it has to traverse. Feed it a recording from a phone that captured a coordinate every second, and the grid work becomes unacceptably slow.

props.caption: Route searches cover an area around the path. Image: SatGuide, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What happened when points were removed

The researchers inserted a simplification step ahead of the search. The Douglas-Peucker algorithm redraws a path using fewer points while keeping its shape, discarding coordinates that sit close to a straight line between their neighbours. A curvy recorded track becomes a handful of well placed corners.

The measured effect was large. Simplification removed up to 99 percent of the points in a path. The original RouteBoxer calculation ran up to 87.8 times faster. Precision stayed above 92.6 percent, meaning the boxes still covered the route well enough to be useful.
The lesson generalises beyond this one algorithm. When a routine is slow because of how much it receives, the cheapest fix is often to send it less rather than to rewrite it.

Source: Aryo Pinandito and Chandrawati Putri Wulandari (2021). Integrating Douglas-Peucker Line Simplification into Routeboxer Algorithm on a Map-Based Android Application. Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: A Small Upfront Cost for a Large Speedup
article.subtitle: The trick is not a faster search. It is a smaller problem to search.

content.text: Performance work often looks like a hunt for a better algorithm. This paper shows a quieter alternative: keep the algorithm, shrink the input. Dijkstra stays exactly as it is. What changes is the graph it gets handed.

props.caption: A transit route map. Search speed depends on how many points carry the line. Image: CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That distinction matters for anyone maintaining a routing service. Replacing a shortest path algorithm is risky and expensive. Pre-processing the data is neither. The Douglas-Peucker routine the team used is a documented line simplification method that cartographers have relied on for decades.
Reading the trade-off
The reported numbers describe a lopsided deal. Simplification adds a small amount of work up front, then removes a very large amount of work from everything downstream.
Added cost: 0.5% memory and 5.13% processing time.
Removed cost: 72.56% memory and 80.83% processing time.
Constraint: the drawn route must still follow the road closely enough to look correct.

props.caption: Dijkstra searches every reachable node, so node count drives its cost. Image: Bensterbenk, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That constraint is the interesting part. Simplification has a tolerance setting, and pushing it too far produces a path that is technically reachable but visually wrong. The authors tuned the setting instead of optimizing it away, which is what real engineering usually looks like.
Where this pattern applies

The same idea shows up anywhere a search runs over map data: fleet tracking, delivery routing, ride hailing, and pedestrian navigation. All of them carry far more geometric detail than the search actually needs. Dropping that detail before the search is cheap, reversible, and easy to test against existing results.

props.caption: Paratransit fleets generate dense route data. Image: Mujiono Ma'ruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Pinandito, Kharisma, and Akbar (2023). Improving Route-Finding Performance of Dijkstra Algorithm and Maintaining Path Visual Cue Using Douglas-Peucker Algorithm. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Planning a Mikrolet Trip With a REST Service
article.subtitle: A prototype service generates paratransit trip plans for a city where route information is hard to find.

content.text: Malang has long been served by mikrolet, a form of paratransit that runs like a shared minibus on fixed routes. It was once a default way to get around the city. Ridership fell as newer, app based transport arrived, and one reason is unglamorous. Passengers often cannot find out which mikrolet goes where.

props.caption: An angkot in Malang traffic. Image: Annidafattiya, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A study from Universitas Brawijaya describes a prototype that tries to close that information gap. It generates trip plans for mikrolet journeys and serves them through a REST web service, so any client, whether a phone or a web page, can request a route over standard HTTP.
How the planner works

The service follows a location-based style. A request carries a starting point and a destination, and the system returns candidate journeys through the mikrolet network. The search is built on depth-first search, chosen for a practical reason rather than a theoretical one.
Depth-first search is simple to modify, which matters while the routing rules are still being worked out.
The output is a web service, so it stays independent of any single app.
Each plan lists the sequence of routes a passenger would take.

props.caption: A route unit parked at Mulyorejo terminal. Image: Mujiono Ma'ruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Functional testing gave the team the result they wanted. The system produced all the trip plans expected from the test cases, with none missing.
Where it strains

Performance is the weak point, and the authors say so plainly. As the number of routes and possible plans grows, the system slows down. Depth-first search explores aggressively, and a denser network multiplies the paths it has to consider.

The paper presents the prototype as a working foundation rather than a finished product, and points to optimization as the next task. For a city trying to improve information about a legacy transport system, a prototype that generates correct plans is already a useful step.

Source: Kharisma and Pinandito (2019). Prototype of REST Location-based Service for Trip Planning by Paratransit (Mikrolet) in Malang City. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Sketching a REST API for Malang Public Transport
article.subtitle: The proposed service would answer cost, time, and booking questions for local transport riders.

content.text: Information technology has already improved public transport in many cities, but Malang had little of it in 2017. Riders had no reliable way to find out which vehicle serves a route, how long the trip takes, or what it costs. Two researchers from Universitas Brawijaya responded with a design for a REST API that local transport services could expose.
What the proposed API should offer
The paper is a design proposal, and its main output is a list of capabilities the interface should carry.
A search facility that finds the right mode of transport for a trip.
Cost estimation and time estimation for that trip.
The ability to call or book a public transport vehicle.
A list of every mode available, plus detailed records for a single mode, including its route.

props.caption: An angkot, the share taxi format common in Indonesian cities. Image: Bayu Oktarino, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: Six indices per mode

The detailed record for each mode carries more than a name and a line on a map. The design calls for an index of comfortability, security, safety, privacy, availability, and accessibility. Those six values give an application something to compare and filter on, which is what turns a transport directory into a service that helps someone choose.

props.caption: Angkot queued along a street. Image: Teguhj, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why a web service rather than an app

The authors frame the work as service-oriented architecture and expose it through REST, with the keywords listing web service design as the approach. Putting the data behind an interface means any developer can build a rider application on top of it, and the transport operator manages one source of truth.

It is worth being clear about the stage. The paper presents a draft proposal of the interface. It does not report a deployed service or a measured outcome, so the value here is the specification itself.

Source: Agi Putra Kharisma and Aryo Pinandito (2017). Design of REST API for Local Public Transportation Information Services in Malang City. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Reading Time Is the Hidden Variable in Concept Mapping
article.subtitle: What students do with the text while they map matters more than whether the text is there.

content.text: Two students get the same activity, the same text, and the same time limit. One learns something durable. The other walks away with a short lived boost and nothing else. A study on concept mapping suggests the divider is simple: how long the student actually spent moving between the text and the map.

props.caption: A concept map turns prose into structure. Image: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The finding comes from an exploratory analysis. Participants who spent longer reading while building their maps scored higher on the immediate test and, more importantly, still scored higher two weeks later. Their retention beat the group that only read the text again, and beat the group that mapped without the text as well.
Why moving between media might matter

The authors offer a mechanism. Going back and forth between a text and a map means locating a detail in the prose, then working out where that detail belongs in the structure. Each round trip touches working memory, and repeated access is what seems to lodge the information.
The text supplies the details.
The map supplies the structure.
The learner does the translation, and that is the part that sticks.

props.caption: Reading support looks different depending on the task. Image: Harrison Keely, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: This puts a dent in a common assumption about learning tools. We tend to treat availability as the intervention: give students the resource, and the resource does the work. Here, availability improved only the short term score. The behaviour around the resource decided the long term one.
What to do with this

For anyone designing or teaching with such a tool, access is a starting condition rather than a strategy. If reading time separates the outcomes, then the interesting design work sits in encouraging the back and forth. The paper notes that whether incentives can shift reading behaviour is a study still waiting to be run.

props.caption: Time on task, not access alone, separated the groups. Image: Heidy Garcia, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Furtado et al. (2021). Influence of Access to Reading Material during Concept Map Recomposition in Reading Comprehension and Retention. IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems. DOI:

article.title: Python, PHP, or Ruby for a Genetic Algorithm
article.subtitle: The same algorithm was written three times and measured on line count, file size, and runtime. The three languages did not agree on a winner.

content.text: Choosing a language for an algorithm is usually settled by preference. The team behind this study turned it into a measurement instead, by writing the same genetic algorithm in three languages.

The problem was the Travelling Salesperson Problem, the classic task of finding the shortest route that visits every city once. It is NP-hard, which makes it a natural target for a genetic algorithm. Instead of searching every route, the algorithm evolves a population of candidate routes over generations and keeps the better ones.
What was measured

The same pseudo code became a Python, a PHP, and a Ruby implementation. Every method was unit tested so that the three behaved identically, then each was run with the same settings: 100 maximum generations, five individuals per generation, a 90 percent crossover rate, and a 1 percent mutation rate.

Runs covered routes of five cities up to ten, and each configuration was measured ten times so the averages meant something. All three produced the same best individual at the same generation, which is what makes the timing comparison fair.

props.caption: Source code with highlighted functions on a monitor. Image: Martin Vorel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What came back
Python was shortest to write, at 237 lines. PHP took 280, and Ruby 302. The reason is syntax. Python does not need closing tags on its functions and loops, so the same logic fits in fewer lines.
File size told the opposite story. Python needed the most space at 7771 bytes, against 6786 for PHP and 5703 for Ruby. The authors point to Ruby's style, which packs more into each statement.

Runtime is where the decision gets made. Ruby was faster than both, improving on Python by roughly 6.5 to 9.99 percent, while PHP ran 0.22 to 6.09 percent slower than Python. That is why the authors recommend Ruby for this kind of work.

props.caption: A Python script beside its plotted output. Image: MikeRun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The limits are worth keeping in view. This is one algorithm, one problem, and a test set of at most ten cities. The finding is about the interpreter and the style it encourages, not about which language is fastest in every situation.
Source: Pinandito et al. (2018). Web-Based Implementation of Travelling Salesperson Problem Using Genetic Algorithm: A Comparative Study of Python, PHP, and Ruby. arXiv preprint. DOI:

article.title: Two Quality Scores That Rarely Move Together
article.subtitle: A Japanese learning experiment shows why a usable app can still feel cold, and what a design team can do about it.

content.text: An app can be easy to use and still leave people flat. Usability research separates that feeling into two measurements: pragmatic quality, which covers getting a task done, and hedonic quality, which covers stimulation, novelty, and how the product makes someone feel. The two do not have to agree.
Pragmatic quality is about finishing the task

In the Japanese m-learning study, both apps let students complete every learning scenario. On perspicuity, efficiency, and dependability the existing app scored 2.23 and the newly designed one scored 2.15. That difference is small enough to call a tie. Whatever the new design changed, it did not make the app harder to operate.
Hedonic quality is about wanting to come back

Here the gap was wide. The proposed app scored 1.45 while the existing app dropped to -0.44. Participants described the new version as conversational and natural, which traces back to a single design decision: building speaking and listening into the core learning loop instead of treating them as extras.

props.caption: A kana chart, the starting point for most self study. Image: W-dcem, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The team reached that decision by studying how learners picture the task in their heads, then writing user stories from that picture rather than from a feature list.
Collect the mental model first, with a diary study rather than a survey.
Turn the notes into personas and a user journey, then into user stories.
Test the redesign against the real competitor, not against an older version of the same app.

props.caption: Learners in a Japanese language class. Image: Sweeper tamonten, public domain.

content.text: The caution worth repeating

A better experience score is not the same as better learning. The authors are explicit that this study measured user experience only, with 20 students from similar backgrounds, and did not test whether the participants actually learned Japanese faster.
The transferable lesson holds anyway. When two apps are equally usable, the one that helps people practise the skill they came for is the one they will describe with enthusiasm.

Source: Komang Candra Brata and Adam Hendra Brata (2020). User experience improvement of japanese language mobile learning application through mental model and A/B testing. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering. DOI:

article.title: Placing AR objects on site with nothing but a phone
article.subtitle: An authoring tool that fuses visual and inertial sensor data lets developers build outdoor AR content while standing at the spot itself.

content.text: Location-based augmented reality puts virtual objects into real streets, campuses, and tourist sites. Building those objects has always been the slow part. Most authoring tools run on a desktop, so a developer visits the location, records coordinates, goes back to a computer, and hopes the placement still lines up when the content goes live.

A team from Okayama University, Universitas Brawijaya, and Politeknik Negeri Malang proposed a shorter route. Their in situ authoring tool lets a developer create and store an AR object directly on a smartphone while standing at the point of interest. No SDK, no desktop, no separate coordinate hunt.

props.caption: A handset running a location-based AR app. Photo: Pixabay, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How the tool works

The tool combines two positioning sources. Visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM) reads the camera feed and builds a map of the surroundings. Google Street View supplies reference imagery of the same street. Fusing those with the phone's inertial sensors gives the system a fix that holds up against changing light, moving crowds, and the flat textures that trip up VSLAM on its own.
The developer points the phone at the target spot.
The tool localizes the position and locks a virtual anchor to it.
The object is stored to the server without leaving the location.

props.caption: Technicians working with AR overlays on site. Photo: HAHN Group, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the tests showed

Fifteen participants each completed practical pedestrian navigation tasks, and every one of them finished successfully. Creating a single AR object inside a 50 metre radius took 16.76 seconds on average.
