The desktop based methods described in earlier literature need one to eight minutes, depending on how experienced the developer is.
Usability reached 89.44 for manipulability and 85.14 for comprehensibility on the Handheld Augmented Reality Usability Scale.
All 15 participants completed their assigned tasks with no failures.

The authors present this as a proposal rather than a finished product. The study covers a small group and pedestrian scenarios only. Even so, the gap it targets is real. If placing an AR object takes seconds instead of minutes, the cost of building a rich LAR experience drops sharply, and more of the work happens where the user will actually stand.

Source: Brata, K.C., Funabiki, N., Panduman, Y.Y.F., et al. (2025). A Proposal of In Situ Authoring Tool with Visual-Inertial Sensor Fusion for Outdoor Location-Based Augmented Reality. Electronics. DOI:
10.3390/electronics14020342

article.title: Dua Langkah Kecil yang Membuat Aplikasi Rute Terasa Cepat
article.subtitle: Merapikan data rute memberi perbaikan yang lebih besar daripada mengganti algoritme pencarian jalur.

content.text: Pengguna menilai aplikasi transportasi dari satu hal saja: berapa lama mereka menunggu jawaban. Animasi yang halus tidak akan menutupi rute yang butuh tiga detik untuk muncul.

Penelitian tentang aplikasi angkutan kota Malang menunjukkan bahwa dua perubahan kecil di sisi data bisa memangkas waktu tunggu itu secara drastis. Keduanya tidak menyentuh algoritme pencarian jalur sama sekali.
Kenapa data rute membengkak

Jaringan trayek angkutan umum terdiri dari banyak titik koordinat. Sebagian besar titik itu hanya menggambarkan lekukan jalan, bukan persimpangan atau halte. Ketika semuanya dikirim ke ponsel dan dihitung satu per satu, pekerjaan yang sebenarnya tidak perlu ikut menumpuk.

props.caption: Angkutan kota trayek MM dan GM di Terminal Mulyorejo, Malang. Foto: Mujiono Ma'ruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Dua langkah yang bisa ditiru
Kompres payload JSON dengan Zlib sebelum dikirim, lalu bungkus hasilnya dengan Base64. Ukuran data yang dikirim turun, dan ponsel tidak perlu menunggu lama.
Sederhanakan garis rute dengan algoritme Douglas Peucker. Titik yang hampir segaris bisa dibuang tanpa membuat bentuk rute terlihat berbeda di layar.
Ukur dulu, baru ubah. Eksperimen ini memisahkan setiap komponen supaya terlihat mana yang benar-benar memberi dampak.

props.caption: Shelter angkutan kota di Terminal Landungsari, Malang Raya. Foto: Mujionomaruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Hasil pengukurannya cukup meyakinkan. Bandwidth yang dihemat mencapai 64,61% dengan tambahan beban memori server hanya 0,44%. Setelah graf disederhanakan, waktu rekomendasi rute turun 81,24% dan memori yang dipakai berkurang 72,99%.

props.caption: Jalanan di Kota Malang, Jawa Timur. Foto: sugeng widodo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Pelajaran praktisnya sederhana. Sebelum mengganti algoritme atau menambah server, periksa dulu apakah data yang diproses memang perlu sebesar itu. Pada kasus ini, merapikan data memberi perbaikan yang lebih besar daripada perubahan di lapisan logika.

Sumber: Pinandito et al. (2024). Peningkatan Performa Komputasi Sistem Navigasi Transportasi Publik Pada Perangkat Bergerak Melalui Penerapan Teknik Kompresi Data Dan Penyederhanaan Graf. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: Partial Concept Maps Cut Cognitive Load Without Cutting Learning
article.subtitle: Leaving some connections in place eases the task while comprehension holds steady.

content.text: Concept maps ask learners to link ideas into propositions. The Kit Build approach goes further: a teacher builds an expert map, software breaks it into loose concepts and links, and students rebuild it without seeing the original. It works, but it strains working memory.

props.caption: A concept map links ideas into propositions. Image: Komila Olimova, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A team from Hiroshima University and Universitas Brawijaya tried a lighter version. They leave each link attached to its source concept and detach only the target, so learners search for one endpoint per proposition instead of two. They call it Target Search Decomposition.
How the study worked

Seventy eight participants split into two groups. One recomposed a map from a fully decomposed kit, the traditional method. The other used a partially decomposed kit. Both read the same narrative, took a comprehension pretest, completed the activity, then reported cognitive load and flow before a post test. Data from 74 was usable.
Full decomposition: every concept and link arrives disconnected.
Partial decomposition: links stay attached to their source concept.

props.caption: Mind maps group related ideas around one topic. Image: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the team found

Cognitive load fell significantly across four dimensions at once: perceived difficulty, perceived effort, time on task, and the number of actions needed to finish. The effect held under a non parametric multivariate test and was consistent across every metric.
Lower difficulty and effort, less time, fewer actions.
Reading comprehension scores stayed comparable.

Motivation held too. The partial group reported a similar, slightly higher flow state, which matters because a task made too easy drains engagement as fast as one made too hard. The authors note a caveat: keeping part of each proposition visible makes the task easier by design, so long term effects on metacognition still need study.

For teachers the takeaway is practical. If a recomposition exercise eats a whole class period and leaves students frustrated, keeping the source side of each link in place frees attention without costing comprehension. Spend the saved time on discussion or review.

Source: Nawras Khudhur et al. (2024). Investigating the Efficacy of Partial Decomposition in Kit-Build Concept Maps for Reducing Cognitive Load and Enhancing Reading Comprehension. IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems. DOI:

article.title: Small Circles, Big Tradeoffs in Paratransit Tracking
article.subtitle: Sampling rate and geofence radius pull effectiveness and efficiency in opposite directions.

content.text: There is a design trap in tracking anything that moves. Sample often and the data is rich but the battery and the server pay for it. Sample rarely and the record becomes thin in ways that are hard to notice until analysis begins. A study of angkot tracking in Malang walked straight into that tradeoff and mapped it.

props.caption: Angkot waiting at a terminal in Malang. Image: Mujiono Ma'ruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why pseudo-stops

Mikrolet have no stops to instrument. So the researchers invented them. A pseudo-stop is a circle placed on the route, and the moment the vehicle enters that circle the system logs a stop event. The design borrows the logic of geofencing and applies it to a transport mode that was never designed to be measured.
Two knobs control the behaviour. One is the tracking interval, how often the phone reports its position. The other is the radius of each circle. Turn one and the other has to follow.

props.caption: The measurement problem starts on the street. Image: Rudi M, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The tradeoff in plain terms
Shorter interval, smaller radius: efficient, but stop events get missed
Longer interval, larger radius: more complete records, more wasted work
Radius too large and neighbouring circles overlap, which makes stop records ambiguous

One more constraint sits outside the designer's control. Android manages location updates with battery life in mind, so the actual interval drifts above or below what the app requested. The authors note that a longer real interval can lower efficiency while a shorter one can reduce effectiveness, which means the tuning has to absorb that variability rather than assume a fixed rate.

The experiment recorded effectiveness near 90 percent and efficiency near 30 percent, so the system works but is not finished. The authors point to two next steps: correcting errors from missed pseudo-stops, and filtering the tracking data either on the phone or on the server before it enters the archive.
For anyone instrumenting informal systems, the lesson is that the interesting decisions happen at the boundary between what you can measure and what the platform will let you measure.

Source: Agi Putra Kharisma, Eriq Muh. Adams Jonemaro, and Issa Arwani (2021). Paratransit Trip Data Collection System with Smartphone GPS and REST Web Service in Malang, Indonesia. Indonesian Journal of Electrical Engineering and Informatics. DOI:

article.title: Tracking Angkot Trips with the Phone in the Driver's Pocket
article.subtitle: A research team turned ordinary smartphone GPS into a data feed for Malang's least predictable transport.

content.text: Ask anyone in Malang about the angkot and the first word is usually uncertainty. Mikrolet, as the city calls them, have no fixed stops and no published operating hours. A driver may take a shortcut, turn back early, or simply stop running for the day. Passengers cannot reliably answer the simplest questions: when is one coming, and how long will the trip take?

props.caption: Mikrolet still serve Malang without fixed stops. Image: Annidafattiya, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That unpredictability is also what makes the service hard to improve. You cannot promise a schedule you have never measured. The team behind this study set out to build the measurement first, with a design goal of changing almost nothing about how the angkot actually operates.
The system in brief

A smartphone in the vehicle reads GPS positions and sends them over a REST web service to a server that stores the trip data. The researchers picked a phone rather than a dedicated GPS module because phones are easier to obtain and maintain, and because their accuracy is good enough for this kind of tracking. The driver keeps driving and the app stays out of the way.

To decide when the vehicle is at a stop, the team used circle based geofencing. Instead of relying on physical bus stops that do not exist, they defined pseudo-stops as circles along the route. Entering a circle registers a stop event, which is what turns a raw trail of coordinates into a usable trip record.

props.caption: Routes follow the city rather than a timetable. Image: Evan Pasha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the experiments found

Two settings dominate the results: how often the app samples location, and how wide the pseudo-stop circles are. A shorter tracking interval tends to allow a smaller radius. That combination is efficient but less effective, because events slip past. A wider interval pushes the radius up, which improves effectiveness and costs efficiency.

Measured across the trials, effectiveness reached around 90 percent while efficiency sat near 30 percent, so both have room to grow. Energy use, notably, stayed low even though the app polls location services periodically. The authors report that consumption settled at a modest level after the initial start up spike.
The value of the study is that it produces the dataset that later prediction work will need. Before anyone can forecast angkot arrivals, someone has to record what the angkot actually did.

Source: Agi Putra Kharisma, Eriq Muh. Adams Jonemaro, and Issa Arwani (2021). Paratransit Trip Data Collection System with Smartphone GPS and REST Web Service in Malang, Indonesia. Indonesian Journal of Electrical Engineering and Informatics. DOI:

article.title: Naive Bayes Beats Nearest Neighbour on Short Messy Text
article.subtitle: Two simple classifiers, one clear gap, and a lesson about how much labelling is enough.

content.text: Choosing a classifier for a small mobile task is rarely about the state of the art. It is about what runs fast, trains on a modest sample, and behaves predictably. A 2017 study on spam detection in tweets offers a clean example of that trade.

props.caption: A phone in use. Image: Océanos y dados, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Two classifiers went head to head on the same job. Naive Bayes estimates the probability that a tweet belongs to a class from the words it contains. Nearest neighbour skips the probabilities and compares a new tweet against the labelled examples it most resembles.
How they differed in practice

The neighbour approach used a weighting scheme that gives rare words more influence, which suits short messages where common words carry little signal. Even with that help it trailed Naive Bayes by eleven percentage points.
Naive Bayes: 82 percent accuracy and simple to retrain.
Nearest neighbour: 71 percent, with more tuning required.

props.caption: A spam message in a mailbox. Image: Pavouk, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What to take from the comparison

Accuracy climbed as more labelled examples were added, and the study tested training sets from ten tweets up to a hundred. That curve matters more than any single figure, because it tells a team how much labelling work to budget.
The other lesson is about preprocessing. Cleaning, tokenising, and stemming the text before training did part of the work that a heavier model would otherwise have to do.

None of this is settled science. Both classifiers were tested on one hundred Indonesian tweets, so the ranking could move with a different language or platform. The durable outcome is the method: label a small set, compare two simple models, and ship the one that holds up.

Source: Pinandito et al. (2017). Spam Detection Framework for Android Twitter Application Using Naive Bayes and K-Nearest Neighbor Classifiers. Proceedings of the 2017 International Conference on Software and Computer Applications. DOI:

article.title: Rebuilding a Mind Map to Learn It Better
article.subtitle: A classroom experiment compared rebuilding a whole mind map with rebuilding only its leaves.

content.text: A mind map is a thinking tool. It lays out understanding as branches, with a central idea at the root and related concepts spreading outward. People draw them to organise their own thinking, and they share them so others can follow along. The catch is that reading a map someone else built is not the same as understanding it.

props.caption: A mind map lays out understanding as branches. Image: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The researchers borrowed a technique that already worked for concept maps: the recomposition method. A map is taken apart into its pieces, and the learner has to put it back together. Doing that requires actually knowing how the pieces relate. Applied to a mind map, the full version means decomposing the entire map and rebuilding all of it.
Two ways to rebuild

The authors proposed a lighter option. In the Leaves Recomposition method, students rebuild only the leaves, the endpoints at the edge of the map. Their reasoning is neat: to place a leaf correctly, you still need to understand the whole path that runs from the root to that leaf. So the thinking stays, but the typing shrinks.

props.caption: Concept maps follow the same rebuild principle. Image: Dvitalo12, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the tests showed

The team ran comparative experiments between the two methods and measured students before and after. Both groups improved significantly. Just as importantly, the difference between the full method and the leaves method was not statistically significant, so the lighter version gave up nothing on the test scores.

The map scores told a second story. Growth rates were much higher for the leaves method than for the full one, and the questionnaire responses described the leaves version as the easier exercise. Students spent less effort and still built maps that moved closer to the target structure.

Two conclusions follow. Rebuilding a mind map has a measurable learning effect, and that effect survives when the exercise is made lighter. The authors frame this as reducing cognitive load while keeping the learning, which is a rare and useful combination in classroom tool design.
Source: Kodai Watanabe et al. (2023). Application of the Recomposition Method to Mind Map and Experimental Verification of Learning Effect. Lecture Notes in Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Less Work, Same Learning: Rebuilding Only the Leaves
article.subtitle: Cutting the effort inside a mind map exercise did not cut what students took away from it.

content.text: There is a comfortable assumption in course design that harder exercises teach more. Students who rebuild an entire diagram must be learning more than students who rebuild a corner of it. A study of mind map exercises tested that assumption and found it wanting.

props.caption: Rebuilding a map forces the learner to trace each branch. Image: Supriyabah, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why the shortcut is not a shortcut

The reasoning behind the leaves method is worth repeating because it explains the result. A leaf sits at the end of a chain. To put that leaf back in the right place, a student has to understand every link that leads to it. The mental work is the same. What disappears is the mechanical work of dragging and placing every node in the middle of the map.

That distinction matters for anyone building learning tools. Effort spent on understanding is the goal. Effort spent on interface chores is a cost, and it is the kind of cost that makes students quit an activity before the learning has a chance to happen.

props.caption: Structure carries meaning, not just the labels. Image: Mirko Lesko, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the comparison found

Students took pre-tests and post-tests around the exercise. Both the full rebuild and the leaves rebuild produced significant gains, and the gap between the two was not statistically significant. The lighter exercise held its ground.
Both methods raised test scores significantly
Map score growth was much higher with the leaves method
Students reported the leaves method as easier to carry out

For lecturers and tool builders, the practical lesson is to look for the part of an exercise that produces the thinking and trim the rest. If a student can demonstrate that they understand a path by rebuilding its endpoint, asking them to also rebuild the trunk adds minutes without adding understanding. That is an easy trade to make, and this experiment suggests it costs nothing in results.
Source: Kodai Watanabe et al. (2023). Application of the Recomposition Method to Mind Map and Experimental Verification of Learning Effect. Lecture Notes in Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: MCCP: A Framework for Apps That Have to Talk to Each Other
article.subtitle: MVC splits an application into parts. A team from Universitas Brawijaya redesigned it for organisations where several applications share one process.

content.text: Model-View-Controller is the pattern most web developers learn first. It splits an application into three roles: the model holds the data, the view shows it, and the controller handles what the user does. Each piece can change without breaking the others.

That separation buys reuse and easier maintenance, which is why MVC is everywhere. It also assumes one application talking to one database on behalf of one set of users. Real organisations rarely look like that.
The problem MVC does not solve

Business processes cross departmental lines. A purchasing record starts in one unit, gets approved in another, and lands in finance. When each unit runs its own software, the work becomes a conversation between applications, and MVC offers no built in way to hold that conversation.

props.caption: Separation of concerns is the whole point of a design pattern. Image: CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the team proposed

The authors propose Model-CollectionService-Controller-Presenter, a modification of MVC rather than a replacement. Two roles join the pattern. The CollectionService handles data exchange between applications, and the Presenter takes over part of the work the controller used to do.

The framework lets several different applications run against the same foundation and exchange data with each other. The authors also report performance comparisons against another widely used web framework, though the abstract gives no figures.

props.caption: Integration work happens on the server side. Credit: Esquilo, CC BY-SA 3.0.

content.text: The interesting move is the restraint. Modifying a pattern that thousands of developers already know is a hard sell, and the team kept the familiar pieces intact while adding what the business case needed.

Source: Aryo Pinandito, Ferdika Bagus Pristiawan Permana and Rizal Setya Perdana (2017). Framework Design for Modular Web-based Application Using Model-CollectionService-Controller-Presenter (MCCP) Pattern. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science, 2(1), 41-65. DOI:

article.title: Map Quality and Higher Order Thinking in Kit Build Classrooms
article.subtitle: When students draw better concept maps, their answers to harder questions get better too.

content.text: Higher order thinking asks students to analyze, evaluate, and create rather than recall. It is also hard to see. Marking a right answer is quick, but judging whether a student has genuinely restructured their understanding takes time few classes have.

props.caption: A mind map laying out how ideas connect. Image: Mirko Lesko, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Concept maps offer a way in. A map shows which ideas a learner treats as related, and that structure is visible to a teacher and to a machine. Kit Build takes advantage: students rebuild a map from a fixed kit, so the result can be compared against an expert version automatically.
What the study tested

Earlier work showed that raising map quality through Kit Build improves achievement, but nobody had checked whether it also stirs higher order thinking. The authors tested that link, and asked a second question: does automatic scoring agree with human judges?
Higher order thinking was measured through performance on higher order questions.
Map quality was scored automatically, then checked against manual assessment.

props.caption: A map built from linked nodes and phrases. Image: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What came out of it

Improving map quality went together with stronger higher order thinking. Students who produced better structured maps handled the demanding questions better, which supports the idea that map quality is not just a neatness score. It shows how well the material is organized in the learner's head.

The automatic assessment held up too. Its results lined up closely with manual grading, and the authors call it a promising way to judge map quality. That matters, because manual scoring is the step that usually stops teachers from using concept maps.

props.caption: A class working through new material. Image: RainaKate, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The practical value is a shorter feedback loop. If software can score a map the moment a student finishes it, teachers keep the hours manual marking would take, and students get a signal while the topic is fresh. The study stops short of promising a replacement for human judgement, but the automatic version looks close enough to help.

For schools weighing mapping activities, the finding is encouraging. The same task that produces a gradeable artefact also pushes students toward the thinking skills that are hardest to teach directly.

Source: Nurmaya et al. (2023). Investigation of the Relationship Between Map Quality and Higher-Order Thinking in Kit-Build Concept Map. Human Interface and the Management of Information, Lecture Notes in Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Map or Camera View? What the Taiwan Study Suggests
article.subtitle: Familiarity drives task performance, but the augmented reality view is what participants remembered fondly.

content.text: When two interfaces both get users to the destination, the interesting question is not which one is better. It is which one people will open next time.

The Taiwan study found a clean split. The 2D map produced faster task completion and higher pragmatic scores. The AR view produced higher hedonic scores and a higher overall rating. Same data, same participants, opposite conclusions depending on which measure you trust.
Why familiarity keeps winning

Participants described the map as familiar. They already knew how to read a blue dot, a route line, and a list of turn instructions, and that fluency showed up in the times. The AR interface asked for a new kind of reading, where you match what the camera shows against what the overlay says.

The AR view had an advantage the stopwatch could not capture. Putting digital labels directly onto the real street removes the mental step of translating an abstract map into what you see in front of you. Participants rated that immediacy highly.

props.caption: An augmented reality view layered over a live camera feed. Image: Mimzy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What this means for navigation apps
Do not drop the map just because the camera view is novel.
Use AR where it is strongest: short distances and spotting something visible ahead.
Keep the map for planning and longer trips, where overview beats immediacy.
Measure enjoyment as well as time, or you will miss what users actually like.

props.caption: A bus stop, the kind of destination the study used. Image: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: There is a limit to how far the findings travel. Ten participants, all students, in one district of one city, all using their own phones. The authors report small differences in task time and call the two interfaces close on usability. Treat the numbers as a signal, not a verdict.

The durable lesson is about measurement. A team that tracks only completion time will build something that works and that nobody enjoys. Tracking pragmatic and hedonic quality together catches the whole picture.

Source: Brata and Liang (2020). Comparative study of user experience on mobile pedestrian navigation between digital map interface and location-based augmented reality. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering. DOI:

article.title: Hand Gestures That Make Rehabilitation Games Easier to Play
article.subtitle: A study ranks 32 hand gestures and tests the best ones in a rehab game.

content.text: Hand and finger exercises only work if patients do them, and repetition makes many people stop. Exergames hide the exercise inside the game: the player moves their hands to control the screen. The open question is which gestures a person can comfortably make.

props.caption: Hand therapy in a clinic. Image: U.S. Navy, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A team from Okayama University, Universitas Brawijaya and partner institutions built a small exergame to answer that. The system uses a web camera and the Mediapipe library to recognise hand shapes in real time. Five gestures map to five controls: up, down, left, right and release.
From 32 gestures to ten

The team began with 32 simple one hand gestures. Sixteen students made each one and rated how easy it felt on a five point scale. Ten survived. The weakest was gesture 27 at 1.7 out of 5, a shape that forces the middle and little fingers together.

props.caption: A web camera drives the gesture recognition. Image: Zsinytwiki, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Because the maze needs five controls, the team split the top ten into two groups. The best used gestures 1, 2, 4, 12 and 29, the second best 3, 7, 11, 21 and 8. Any gap in performance then comes from the gestures themselves.
What the results show
Fifteen students played the maze with both groups. Scores averaged 88.2 with the best group against 76.6 with the second best, and every participant scored higher.
Usability reached 84 on the System Usability Scale for the best group, rated excellent, against 79.3 for the second best group, rated good.
On the User Experience Questionnaire, four scales rated excellent and two, dependability and novelty, rated good.

A separate test with 30 students measured how often the camera read each gesture correctly. The best group was recognised more reliably. The misses had practical causes: dim lighting, low camera resolution, overlapping fingers, and hands held too far away.

The study has limits. Most participants were young students rather than rehabilitation patients, so the ratings could shift with age or with an injured hand. Even so, the pattern is clear: easy gestures produced better play and better usability scores without changing the game underneath.
Source: Husna et al. (2025). An Investigation of Hand Gestures for Controlling Video Games in a Rehabilitation Exergame System. Computers. DOI:

article.title: GetX vs Riverpod: Measuring Two Flutter State Managers
article.subtitle: A benchmark on a real marketplace app finds a gap in memory and speed, but not in processor load.

content.text: Flutter developers face a decision early in every project: how should the app manage its state? Two libraries dominate the conversation, and they take opposite approaches. GetX bundles state, routing and dependency injection into one package. Riverpod splits concerns and leans on providers. Both are popular, and until recently there was little head to head measurement on a realistic app.

props.caption: Application code under measurement. Image: Markus Spiske, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A team set out to compare them properly. Instead of a toy example, they used Flutter ecommerce, an open source marketplace application available on GitHub. That choice matters, because marketplace apps carry the workloads that state managers struggle with: product lists, images, filters and search.
What was measured
The team ran the same three features under both libraries and recorded three numbers for each: memory usage, execution time and processor utilisation.
Displaying the home screen, the first thing a user sees and the heaviest screen to build.
Search, which fires repeated queries and rebuilds results as the user types.
Adding an item, which writes to the cart and updates several parts of the interface at once.

props.caption: A mobile development session. Image: Thamizhpparithi Maari, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The results

Across the three features and the scenarios tested, memory usage and execution time differed. GetX used less memory and finished faster. The processor numbers told a different story: there was no meaningful difference between the two libraries on that measure.

The split is the interesting part. If one library had won on every axis, the choice would be simple. Instead, the result points to a trade off between how often a state manager rebuilds parts of the interface and how much raw work it asks the processor to do.

The authors draw a practical conclusion: GetX came out ahead on memory and speed in this test. That is a narrow claim, tied to one application and one set of features, and the paper presents it as such. It is still more than most teams have when they make the choice, which is usually based on documentation, community size and personal preference.

Source: Jatnika, Akbar and Pinandito (2023). Comparative Analysis of the Use of State Management in E-commerce Marketplace Applications Using the Flutter Framework. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Extending a Concept Map: Two Methods, Two Outcomes
article.subtitle: A study with 55 university students compared free-form extension with rebuilding the teacher's map first.

content.text: A concept map draws what a student understands. Ideas sit in nodes, labelled lines connect them, and each connected pair is a proposition, the smallest unit of meaning in the map. Count the propositions and you get a rough measure of how much the student knows.

A question follows from that. If one map holds more propositions than another, is it better? A study from Hiroshima University, Universitas Negeri Malang and Universitas Brawijaya tested this with two ways of extending a concept map.
Two ways to extend a map

The Extended Scratch-Build approach stays open-ended. Students add concepts, links and examples however they like. The Extended Kit-Build approach starts from a closed set of components. Students recompose the teacher's map first, then extend it with their own additions on top.

props.caption: A concept map on water and its patterns. Image: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Fifty-five second-year university students took part, split into a control group using the scratch-build tool and an experimental group using the kit-build one. A pretest confirmed the two groups started level.
What the team found
Structural map scores were significantly higher in the kit-build group.
Quality of propositions was also higher there. The kit-build group wrote fewer propositions on average and still scored better on quality.
The kit-build group showed a strong positive correlation between structural map scores and proposition quality.
On the Technology Acceptance Model, kit-build scored higher for perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness and behavioral intention.

props.caption: A hand drawn knowledge map. Credit: Renata t quevedo, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: The original maps from both groups looked much the same, which suggests neither group had an early advantage. The difference appeared in the extension step, where the kit-build students had to reason about how new material attaches to a structure they had already rebuilt.
Source: Prasetya et al. (2022). Analysis of quality of knowledge structure and students' perceptions in extension concept mapping. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 17(14). DOI:

article.title: Extended Scratch-Build: a map students grow instead of replace
article.subtitle: The activity starts open ended, then adds a second phase so new material has to attach to what the learner already built.

content.text: Concept mapping has a long standing tension built into it. Ask a class to map a topic from scratch and every map comes out different, which is exactly what makes the activity useful for seeing how a student thinks. It is also what makes the results painful to compare or grade.

Hand out a fixed set of concepts and links instead, the Kit-Build way, and grading becomes tractable. The trade is that the map now says more about the teacher's structure than the learner's. The Extended Scratch-Build method was designed to keep both properties at once.

props.caption: A student working at a computer. The mapping activity runs on a desktop tool. Photo: Syced, CC0.

content.text: How the two phases work
The activity splits one mapping session into two rounds separated by a block of new material. Nothing about the first round is constrained, and that is deliberate.
Phase one: read the original material and build an open map, choosing your own concepts and links.
Between phases: study the additional material, in class or during online study time.
Phase two: extend the map you already made with new concepts, new links, and new propositions.
Where the learning signal shows up

The extension step is where this method earns its keep. A student cannot quietly start a fresh diagram. Keeping the earlier map means every new idea has to find a place among the old ones, and the links that cross between the two rounds are visible to the teacher.

props.caption: Students at work in a computer lab. Maps are built and extended on screen. Photo: Michael Surran, CC BY-SA 2.0.

content.text: A study of university students in a blended learning course compared the method against a more familiar combination of whole class discussion and summarization. The students who worked through the extended mapping activity came out ahead on the immediate test that followed the lesson.

The authors are careful about the scope of that claim. It rests on a single course, a single topic, and a small group of learners, so it is best read as a promising signal rather than a settled result. What the design offers in the meantime is a way to run concept mapping that is personal for the student and legible for the teacher.

Source: Prasetya, D.D., Pinandito, A., Hayashi, Y., et al. (2020). The Performance of Extended Scratch-Build Concept Mapping Tool in Blended Learning. Proceedings of the International Conference on Vocational Education and Training (ICOVET 2020). DOI:

article.title: Building an AR Guide That Survives a Real Street
article.subtitle: Sensors drift, light changes, and the interface still has to point the right way.

content.text: An augmented reality walking guide sounds like a rendering problem. Most of the difficulty sits underneath, in knowing where the user is, where the target is, and how far to trust the sensors in between.

props.caption: A bus shelter at the roadside. Image: Pi.1415926535, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: BusAR was built in three layers. The phone handles the camera and the overlay, a middle layer holds the guidance logic, and web services supply stop locations and route data. Keeping them apart meant sensor handling could change without touching the interface.
Sensors, and what to do with them

Location comes from GPS. Heading needs the magnetometer, which drifts near metal and among tall buildings, so the accelerometer and gyroscope help steady it. Distance to each stop comes from the great circle formula.
Layered design keeps sensor code away from the interface.
A compass arrow turns raw heading into an instruction.

props.caption: A phone overlaying measurements on a room. Image: Fmalka, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the field test suggested

The app was tested on real streets rather than in a controlled setup, which is the only way to learn whether a walking guide holds up. Sensor drift and shifting light are exactly what a desk test cannot reproduce.
The efficiency result is encouraging for adoption. Around 0.25 kilobytes per second is light enough for a limited data plan, and it came in lower than the route planning apps used for comparison.

The design lesson is to spend effort where the user actually gets confused. A list of stop names is accurate and useless when you are on the wrong side of the road, while an arrow drawn over the camera answers the only question that matters.
Source: Brata, Liang, and Pramono (2015). Location-Based Augmented Reality Information for Bus Route Planning System. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering.

article.title: Your Phone Already Has Everything a VR Controller Needs
article.subtitle: A body controlled labyrinth game shows where the real engineering effort goes once the hardware is free.

content.text: Before buying a controller, check the phone. A modern handset already carries an accelerometer, a gyroscope and a magnetometer. The project behind this paper uses nothing else to drive a 3D labyrinth with the player's head and body.

props.caption: The shell is the only extra hardware needed. Image: SimonWaldherr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The inexpensive part

A dummy head mount in the style of Google Cardboard costs a fraction of dedicated hardware, and the sensing happens inside the phone. Display, sensors and game loop all live in a device the user already owns. That changes who gets to try a virtual reality experience at all.
Where the difficulty actually sits
Reading a gyroscope is easy. Turning that stream into a stable, comfortable view is not, and the paper spends most of its detail on that gap.
The phone and the game engine use different handedness, so attitude values need conversion before they can drive a camera.
Screen orientation changes the frame of reference, so the same values must be rotated for landscape and portrait.
Sensor output is noisy, and a camera that follows it directly will jitter, so interpolation smooths the movement.
Walking is invisible to a gyroscope, so step detection needs its own logic and its own thresholds.

props.caption: Movement is the input, not a gamepad. Photo: James Blair, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the thresholds teach

The most transferable result is a set of numbers. Walking and rotating produce rotation rate magnitudes of different sizes, so two thresholds can separate still, walking and turning. That detector handled 84.5 percent of walking cases alone, and pairing it with a second comparison of accelerometer values improved the score on every measure.

props.caption: A cardboard shell turns a phone into a display. Photo: Donald Trung Quoc Don, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The rest is design judgement. A player who must walk and spin needs open floor, so the game belongs in a hall rather than at a desk. The same sensing stack can drive training, guided tours or rehabilitation, anywhere that movement itself is the input.
Source: Tolle, H., et al. (2015). Virtual Reality Game Controlled with User's Head and Body Movement Detection Using Smartphone Sensors. ARPN Journal of Engineering and Applied Sciences.

article.title: Walk to Move Through a Virtual Labyrinth
article.subtitle: Six movements, two phone sensors and a cardboard headset add up to a game you steer with your body.

content.text: A labyrinth is a strange test case for motion sensing, which is why it works so well. To find the exit, players have to walk, turn and look around. That is exactly what a phone strapped to the head can measure.

props.caption: A tiny inertial measurement unit by a penny. Photo: University of Michigan, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Six movements, two sensors

The authors list six movements the system must recognise: walking, rotating the body, and the head looking left, right, up and down. No single sensor covers all six. The gyroscope handles turning the head sideways, while looking up and down is derived from accelerometer data as a pitch angle.
Telling walking apart from rotating

Body movement was the harder half. The team combined two existing approaches. The first reads rotation rate and accumulates its magnitude, then compares that number against two thresholds: below the first the user is still, between them the user is walking, above the second the user is rotating. On its own that method reached 84.5 percent accuracy, and it slipped when someone walked much slower or faster than usual.
The second approach compares accelerometer values between the current and the previous frame, and calls it walking when the difference lands between 0.9 and 0.994.
Combining both approaches gave the best score on every measure, so the prototype runs the pair together.

props.caption: A dummy headset turns one phone into a display. Photo: Benjamín Núñez González, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Making the view feel natural

Rendering was done in Unity3D for Android and iOS with two viewports, shifted a short distance apart for the left and right eye. The gyroscope reports attitude in a right handed coordinate system while Unity3D uses a left handed one, so the quaternion values need conversion. Spherical interpolation smooths the camera between frames so the view does not jump.

The speed study adds practical limits. Rotation was detected reliably between 18 and 45 degrees per second, and walking between 0.5 and 2 steps per second. Outside those bands the detector loses track of the player.

props.caption: A headset view driven by the sensors in a phone. Photo: FloppaIngenieur, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Thirty users played the game and all of them enjoyed the controls. The authors also name the obvious constraint. This kind of control needs room, because a player who has to walk and spin cannot do it at a desk.
Source: Tolle, H., et al. (2015). Virtual Reality Game Controlled with User's Head and Body Movement Detection Using Smartphone Sensors. ARPN Journal of Engineering and Applied Sciences.

article.title: Show One Marker, Not Twenty
article.subtitle: The hardest part of building an AR overlay is deciding what to leave off the screen.

content.text: Open a typical AR navigation app and the camera view fills with markers. Each one points at a real place, so each one is technically correct. Together they are useless, because the user cannot tell which of the twenty pins matters right now.

props.caption: A map can show every point at once. A camera view cannot. Image: OpenStreetMap contributors, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: Crowding is a design problem, not a data problem

The team behind this study found the crowding issue in a field study, not in a diagram. Walking with real users showed that overlapping markers were the single largest source of confusion. Their fix rests on a simple assumption about attention: a place further away is usually less important than a place nearby, so it is acceptable for a far marker to disappear behind a closer one.

props.caption: Real stops sit close together and are easy to miss. Photo: Diamo Laung Bobpuao, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The rules the team settled on
Choose which markers to draw from the user's position, heading and search radius.
Hide a distant marker behind a nearer one instead of drawing both.
Give the active marker a direction arrow and a remaining distance.
Switch the marker icon once the user is within 20 metres of the target.

props.caption: The final metres are the hardest part of the trip. Photo: Solomon203, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why the restraint works

Hiding information sounds like a loss. In testing it was the opposite. Participants found destinations in about a third of the time they needed with a standard AR app, while scoring the same 100 percent success rate. Nothing was added to the data. The screen simply stopped competing with itself.

The lesson travels well beyond buses. Any overlay that labels the physical world, whether it points at museum exhibits, shop shelves or machine parts, faces the same crowding problem. Deciding what to leave off the screen is the real design work.
Source: Brata, K. C., & Liang, D. (2019). An effective approach to develop location-based augmented reality information support. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering. DOI:

article.title: User Journey Maps Show Why AR Navigation Fails Pedestrians
article.subtitle: Ten walkers, two search tasks and one chart of frustrations produced a bus finder that cut travel time by roughly two thirds.

content.text: A pedestrian hunting for a bus stop is not driving. There is no lane to follow and no turn coming up. The person stands on a pavement, turns in a circle, and tries to line up a phone screen with the street in front of them. That mismatch is where location based AR usually stumbles.

props.caption: In car navigation assumes a road to follow. Photo: bizmac, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Watching ten people get lost

The authors ran a field study with ten university students aged 20 to 28. All used Android phones, and none knew the test area. Each participant completed two tasks. In blind search the app named a random destination about 300 metres away. In directed search the participant picked a place from the map. Every step was recorded.

Those records became a user journey map. Along the top sits the sequence of steps a user takes. Down the side sit five rows: actions, questions, happy moments, pain points and opportunities. The last two rows are where the software requirements come from.
Markers overlap when two or more points of interest sit in the same direction on screen.
The screen gives no clue about how to walk to a point.
A destination hidden behind another building is nearly impossible to find.
Users cannot tell how far they still have to walk.

props.caption: A bus stop sign and shelter on a city street. Photo: JustYou80, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the prototype changed

The team built an AR app for the bus network of Zhongli District in Taiwan and rebuilt the presentation around one rule: do not show everything at once. Only the next waypoint and the final target appear. When two markers line up, the farther one is hidden. A marker changes shape once the user is within 20 metres of the destination.

props.caption: A 360 degree view of an indoor space. Photo: Szilas, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Ten participants then repeated both tasks on the prototype and on a standard location based AR app. Both scored 100 percent success, so accuracy was never the issue. Time was. Blind search fell from 14.9 minutes to 5.4, and directed search from 7.86 to 5.12. Questionnaire scores for satisfaction and learnability climbed by roughly 15 to 25 points.

One complaint survived the redesign. Several users reported drift, where a marker floats slightly away from the real object. That is a sensor and GPS limit rather than an interface one, and the authors note that more precise coordinates would be needed to fix it.
Source: Brata, K. C., & Liang, D. (2019). An effective approach to develop location-based augmented reality information support. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering. DOI:

article.title: Turning Paired Talk Into Something You Can Count
article.subtitle: Recording the conversation turns a vague claim about collaboration into something you can count.

content.text: Every paper about collaborative learning says that talking helps. Very few of them show you the talking. This study recorded what pairs said to each other while they worked, then coded the transcripts so the conversation itself became data.

props.caption: Each pair works through the same material. Photo: Dandarmkd, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Turning talk into categories

The authors built a coding scheme for the pair talk and sorted each utterance into a category. Two broad groups emerged. Some turns moved the task forward, such as proposing a link or checking a reading. Others managed the pair itself, such as asking a partner to explain or deciding who does what next.
Where the two methods diverge

Pairs who rebuilt a supplied map spent their turns differently from pairs who invented a map from nothing. With the parts already on the table, there is no long opening debate about which idea deserves a place. The pair goes straight to the harder question of how two ideas relate, which is exactly the reasoning the activity is meant to practise.

props.caption: Diagram of two sets and where they overlap. Image: Metathrope, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The recorded patterns also explain the test result reported in the same study. The Kit-Build pairs scored significantly higher on comprehension after the activity, and their transcripts show more of the specific talk that builds a shared reading of the text.
Why this is worth copying

Conversation analysis is cheap and it changes decisions. A teacher who reads transcripts learns which part of an activity produced the useful argument and which part only produced logistics. That is a better guide than a satisfaction survey, and it takes an afternoon rather than a semester.

props.caption: Screenshot of a spoken sentence as a spectrogram. Image: Emflazie, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The same recipe works for any group task that runs online, because the platform already keeps the log. If pairs work in a shared document or a shared canvas, the record exists. Someone only has to decide what to count.

Source: Pinandito, A., Hayashi, Y., & Hirashima, T. (2021). Online Collaborative Kit-Build Concept Map: Learning Effect and Conversation Analysis in Collaborative Learning of English as a Foreign Language Reading Comprehension. IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems. DOI:

article.title: What a Delayed Test Says About Rebuilding a Map
article.subtitle: Tests taken before, right after, and well after the activity show where the Kit-Build advantage actually shows up.

content.text: A reading exercise is easy to finish and easy to forget. The study behind this paper asks a sharper question than whether students understood a text on the day. It asks whether the way they worked on it changed what they still knew later.

props.caption: Diagram that makes the structure of a system visible. Image: Svleest, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How the comparison was set up

Students learning English as a foreign language worked in pairs on the same reading material. One group rebuilt a concept map from a supplied set of parts, the collaborative Kit-Build condition. The other group composed an open ended map from scratch. Everyone took the same comprehension tests: one before the mapping activity, one immediately after, and one later to check retention.

props.caption: Partners work through a text on a shared screen. Photo: Bright Kwame Ayisi, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The detail that mattered

The tests separated two kinds of question. In-Kit questions covered content contained in the parts that students received. Not-In-Kit questions covered content from the same reading that the kit did not include.
Before the activity, the two groups scored about the same on the In-Kit questions, a difference that was not statistically significant.
After the activity, the Kit-Build group scored significantly higher on those same questions.
On the Not-In-Kit questions, the two groups stayed level throughout.
Reading the retention result

The delayed test adds nuance. Students who had scored higher right after the activity also scored higher later, and the analysis suggests the retention gap traced back to that immediate understanding rather than to the teaching method by itself. The method matters because it produces the understanding in the first place.

props.caption: Chart comparing reading scores across school systems. Image: Nerd271, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The finding carries a practical warning as well. Because the kit defines the content, students get better at what the kit contains. Anything left out of the parts, and therefore outside the reconstruction task, gains no measurable advantage. Teachers who adopt the approach should decide deliberately what belongs in the kit.

Source: Pinandito, A., Hayashi, Y., & Hirashima, T. (2021). Online Collaborative Kit-Build Concept Map: Learning Effect and Conversation Analysis in Collaborative Learning of English as a Foreign Language Reading Comprehension. IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems. DOI:

article.title: What Real Time Collaboration Adds to a Study Tool
article.subtitle: Two students editing the same concept map at once is a small feature with a large effect on how they talk about the material.

content.text: Most learning tools are built for one person at a time. That works until the course asks students to learn together, and suddenly the software becomes a shared document that nobody can edit without stepping on someone else. Distance learning makes that mismatch visible very quickly.
The problem with passing a file around

A conventional workflow has one student map, send the file, and wait. Each hand off costs a day, and the discussion that would have happened while building is lost. The energy of collaboration lives in the moment when two people disagree about a link and have to settle it.

props.caption: A discussion session where partners compare notes. Photo: IAEA Imagebank, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Building the shared workspace

The system described in the paper removes the hand off entirely. Two students open the same concept map and work on it simultaneously, seeing each other's changes as they happen. The implementation keeps both clients in sync in real time, so the map on one screen matches the map on the other within moments.

props.caption: Online sessions replace the shared table. Photo: Bright Kwame Ayisi, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why the Kit-Build parts help the pair

Real time editing alone does not tell students what to do. In this study the pairs did not start from an empty canvas. They received a fixed set of nodes and links, taken from the teacher's map, and rebuilt the structure together. That constraint gives the pair a shared vocabulary from the first minute, which is precisely what makes the discussion productive.

The comparison against open ended mapping supports that reading. Pairs using the supplied parts reported that they could monitor and manage their joint work more easily than pairs inventing a map from nothing, and they scored higher on the comprehension test that followed the activity.

props.caption: Chart with fixed labelled categories. Image: Ed Hawkins, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What this means for course design

Two lessons carry over to any tool a teacher chooses. First, collaboration needs to happen live, because a hand off kills the argument that produces understanding. Second, students need an entry point, and supplying the raw materials is a cheap way to provide one without doing the thinking for them.

The experiment ran with graduate students learning English as a foreign language, but nothing in the design is specific to that subject. Any course that asks students to turn a text into a structure can reuse the pattern.

Source: Pinandito, A., et al. (2021). Efficient Online Collaborative Learning Through Concept Mapping with Kit-Build Concept Map. 6th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: What Survives the Move From Paper to a VR Headset
article.subtitle: Turning a physical eye routine into software is mostly an exercise in deciding what to leave out.

content.text: Any therapy that lives in a textbook faces the same barrier. Patients hear about it, rarely learn the correct way to practise it, and quietly stop. Eye exercises are a clear case, which is why a team at Universitas Brawijaya looked at whether a phone and a cheap headset could carry the routine instead.
The feasibility filter
The Bates method contains several distinct techniques. Before writing any code, the authors checked each one against what a mobile headset can physically do, and three of them failed immediately.
Palming asks the user to close and massage the eyes, which is impossible while wearing a head mounted display.
Sunning needs real sunlight, and a smartphone screen cannot reproduce it.
Colour day would require the user to keep the headset on all day, which nobody will do.

props.caption: Nerves and muscles around the eye. Photo: Patrick J. Lynch, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What remained, and how it was rebuilt

Two techniques made the cut. Head swing became a pointer driven by the phone gyroscope, moving through the 3D axes so the head has something to follow. Optical swing became a moving object that the eyes track while the head stays still. Both target the same muscles that control accommodation, and both map cleanly onto hardware that already exists in every phone.

The application guides the user step by step, logs exercise history so progress is visible, and switches into a dedicated VR mode once an exercise begins. Small choices like the history log matter more than they look, because they turn a routine into something a person can actually keep up.

props.caption: An optometrist uses instruments to measure sight. Photo: M.O. Stevens, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Measuring the result inside the app

To let users see whether the effort pays off, the app also measures refraction. It uses the front facing camera to capture the face, locates the eye position, and converts the measured distance into a diopter value that is shown on screen. That closes the loop between doing the exercise and knowing what changed.

props.caption: Acuity is normally checked in a clinic. Photo: Ptrump16, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Across a five week trial with 14 participants, the average change was a 0.13 diopter reduction, and participants said the guided format made the exercises simpler, faster and more enjoyable. They also flagged eye fatigue after long sessions in the headset, a limit the authors connect to earlier findings about prolonged VR use.
Source: Brata, K. C., et al. (2023). Virtual reality eye exercises application based on bates method: a preliminary study. Indonesian Journal of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: How Coloured Links Turn a Concept Map Into Feedback
article.subtitle: The quiet engineering behind Kit-Build is a comparison engine that grades a student map the moment it is finished.

content.text: Marking a concept map by hand is slow work. A teacher has to read every node, follow every arrow, and decide whether each link makes sense. That cost is one reason concept mapping never spread as widely as its learning benefits suggest it should. The Kit-Build tool attacks the problem by automating the comparison.
Three colours, three meanings
Once a student finishes rebuilding the map, the tool compares it against the teacher's original and colours every link by what it found.
Green links match propositions that appear in both maps.
Red dashed links mark propositions the student missed, which exist only in the teacher's map.
Blue links mark propositions the student added beyond the reference map.

props.caption: A mind map groups related ideas into branches. Photo: Useamuse, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A kit that builds itself

The teacher only has to author one map. From that map the tool generates the set of nodes and links that students receive, so the same artefact serves as both the exercise and the answer key. No separate marking step is needed, and feedback arrives immediately rather than a week later.

The tool itself is built with standard web technology, HTML5 and JavaScript with the CytoscapeJS graph library. It supports colourisation, undo and redo, node duplication, automatic layout, and search, which are the small conveniences that decide whether students keep using a study tool.

props.caption: Diagram of a network where colour marks each cluster. Image: Martin Grandjean, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What this changes in a classroom

Instant feedback turns the map into a conversation. A student sees a red dashed link and knows exactly which idea they failed to notice, while a blue link opens a different question about whether their extra connection is justified. Both are more useful than a bare score.

The student review that accompanied the tool supports this direction. When undergraduates compared four study strategies across a four week course, they rated Kit-Build recomposition as the preferred way to learn efficiently and meaningfully.

props.caption: A reference map can double as the exercise and the answer key. Photo: Mindomo, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Pinandito, A., et al. (2022). Knowledge Reconstruction with Kit-Build Concept Map: A Review from Student Experience. 7th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Four Ways to Study, Ranked by the Students Who Tried Them
article.subtitle: A classroom review asked undergraduates to try four study strategies and report which one actually helped them learn.

content.text: Concept mapping is a well known study strategy. Students draw the ideas of a topic as nodes and connect them with labelled links, which forces them to think about how the pieces relate. The method has a stubborn weakness: learners who do not yet understand the topic cannot build a good map, and a bad map teaches them very little.
Four strategies, one class

The authors ran a short course with 32 undergraduate computer science students. The class met for 14 sessions of 100 minutes across four weeks. Along the way, students worked through four different learning strategies on the same material.
Free note taking during the lecture.
Composing a concept map with paper and pencil.
Composing a concept map from scratch with a digital tool.
Recomposing a concept map with the Kit-Build tool, which hands students a ready made set of parts.

props.caption: Diagram of nodes joined by labelled links. Image: Mattias.Campe, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Rebuild instead of build

Kit-Build takes the teacher's finished map, breaks it into its individual nodes and links, and gives that pile to the students. The task is no longer inventing a map but reconstructing one. Students still have to reason about every connection, yet they are never stuck staring at an empty canvas without the vocabulary to fill it.

props.caption: A cycle of ideas linked into a single structure. Photo: Paolo Anghileri, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the students said

After experiencing all four approaches, students reported the benefits and drawbacks of each. The conclusion of the review is that Kit-Build concept map came out as the preferred strategy to support learning that is both efficient and meaningful.

props.caption: Study strategies are compared inside one class. Photo: Thomas Taylor Hammond, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The result is worth reading carefully. It comes from one class, one course, and a single short term, so it speaks about student experience rather than exam scores. Still, the message is practical: lowering the cost of getting started matters, because the real learning happens in the reasoning that follows.

Source: Pinandito, A., et al. (2022). Knowledge Reconstruction with Kit-Build Concept Map: A Review from Student Experience. 7th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Membaca Peran Shader dalam Augmented Reality di Peramban
article.subtitle: Satu laporan menunjukkan bahwa lapisan penggambaran yang jarang disentuh pengembang justru menentukan hasil akhir.

content.text: Membuat augmented reality di peramban berarti menumpuk dua pekerjaan berat sekaligus. Kamera harus terus membaca dunia nyata, sementara grafis harus menggambar objek virtual dengan mulus di atasnya. Penelitian dari tim Universitas Brawijaya membedah bagian yang paling sering diabaikan dalam tumpukan itu.
Augmented reality yang tidak perlu dipasang

Aplikasi yang harus diunduh lebih dulu selalu kehilangan sebagian calon pengguna. Versi berbasis web menghapus hambatan itu. Pengguna membuka tautan, mengizinkan akses kamera, dan pengalaman langsung berjalan. Cara ini cocok untuk katalog produk, materi belajar, sampai penunjuk arah di sebuah gedung.

props.caption: Tahap geometry shader di dalam pipeline grafis. Photo: MaxDZ8, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Empat komponen yang bekerja bersama
WebGL, standar rendering grafik 3D di antarmuka web.
GLSL, bahasa skrip yang mengatur tampilan visual yang dihasilkan WebGL.
Three.js, perangkat JavaScript untuk grafik 3D interaktif.
AR.js, lapisan yang menyatukan objek virtual dengan gambar kamera.

props.caption: Komponen penyusun WebGL. Diagram: Scriptor universalis, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Pelajaran untuk pengembang

Studi ini menemukan bahwa shader GLSL memberi kinerja lebih baik daripada jalur WebGL biasa ketika menampilkan objek virtual di augmented reality berbasis web. Artinya, menulis shader sendiri bukan sekadar latihan teknis. Keputusan itu berpengaruh pada hasil yang dirasakan pengguna.

Bagi tim yang membangun produk, urutan prioritasnya menjadi lebih jelas. Mulai dari fitur yang berjalan, lalu turun satu lapis ke penggambaran ketika perangkat pengguna mulai beragam dan tuntutan kelancaran naik.

props.caption: Transformasi titik di jalur grafis WebGL. Diagram: Scriptor universalis, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Untuk kelas dan proyek mahasiswa, kasus ini juga berguna sebagai contoh bahwa keputusan teknis yang terdengar mendalam tetap punya konsekuensi praktis yang bisa diukur.

Sumber: Hamzaturrazak, M., et al. (2024). Analisis Kinerja Augmented Reality Hypertext Markup Language Dengan Pemanfaatan Web Graphics Library Dan OpenGL Shading Language Untuk Pengembangan 3D. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: Small Interface Choices Decide Who Finishes a Campus Tour
article.subtitle: A faculty building tour shows how small interface choices decide whether beginners reach the last room or give up halfway.

content.text: Orientation used to mean walking a new student around a building. Online study pushed that job onto software, and the software rarely gets tested against the people it is meant to help. A team at Universitas Brawijaya took one campus tour and redesigned its navigation from scratch.
The interface problem

A virtual tour that shows every arrow at once trusts the visitor to plan a route. Beginners cannot do that yet, because they do not know what the building contains. The paper frames this as a working memory problem: people who are busy deciding where to go stop encoding the place itself.

props.caption: A virtual tour interface with on screen navigation controls. Image: ESO, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Three decisions that shaped the tour
Reveal arrows one at a time. The path is fixed, so a visitor always has exactly one next step to consider.
Make the visitor earn the next arrow. It appears only after they open the information panel of the room they are standing in, which keeps them searching rather than watching.
Colour the arrows by memory. White means a room not yet seen, blue means one already visited, so the tour shows progress without a separate map.

props.caption: A public interior rebuilt as a walkable panorama. Photo: ESO, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What builders should take away

Guidance and learning are often treated as a trade off. Give people a guide and they finish quickly but learn less. This study tested that assumption directly, and the trade off did not appear. The guided group finished sooner and scored the same on the landmark knowledge test.

The reason seems to be the middle bullet. The guide does not do the work for the visitor. It removes the route planning load and leaves the looking, reading and clicking in place, which is exactly the part that builds memory.

props.caption: A room recorded as a full panorama for a tour. Photo: DerMische, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Where this could apply next

The experiment used 360 degree photo tours of 19 rooms, so the same recipe should transfer to museums, hospitals, hotels and plant walkthroughs. Anywhere a first time visitor has to find every stop without prior knowledge, a sequential guide with a visible sense of progress is a cheap addition to build and an easy one to test.
Source: Akbar, M. A., et al. (2024). Performance Analysis of Virtual Tour Navigation Guides for Landmark Recognition. JOINCS (Journal of Informatics, Network, and Computer Science). DOI:

article.title: A Guided Virtual Tour Helps Newcomers Find Every Room
article.subtitle: A campus study compared free exploration with a step by step navigation guide, and timing was not the only thing it measured.

content.text: Virtual tours built from 360 degree photos have become a common way for universities to introduce a campus to people who cannot visit. One problem keeps showing up. When every navigation arrow is visible from the start, beginners tend to wander, miss rooms, and stop before they have seen the whole building.
The problem with free navigation

Most virtual tours work like a room with all the doors open at once. Arrows point in every direction, and users move wherever they like. The authors call this non linear or free exploration. It suits experienced users, but the paper notes that novices often fail to reach all the locations.

props.caption: The study toured a Faculty of Computer Science building in Malang. Photo: Lorrainevyu, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A linear guide with a memory

The team built a second version of the same tour. Here the arrows appear one at a time. The next arrow only shows up after the visitor finds the current room and clicks its information icon, so the guide never turns the tour into a passive slideshow. Arrows also carry colour: white when they lead somewhere new, blue when they lead somewhere already seen.

props.caption: An interior photographed as a full 360 degree panorama. Photo: Alexis Markwick, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How the test worked
The tour covered 19 rooms in one faculty building, all shot as 360 panoramas.
Participants were students who had never visited the building, split into a guided group and a free navigation group.
They first raced to find every room online, then walked the real building and matched room names to code letters posted on the doors.
What the results showed

Completion time differed significantly between the two groups. Students using the linear guide finished faster. In the raw times, several free navigation runs passed 2000 seconds, while the guided group stayed far lower.

Landmark knowledge showed no significant difference. People who followed the guide remembered the rooms just as accurately as people who explored on their own. That is the reassuring half of the result: the guide bought speed without costing spatial memory.

props.caption: Participants walked real corridors afterwards to test recall. Photo: Warren LeMay, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Akbar, M. A., et al. (2024). Performance Analysis of Virtual Tour Navigation Guides for Landmark Recognition. JOINCS (Journal of Informatics, Network, and Computer Science). DOI:

article.title: Kit Build Versus Scratch Mapping: Which Pushes Students Further
article.subtitle: A free form map and a constrained one teach differently, and the test scores show where.

content.text: Give students a blank canvas and they will draw something. Whether that something reveals their understanding is a separate question. The Kit Build method trades the blank canvas for a kit of parts, and a 2023 study set out to measure what that trade buys.

props.caption: A map of ideas linked to one topic. Image: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The comparison ran with 54 undergraduates split across the two methods. Everyone covered the same topic and sat the same test before and after. The questions came in two flavours: the kind that asks for recall, and the kind that asks for reasoning.
Where the two methods diverge

Scratch mapping is the familiar route. Students place concepts and draw their own links, which leaves room for unusual connections that a textbook would never suggest. The cost is that two maps of the same topic can look nothing alike, so comparing or marking them at scale is awkward.
Scratch maps reward originality but resist automated scoring.
Kit Build maps constrain the shape, which makes every submission comparable.

props.caption: Students working through a lesson. Image: RainaKate, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the result means for a classroom

Kit Build came out ahead on higher order thinking, and the effect was moderate rather than overwhelming. The recall questions showed no meaningful gap. Read together, that pattern suggests the constraint does not make the task harder in general. It steers effort toward reasoning.

The scores on the maps themselves lined up with the later test results. That is the practical payoff. If a map can be scored automatically, a teacher gets a usable reading of understanding without marking a stack of diagrams by hand.

There is a limit worth stating. The study covers one topic and one group of students, so the size of the advantage will move with the material and the class. What travels better is the mechanism: a constrained build forces every link to be a deliberate choice.

For anyone choosing between the two, it is not either or. Scratch mapping suits open exploration early in a topic, when students need room to wander. Kit Build suits consolidation, when the goal is to confirm that the structure of the topic has actually landed.
Source: Nurmaya et al. (2023). Promoting Students' Higher Order Thinking with Concept Map Recomposition. IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems. DOI:

article.title: Kapan pedagang sebaiknya memakai QRIS dinamis
article.subtitle: Pilihan jenis QRIS paling bergantung pada satu hal sederhana: apakah nominal transaksi Anda berubah atau tetap.

content.text: Bagi pemilik usaha kecil, pertanyaan soal QRIS bukan lagi soal perlu atau tidak. Lebih dari 29,4 juta merchant sudah terdaftar, dan lebih dari 99 persen di antaranya adalah usaha mikro, kecil, dan menengah. Pertanyaan yang lebih berguna adalah jenis QRIS mana yang cocok untuk pola jualan tertentu.
Mulai dari pola transaksinya

Sebuah penelitian di Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer membandingkan dua jenis QRIS yang memakai Merchant Presented Mode. Kesimpulannya sederhana dan praktis: pilihan terbaik bergantung pada apakah nominal transaksi Anda berubah-ubah atau tetap dari waktu ke waktu.

props.caption: Kode QRIS di sebuah masjid. Jaringan merchant QRIS menjangkau usaha paling kecil. Foto: Fahmihidayatullah, CC0.

content.text: Kalau nominalnya selalu berubah

Untuk warung makan, kafe, atau toko yang menjual barang dengan harga berbeda di setiap transaksi, QRIS dinamis lebih cepat. Kode yang ditampilkan penjual sudah membawa nominal, sehingga pembeli langsung memindai dan membayar tanpa perlu mengetik angka terlebih dahulu.
Waktu transaksi lebih singkat karena nominal tidak perlu dimasukkan manual.
Jumlah langkah yang dibutuhkan penjual dan pembeli ikut berkurang.
Kalau nominalnya berulang dan sama

Untuk transaksi berulang dengan nominal yang sama, misalnya iuran bulanan atau paket langganan, QRIS dinamis juga dinilai mampu meningkatkan efisiensi koreografi proses bisnis. Alurnya menjadi lebih pendek dan lebih sedikit menuntut konfirmasi antara kedua pihak.

props.caption: Peta sistem pembayaran kode QR di Asia, dengan QRIS sebagai salah satu standar nasional. Gambar: Bamboofirdaus, CC0.

content.text: QRIS statis bukan pilihan yang salah. Kode tetap lebih murah dan lebih sederhana untuk usaha yang transaksinya jarang, atau bagi pedagang yang masih menimbang biaya perangkat tambahan. Yang menjadi masalah adalah memakai jenis yang keliru untuk pola transaksi yang tidak cocok.

Satu catatan penting dari penelitian ini: pengukuran hanya mencakup waktu dan jumlah langkah, sedangkan penggunaan sumber daya sistem diabaikan. Jadi rekomendasinya berbicara soal pengalaman orang di depan meja kasir, bukan soal beban server di belakangnya.
Sumber: Pinandito, A., Brilliansyach, R.F. (2024). Efisiensi Penggunaan Qris Dengan Merchant Presented Mode Dalam Transaksi Pembayaran Non-Tunai. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: When the Setup Assistant Gets It Wrong
