article.subtitle: The most useful results in the SEMAR trials are the three places the assistant failed, and how users worked around them.

content.text: A setup assistant is only as good as its worst answer. When a novice follows instructions line by line, one wrong constant can stop the whole project. The SEMAR team logged every stumble during their trials.
The pin that would not compile

In the smart light case, the assistant told the user to assign the sensor to pin D4. The code did not compile, because the NodeMCU board expects the bare pin number, not the label. Once the user pasted the compiler error back into the chat, the service corrected itself.

props.caption: An Arduino Uno, one of the boards the assistant gave guidance for. Image: Dllu, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Missing libraries and newer boards

Two other problems surfaced. The room temperature monitor imported PubSubClient for MQTT, a library the Arduino IDE does not ship; the assistant talked the user through installing it, which is the failure mode you want. The water heater case was worse. The user swapped in a Raspberry Pi 5, and the package the assistant recommended for the DS18B20 sensor does not work on it. The model's training data stopped in October 2023, before that board shipped, so the team read the package documentation and changed settings by hand. The authors flag this as a clear limit.

props.caption: A Raspberry Pi 4. The assistant struggled with the newer Pi 5. Image: Laserlicht, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What held up

The board swap itself is worth noting. The assistant moved the project from an ESP8266 to a Raspberry Pi, rewrote the pin assignments, and produced Python code with a discrete time PID controller and dimmer duty cycle control.

In the classroom trial, 16 of 19 students with no IoT background completed the assignment, along with all three experienced students. The most requested improvement was small: let users edit a message after sending it.

The lesson for anyone building this kind of tool is unglamorous. Grounding helps and conversation helps, but the assistant will still hand users a wrong pin or an outdated package. The design question is whether the interface makes mistakes easy to notice and recover from.
Source: Kotama et al. (2025). Implementation of Sensor Input Setup Assistance Service Using Generative AI for SEMAR IoT Application Server Platform. Information. DOI:

article.title: Giving the online half of blended learning a real job
article.subtitle: A structured mapping task turns independent study into an artifact the next lesson can build on.

content.text: Blended learning promises more independent work and less lecturing. What it often delivers is a reading assignment and a short quiz. Students stay busy, but the teacher ends up with a score instead of a picture of what a student understood.

A study on the Extended Scratch-Build concept mapping tool treats that study time differently. The online portion is not a reading slot. Students build a concept map from the first block of material, then extend that same map after studying the next block.

props.caption: A university classroom. Blended courses move work outside this room. Photo: Tulane Public Relations, CC BY 2.0.

content.text: What the activity asks of the teacher
The preparation is modest, but it has to be done in a particular order. Splitting the material correctly matters more than any tool setting.
Choose two blocks of material that genuinely relate, so the second block has something to attach to.
Leave the first mapping round open ended. Handing out a component list at this stage defeats the purpose.
Give the extension phase its own time, and tell students the earlier map is the starting point, not scrap paper.
Why a map beats a quiz here

A quiz reports a number. A map shows placement. The teacher can see which ideas sat next to each other, which ones carried a labelled link, and which ones floated alone at the edge of the diagram. That is enough to steer the next session.

props.caption: A concept map with labelled relationships. Links show how ideas were placed. Image: NASA, public domain.

content.text: The extension phase adds a second signal. Propositions that reach from the earlier map into the new material show that a learner connected the two blocks rather than memorising them separately. Those crossing links are the clearest evidence of integration the method produces.

In the study, the class that worked this way outperformed a class that used whole class discussion and summarization instead. The evidence is limited to one course with a small number of students, so the sensible move is to try it on one topic and see what the maps reveal. The cost is low and the output is something a teacher can read at a glance.

Source: Prasetya, D.D., Pinandito, A., Hayashi, Y., et al. (2020). The Performance of Extended Scratch-Build Concept Mapping Tool in Blended Learning. Proceedings of the International Conference on Vocational Education and Training (ICOVET 2020). DOI:

article.title: Extended Concept Maps and the Shape of What Students Know
article.subtitle: Fifty five students, two starting points, and a gap that widened as the material went on.

content.text: A concept map shows what a student thinks the pieces of a topic have to do with each other. Extend that map across several subtopics and you get something more useful: a picture of how their understanding grows as the material does.

props.caption: A map built from linked nodes and phrases. Image: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A 2021 study followed 55 college students through that kind of extended mapping. Both groups worked across four subtopics in two phases. One group started from a blank canvas, and the other started from a kit of parts taken from the teacher's own map.
Two routes through the same material

The blank canvas group built a first map freely, then expanded it when the next subtopic arrived. The kit group reconstructed the teacher's map first, then extended it in the same open way. Both groups ended up extending a map. The difference was where they started.
Free form start: room to shape the map your own way.
Kit start: every student begins from the same structure.

props.caption: A class working through new material. Image: Kambai Akau, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the scores showed

The kit group came out ahead on knowledge structure quality, and the margin grew as the material went on. On the first two subtopics the groups were close. By the third, the gap had opened wide enough for the authors to call the effect large.

The other finding is about spread. Scores in the kit group were distributed more evenly across subtopics, and students held their performance steady from the first subtopic to the last. Fewer of them fell behind partway through.

The mechanism is easy to describe. Working from the teacher's structure first clears up early confusion about what a map should look like. Later, when students expand it, they have a solid base to build on.
One cohort and one set of materials is a local result, so read the size of the gain that way. The pattern is the portable part: a shared starting structure helps most once the material gets harder.

Source: Prasetya et al. (2021). Investigating the Distribution of Knowledge Structure in Extended Concept Mapping. Proceedings of the Business Innovation and Engineering Conference 2020, Advances in Economics, Business and Management Research. DOI:

article.title: Dijkstra or A star? What the timings actually say
article.subtitle: On a small campus road network the heuristic search wins clearly on a single route, and loses most of that edge as the destination moves farther away.

content.text: The usual summary is that A star beats Dijkstra and you should just use it. Timings from an Android navigation prototype put a condition on that advice. The gap between the two algorithms is real, but it depends on how far the route has to travel.

The measurements come from a prototype running on a Google Nexus 6 with Android 7.0, working over a campus road network of 134 nodes and 154 edges. Queries were grouped by how close the start and end points were, which is what makes the result interesting.

props.caption: A handheld GPS unit. Short routes leave a search little room to prune. Photo: Voschix, CC0.

content.text: The gap depends on distance
Nearby nodes: A star finished in about 0.10 ms, against an average of 1.22 ms for Dijkstra overall.
Nodes on opposite sides of the network: A star took about 1.16 ms, close to the plain algorithm.
Heuristic overhead: estimating distance with the Euclidean formula added roughly 0.26 ms per query.

The pattern follows from how the heuristic works. A star gains when the estimate can steer the search away from large parts of the graph. Over a short distance there is not much to steer away from, and the estimation cost takes a bigger share of the total.
Where the plain algorithm still earns a place

Dijkstra solves a different problem. It finds the shortest path from one source to every other node in a single pass, so its work carries over when an app needs several destinations from the same origin. The authors suggest pre-caching routes with Dijkstra when the next destination can be predicted, and reserving the guided search for one off requests.

props.caption: Roads, signs and daily travel. Route data is fetched as JSON and cached locally. Photo: LondekaT, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: The honest conclusion for a working app is that neither number is uncomfortable on a graph this size. Both algorithms answer in milliseconds on hardware from a few years back. Where the difference starts to matter is at scale, or when an app fires many queries in a row.

There is also a design lesson that has little to do with either algorithm. The framework keeps road data on the device after the first fetch, so a route can be computed without waiting on the network. For how fast the app feels to use, that choice does more work than any milliseconds saved inside the search loop.

Source: Pinandito, A., Kharisma, A.P., Perdana, R.S. (2018). Framework Design for Map-Based Navigation in Google Android Platform. Journal of Telecommunication, Electronic and Computer Engineering (JTEC), 10(1-8).

article.title: Designing Hand Gestures People Can Actually Make
article.subtitle: What a rehabilitation exergame study teaches about choosing controls that fit the hand.

content.text: Gesture interfaces make a promise: move naturally and the machine will understand. That promise breaks when the gesture set is chosen for technical convenience rather than for the human hand. A recent exergame study looked for the gestures people genuinely find easy.

props.caption: A physical therapy teaching lab. Image: Mikepascoe, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The setup was deliberately plain. A web camera watches the player's hand, the Mediapipe library extracts landmarks, and a Python program turns recognised shapes into game commands. The hardware is nothing exotic, so the same approach runs on an ordinary laptop at home.
Start with too many gestures, then cut

Rather than guess, the team listed 32 possible one hand gestures and asked students to rate each one. Ten survived. The spread was wide. Gesture 27, which asks the middle and little fingers to stay together while the others spread, averaged 1.7 out of 5. Awkward shapes are also harder for a camera to read, because the fingers overlap and the outline blurs.

props.caption: Recognition starts with a commodity web camera. Image: Zsinytwiki, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The link between comfort and recognition accuracy is the practical lesson. The best group of gestures was detected more reliably than the second best, and it produced higher game scores: 88.2 against 76.6 on average. Usability followed the same line, 84 against 79.3 on the System Usability Scale.
Failure modes worth designing around
Poor lighting cuts the contrast the model needs to find landmarks.
Low resolution cameras miss fingertip position, often the only difference between similar gestures.
Occlusion, where fingers hide each other or the hand leaves the frame.
Distance matters: hands too close or too far fall outside the working range.

None of these are exotic engineering problems. They are the ordinary conditions of a living room, so the advice is plain: steady lighting, a decent camera, shapes that keep the hand open enough to read, and a sensible distance from the screen.

The wider lesson for anyone building gesture interfaces is that the gesture set is a design decision, not an afterthought. Test candidates with real people, keep the ones that feel easy, and expect the discarded ones to be the shapes recognition struggles with.
Source: Husna et al. (2025). An Investigation of Hand Gestures for Controlling Video Games in a Rehabilitation Exergame System. Computers. DOI:

article.title: Giving a Kart Racing Game an Opponent to Beat
article.subtitle: A decision tree and a line of waypoints turned a solo template into a race.

content.text: A racing game with nobody to race gets old fast. That was the problem with a Unity karting template a team of developers picked up in 2021. It could only be played alone, because it shipped without an opponent. Their fix was to build a non player character that drives the course and competes for position.

props.caption: A racing game setup at a gaming event. Image: Hilary Murugu, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The work split into two separate problems. The kart has to move around the track without clipping walls or barriers, and it has to choose what to do when the track ahead changes. Both need to run cheaply enough that the frame rate holds.
Driving, then deciding

For movement, the team placed waypoints along the track and let the NPC steer between them. A raycast, a line cast forward from the kart to see what it touches, watches for obstacles and triggers a correction when something blocks the path.
Waypoints tell the kart where the road goes.
A decision tree tells it what to do next.

props.caption: A decision tree branching toward outcomes. Image: Lapollard, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How it tested

The team ran black box testing to check behaviour from the outside, and white box testing to check the logic inside. Both passed. They also drove the NPC for ten laps to watch how it handled corners and contact with other karts.
The performance cost turned out to be small. Adding opponents in pairs cost roughly 0.2 to 0.3 frames per second, so a race can hold several of them on modest hardware without a visible drop.

On lap time, the new NPC beat the machine learning opponent that came with the template. The authors argue the decision tree is the cheaper route, since it needs no training data and its behaviour can be read straight off the rules.
One game and one track is a narrow test, so the exact figures will not carry over to another project. The structure will. Racing AI is easier to build when driving and deciding are solved separately.
Source: Mas'udi et al. (2021). Development of Non-Player Character for 3D Kart Racing Game Using Decision Tree. Fountain of Informatics Journal. DOI:

article.title: Choosing a State Manager for a Flutter Marketplace App
article.subtitle: A benchmark on a real shopping app turns a heated library debate into a countable question.

content.text: Ask five Flutter developers which state library to use and you will get five confident answers. The arguments are real, but they are rarely backed by numbers from an application like the one you are building.

props.caption: State handling shows up as responsiveness on the device. Image: Kskhh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A 2023 study picked a harder test case than usual. The authors benchmarked GetX and Riverpod on Flutter ecommerce, an open source marketplace app from GitHub, rather than on a minimal demo. Marketplace apps stress a state manager in specific ways: long product lists, image loading, filters, and a cart that several screens depend on.
Why the two libraries differ

GetX is deliberately all in one. State, routing and dependency injection live in the same package, and the library tends to rebuild only the widgets that asked for a value. Riverpod takes the opposite route, building from composable providers that give finer control at the cost of more wiring.

props.caption: Choosing libraries is an early project decision. Image: Thamizhpparithi Maari, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the benchmark found

The team measured three features under both libraries: loading the home screen, running a search, and adding an item. For each one they recorded memory usage, execution time and processor utilisation.
GetX used less memory across the features and scenarios tested.
GetX also completed execution faster than Riverpod.
Processor utilisation showed no clear difference between the two.

For a developer, those three lines map onto things users notice. Memory and execution time shape how quickly a screen appears and how smoothly scrolling feels on a mid range phone. Processor load shapes battery drain and heat, and there the two came out level.

It is worth keeping the scope in view. This is one application, one platform and three features, so it does not settle the argument in general. What it does is replace opinion with a measurement on a workload closer to production than most comparisons use.

Source: Jatnika, Akbar and Pinandito (2023). Comparative Analysis of the Use of State Management in E-commerce Marketplace Applications Using the Flutter Framework. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Choosing a Renderer for Web Augmented Reality
article.subtitle: The polygon count of your heaviest model should decide the library, not the other way around.

content.text: If you are building augmented reality for the web, the rendering library is one of the first decisions you make, and one of the hardest to reverse later. Switching means rebuilding the content pipeline.

The study behind this comparison examined that choice directly, in an HTML based AR application built on AR.js, a JavaScript library that runs augmented reality in the browser without asking users to install a plugin.
What AR.js gives you

The library covers three common styles of augmented reality: marker based, where a printed or on screen bookmark triggers the content; image based, where a picture acts as the anchor; and location based, where the scene is tied to coordinates. It also supports visual and audio effects alongside the 3D content.
That breadth is convenient, because it means the rendering decision is not tied to one AR mode. The same application can mix modes and still share a rendering path.

props.caption: An early augmented reality system used for search and rescue. Image: Winged1der, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Questions worth asking before you commit
How many polygons will your heaviest model actually have?
Does the target device have the memory and graphics headroom for it?
Does the library render it close to native speed, or does it fall behind?
Can you swap the renderer later without rebuilding your assets?

The study's own findings give one clear answer. Both approaches handled low and medium polygon models. Only at high polygon counts did WebGL fall away, while GLSL held its ground near native performance.

props.caption: A path traced 3D render produced in Blender. Image: KaiaVintr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The caveat matters as much as the result. This was a rendering benchmark, not a study of a finished application, and actual performance also depends on the device and the browser running it. Use the polygon count of your real content as the deciding input, not the label on the library.

Source: Hamzaturrazak et al. (2023). Performance Analysis of 3D Rendering Method on Web-Based Augmented Reality Application Using WebGL and OpenGL Shading Language. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Cara kerja framework DPE saat kurikulum berubah jadi gim
article.subtitle: Lima lapisan desain yang membantu pengembang menentukan kompetensi sebelum memilih teknologi.

content.text: Membuat gim edukasi bukan sekadar menempel soal ke dalam sebuah permainan. Ada lapisan desain yang harus diputuskan lebih dulu: materi apa yang ingin diajarkan, cerita seperti apa yang membungkusnya, dan bagaimana pemain berinteraksi dengan keduanya.

Tim peneliti di balik gim Gravic memakai framework Design, Play, Experience atau DPE untuk menjawab pertanyaan itu secara berurutan. Kerangka ini merupakan pengembangan dari MDA, tetapi disusun khusus untuk kebutuhan gim serius dan edukatif.

props.caption: Dua anak asyik bermain gim. Framework DPE menata pengalaman belajarnya. Foto: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0.

content.text: Lima lapisan yang harus diisi
DPE membagi pekerjaan desain menjadi lima lapisan. Setiap lapisan diisi sebelum lapisan berikutnya dikerjakan, sehingga keputusan teknis tidak diambil lebih dulu sebelum tujuan belajarnya jelas.
Learning: materi dan soal diambil dari buku aktivitas grafik, dengan fokus menafsirkan dan menyusun grafik.
Storytelling: latar sehari-hari di restoran, rumah sakit, rumah, dan taman, dengan tokoh utama siswa kelas lima.
Gameplay: mekanisme kuis dengan pertanyaan bergambar yang dijawab memakai mouse.
Technology: Unity 2D dengan bahasa C# dan gaya pixel art yang dibangun lewat Tilemap.

props.caption: Siswa mengerjakan tugas di laboratorium komputer. Materi gim disusun bertahap. Foto: Michael Surran, CC BY-SA 2.0.

content.text: Kenapa urutannya penting

Lapisan pengalaman pengguna menutup rangkaian itu. Menu utama menyediakan panduan cara bermain, sementara narasi pembuka menjelaskan kebingungan tokoh utama terhadap grafik. Dengan begitu pemain memahami alasan di balik setiap misi, bukan sekadar mengerjakan soal demi skor.
Pendekatan berlapis ini juga memudahkan evaluasi. Ketika hasil post-test naik dibanding pre-test, tim dapat menelusuri lapisan mana yang berperan, bukan menebak dari keseluruhan gim.

Bagi tim pengembang lain, urutan kerja ini layak dicoba. Tentukan kompetensi lebih dulu, bungkus dengan cerita yang dekat dengan keseharian pemain, baru pilih teknologi paling sederhana yang bisa mewujudkannya.

Sumber: Silitonga, E., Jonemaro, E.M.A., Akbar, M.A. (2023). Pengembangan Gim Simulasi Kehidupan untuk Peningkatan Literasi Grafik Menggunakan Framework DPE. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: Building a Racing Opponent from Waypoints and Rules
article.subtitle: A design pattern for game AI that stays cheap to run and easy to debug.

content.text: Building an opponent for a racing game looks like an animation problem and turns out to be an architecture problem. A 2021 kart racing project split the NPC into two parts that never have to negotiate with each other: one drives, the other decides.

props.caption: A game running on a handheld screen. Image: InclusiveGameLab, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Driving runs on waypoints. Each one is a marker on the track and the kart simply aims for the next in line. It is a plain technique, and it means the designer controls the racing line by moving markers rather than by rewriting code.
Keep the two layers apart

Decisions sit on top. A decision tree checks conditions such as an obstacle ahead or a rival alongside, then returns an action. Because the tree is separate from the steering, behaviour can change without touching the movement code.
Waypoints own the racing line and the route around obstacles.
The tree owns overtaking, braking, and reactions to other karts.

props.caption: A branching tree of decisions. Image: scikit-learn developers, BSD, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why this pattern travels

There is no training phase. Nothing has to be recorded, labelled, or tuned overnight, which matters when a small team is on a deadline. Rules stay readable, so a strange move on the track can be traced back to the branch that produced it.

The testing backed the design. Black box and white box checks passed, and the lap times came out ahead of the machine learning opponent in the original template. The cost to the frame rate stayed low enough for several opponents to share the track.

The honest caveat is scale. This is one karting game, and a crowded track may need more than a small tree. Start with waypoints and a decision tree, then add complexity when a specific behaviour actually demands it.
Source: Mas'udi et al. (2021). Development of Non-Player Character for 3D Kart Racing Game Using Decision Tree. Fountain of Informatics Journal. DOI:

article.title: The bridge between two maps is where the learning shows
article.subtitle: Counting the links that cross from an old concept map to a new one gives teachers a cheap and visible measure of integration.

content.text: Most assessment asks what a student knows at the end. Extension concept mapping asks something slightly different: how well does the new material attach to what the student already had?

That question has a concrete answer in the form of extension relationships. An extension relationship is a proposition that crosses the boundary between the original map and the additional map. It is not a link inside either map. It is a link that exists only because the learner saw a connection between the two.

props.caption: A concept map drawn by hand. Cross links are what extension mapping looks for. Image: Chabre, public domain.

content.text: Why count the crossing links

The measure is attractive because it is cheap and visible. A teacher can scan a map and count how many propositions reach back to earlier material. In an ICCE 2021 study, that count separated two classes sharply: an average of 1.63 crossing links in one group against 5.32 in the other.
A high count suggests the learner is building one connected structure.
A low count suggests two islands of knowledge that never met.
Quality matters as well, which is why the study graded each crossing link for scientific correctness.

That quality dimension is worth pausing on. Ten wrong connections are worse than two right ones. Counting alone would miss the difference, so the study scored every extension relationship on a four level rubric rather than trusting the total.

props.caption: Students in a computer lab. Extension mapping runs on any digital mapping tool. Photo: Michael Surran, CC BY-SA 2.0.

content.text: What a teacher can do with it

The practical lesson is about how the second activity is framed. If students begin the extension phase from a blank canvas, they tend to build a separate map rather than a connected one. If they start from a structured base, whether teacher supplied or previously built, the crossing links appear more often.

It also suggests a change in how teachers read finished work. Instead of only checking whether the new concepts are present, check whether they connect back to the old ones. That single habit surfaces integration problems while there is still time to address them.

The study's own caution applies here too. The sample was small and the evidence is preliminary. But the idea costs nothing to try in a classroom, and the measure is one a teacher can read at a glance.

Source: Prasetya, D.D., Pinandito, A., Hayashi, Y., et al. (2021). Investigating the Tightness of Connection between Original Map and Additional Map in Extension Concept Mapping. Proceedings of the International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2021).

article.title: Panduan Tampilan Dasbor Learning Analytics
article.subtitle: Rancangan ini menetapkan syarat tampilan untuk dasbor pembelajaran, dari tata letak sampai pilihan warna.

content.text: Daftar fitur sering menjadi satu satunya perhatian saat merancang dasbor. Padahal keputusan tentang tampilan turut menentukan apakah dasbor dipakai setiap hari atau ditinggalkan setelah minggu pertama.

Rancangan dalam penelitian ini menetapkan sejumlah kebutuhan non fungsional untuk dasbor Learning Analytics yang menjadi masukan bagi model personalized learning. Isinya sederhana, dan dapat langsung dipakai sebagai daftar periksa.
Apa yang ditetapkan
Platform berbasis web, agar bisa dibuka dari berbagai perangkat tanpa pemasangan.
Tampilan responsif, supaya tata letak tetap rapi di layar kecil.
Tata letak dan kerangka desain yang rapi dan konsisten.
Font yang lugas, tanpa motif, dengan ukuran proporsional.
Warna yang netral dan lembut.

props.caption: Tampilan responsif menyesuaikan ukuran layar. Foto: Muhammad Rafizeldi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Pilihan warna dan tipografi bukan soal selera. Dasbor learning analytics berisi banyak angka dan ringkasan aktivitas. Warna yang mencolok serta huruf yang berhias membuat pembacaan lebih lambat, dan mahasiswa cenderung berhenti membuka dasbor yang terasa melelahkan.

Syarat tentang tata letak yang rapi dan konsisten mudah dianggap remeh. Untuk dasbor, konsistensi adalah alat bantu navigasi. Kalau posisi ringkasan aktivitas selalu sama di setiap halaman, mahasiswa tidak perlu mencari ulang setiap kali membuka dasbor. Waktu yang dihemat terasa kecil, tetapi efeknya menumpuk pada pemakaian harian.

Dua butir pertama juga saling terkait. Sistem berbasis web dipilih supaya mahasiswa tidak perlu memasang aplikasi, dan justru karena itu tampilannya harus responsif. Tanpa tata letak yang menyesuaikan layar, pilihan platform tadi kehilangan sebagian manfaatnya.

props.caption: Laboratorium komputer di sebuah universitas. Foto: Waikato Wordwizard, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Pakai daftar ini sebagai kriteria pemeriksaan sebelum rilis, bukan sekadar hiasan dokumen. Buka dasbor di layar ponsel, periksa apakah kerangkanya masih konsisten, lalu nilai apakah warnanya masih nyaman dibaca dalam waktu lama.
Sumber: Wardhono, Kharisma, dan Jonemaro (2022). Pengembangan Desain Solusi Dasbor Learning Analytics sebagai Input pada Model Personalized Learning. Edunity: Kajian Ilmu Sosial dan Pendidikan. DOI:

article.title: What Matters Most in a Halal Food Tracking App
article.subtitle: Five experts weighed four design criteria, and one of them dominated the result.

content.text: For Muslim travellers, buying food souvenirs raises a question that is not always easy to answer: is this product halal, and who says so? In Indonesia, halal certification is issued by LPPOM MUI, and at the regional level the local MUI office can issue a halal promise certificate for small producers who are not ready for full certification.

props.caption: A food stall in Yogyakarta. Image: Christophe95, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A research team designed an application to track the halal status of culinary products sold at a food souvenir centre, so that buyers can check a producer's status from their phone. The interesting part is not the app. It is how the team decided what the app should prioritise.
Asking experts to rank the criteria

The team used the Analytical Hierarchy Process, a method for turning expert judgement into weights. Five experts took part, giving pairwise comparisons between criteria, and the calculations were run with Criterion Decision Plus. Every comparison passed the consistency check, with ratios below 0.1.
User friendly came first by a wide margin, with a weight of 0.423.
Accessibility followed at 0.156, then content and organisation at 0.142, and design at 0.135.

The gap is the story. User friendly carried roughly three times the weight of the next criterion, which tells a development team where to spend its effort. A tracking app can survive plain visuals. It cannot survive a confusing flow.

props.caption: Halal certified meat on display. Image: Raysonho, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The strategy that scored highest

The same method was applied to alternative strategies for the app, and the winner was ease of access, with a score of 0.249. That fits the criterion ranking: the experts wanted a product that a shopper can open and understand quickly, standing in a souvenir shop with a bag in one hand.

The study has clear boundaries. It gathered opinions from five experts in one city, between September 2015 and January 2016, so the weights reflect that panel and that moment. Halal governance has moved on since then, and a new panel might rank things differently. What holds up is the approach: decide priorities with a documented method instead of a loudest voice.
Source: Sucipto et al. (2018). Halal Culinary Tracking Application at Food Souvenirs Center Based on Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) Method. Pertanika Journal of Social Sciences & Humanities.

article.title: Testing a Learning Tool Against the Technology Acceptance Model
article.subtitle: The Kit-Build study is a template for evaluating a study tool before you try to prove it improves learning.

content.text: When a team finishes a learning tool, the first question is often whether students learned more. That is the hardest question to answer, and it is not the first one worth asking.

A study of a Kit-Build concept map authoring tool for English reading comprehension took the step before that one, asking whether students accept the tool at all. The method is worth copying, because it costs far less than a learning outcome study.
Build the sample deliberately

The authors screened participants instead of taking whoever was available. Seventy three third year undergraduates took part, all with a minimum TOEFL score of 450 and existing familiarity with web applications. Both conditions matter for an English reading task that runs in a browser. One sets a language floor, and the other removes basic usability as a source of noise.
Separate the core from the additions

The questionnaire used a seven point scale, split into two groups. Fifteen items measured the four standard TAM variables: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude towards using, and behavioral intention. Eleven further items measured compatibility, habit, and enjoyment.

Keeping the groups apart is what makes the result readable. You can see whether the standard model still holds, and whether the extra variables earn their place. Here the core was consistent with the original TAM, and compatibility and enjoyment proved significant.

props.caption: A digital concept map built from linked nodes. Image: F22raptor editor, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Read the result as a design brief

Compatibility and enjoyment are not abstract findings. They translate into concrete work: match the tool to the study habits students already have, and make the act of using it pleasant rather than merely functional.

The authors are careful about scope. They measured adoption, not learning gain, among a screened group at one university. That is a fair limit for this kind of study, and it sets up the obvious next experiment.

props.caption: Students reading a book together in class. Image: FramaKa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Pinandito et al. (2021). Students' Acceptance towards Kit-Build Concept Map Authoring Tool in Supporting Learning of English Reading Comprehension. Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Swapping pathfinding algorithms without rewriting the app
article.subtitle: An Android navigation framework treats the shortest path method as a plug in, so the rest of the app never has to care which one runs.

content.text: In most navigation apps, the route calculation is welded into everything else. The map screen calls it, the data layer feeds it, and the drawing code reads its output directly. Trying a different algorithm then means touching half the project.

A framework designed for the Google Android platform takes the opposite approach. It treats the pathfinder as one replaceable piece behind a common interface, and uses the Abstract Factory pattern so the application can choose an implementation at runtime instead of at compile time.

props.caption: A phone running a map app. The framework targets outdoor navigation on Android. Photo: Santeri Viinamaki, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: What sits inside the framework
A graph model built from Node and Edge objects, so the road network is an explicit data structure.
A pathfinder interface with Dijkstra and A star implementations, both selected through the same factory.
A data layer that pulls road geolocation over HTTP as JSON from a web service and caches it on the device.
A map layer built on the Mapbox Mobile SDK, chosen over the Google Maps API for its offline caching support.
What the prototype measured

The team built a working prototype in Java and ran it on a Google Nexus 6 with Android 7.0, using a campus road network of 134 nodes and 154 edges. Both algorithms returned the same routes, as expected. The interesting difference was in time.
Dijkstra averaged 1.22 ms per query across the test cases.
A star averaged 0.49 ms, ranging from 0.10 ms for nearby nodes to 1.16 ms for nodes on opposite sides of the network.

That works out to more than 60 percent faster on average for a single route, with the largest gains in the 71 percent range. The heuristic is not free though. Estimating distances with the Euclidean formula added about 0.26 ms of overhead per query, and the authors note that Haversine would give a more accurate estimate over longer distances.

props.caption: A row of Android and other smartphones. The prototype targets Android devices. Photo: Carlos Varela, CC BY 2.0.

content.text: Source: Pinandito, A., Kharisma, A.P., Perdana, R.S. (2018). Framework Design for Map-Based Navigation in Google Android Platform. Journal of Telecommunication, Electronic and Computer Engineering (JTEC), 10(1-8).

article.title: A Smartwatch Interface Cut Transit Travel Time by Six Minutes
article.subtitle: A twenty person study in Malang moved the journey guidance from phone screen to wrist, and the numbers moved with it.

content.text: Using a transit app inside a crowded bus or angkot is harder than it looks. Passengers have to hold a bag, watch for their stop and stare at a phone screen at once. For visitors who do not know the city, that is stressful.

props.caption: A bus stop where guidance often gets checked. Image: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A team from Universitas Brawijaya studied the problem on the public transit routes of Malang. They recorded how twenty participants actually travelled, then built a prototype that moves guidance onto a smartwatch. The watch shows the itinerary, tracks the route in the background and vibrates near a checkpoint.
What changed with the watch
The same twenty people then ran the trip twice, once with a standard map based phone app and once with the watch prototype. The team recorded trip duration, task completion and user ratings.
Average travel time fell from 26.20 minutes on the phone to 20.40 minutes with the watch.
Both setups reached the destination every time, with a 100 percent success rate.
System Usability Scale scores came out close: 72.13 for the phone against 72.50 for the watch.

props.caption: Guidance on the wrist instead of in the hand. Image: TheArchivistMan, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The six minute gap is the headline, but the per question results explain it. On not needing to keep monitoring the app, the phone scored 0.70 and the watch 2.65. That is the crowded bus problem in one number: riders stopped holding a screen in front of their face.

Several riders said the hands free interaction reduced their anxiety, and the simpler interface was quicker to learn. Since overall usability scores stayed almost identical, the gain did not come from the app feeling better. It came from where the information sat.

The obvious caveat is hardware. Using the design means buying a smartwatch, which not everyone can afford, and the study covers twenty people in one city. The authors present it as preliminary. Even so, it makes a useful point for builders of transit software: the interface is not only what you show, but the device the rider holds while the bus moves.
Source: Brata et al. (2021). Usability improvement of public transit application through mental model and user journey. TELKOMNIKA Telecommunication, Computing, Electronics and Control. DOI:

article.title: Turning Expert Opinion Into a Feature List
article.subtitle: How a halal culinary tracking app was scoped with pairwise comparisons instead of guesswork.

content.text: Requirements gathering often ends the same way. A workshop produces a long list of features, nobody agrees on the order, and the loudest opinion wins. A study on halal culinary tracking took a more deliberate route, borrowing a decision method from operations research to set its priorities.

props.caption: Street vendors selling prepared food. Image: Gunawan Kartapranata, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The application being designed serves a food souvenir centre, where shoppers want to confirm that a product is halal before buying. In Indonesia that confirmation has a paper trail. LPPOM MUI handles formal certification, while regional MUI offices issue a halal promise certificate for producers who are not yet certified. The app's job is to make that status visible on a phone.
The method, briefly

The Analytical Hierarchy Process works by comparison rather than rating. Five experts judged criteria against each other in pairs, and software called Criterion Decision Plus converted those judgements into weights. A consistency check guards the result, and in this case every ratio came in below 0.1, the usual threshold.
User friendly led with 0.423, far ahead of the rest.
Accessibility reached 0.156, content and organisation 0.142, design 0.135.
Among strategies, ease of access scored highest at 0.249.

props.caption: A restaurant in Malang, where the field survey was done. Image: Hugo van den Bos, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Read together, the two rankings line up. The experts put usability first among criteria and simplicity first among strategies, which gives a team a clear instruction: build the shortest path from opening the app to seeing a producer's halal status, and treat decoration as a later concern.

There are limits worth naming. Five respondents is a small panel, and the field work ran from September 2015 to January 2016 in one city. Weights are opinions with arithmetic applied, not measurements, and a different panel would shift them. The value of publishing the numbers is that the reasoning can be checked and repeated.

For teams facing a similar argument about scope, the takeaway is portable. When priorities have to be settled, compare options in pairs, check the consistency of the judgements, and write down the weights. It costs a few meetings and removes a lot of rework.
Source: Sucipto et al. (2018). Halal Culinary Tracking Application at Food Souvenirs Center Based on Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) Method. Pertanika Journal of Social Sciences & Humanities.

article.title: QRIS statis atau dinamis, mana yang lebih cepat
article.subtitle: Penelitian membandingkan waktu dan jumlah langkah pada dua jenis QRIS dengan Merchant Presented Mode.

content.text: QRIS sudah menjadi bagian sehari-hari di Indonesia. Standar pembayaran kode QR ini dipakai lebih dari 29,4 juta merchant terdaftar, dan lebih dari 99 persen di antaranya adalah usaha mikro, kecil, dan menengah. Namun tidak semua QRIS bekerja dengan cara yang sama.

Ada dua jenis yang dibandingkan dalam penelitian ini: QRIS statis dan QRIS dinamis. Keduanya memakai Merchant Presented Mode, yaitu mode ketika penjual menampilkan kode dan pembeli yang memindai. Perbedaan utamanya ada pada nominal yang tertanam di dalam kode tersebut.

props.caption: Kode QRIS ditempel di jendela sebuah gerai makanan. Foto: VulcanSphere, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Apa yang diukur

Penelitian ini membandingkan keduanya dari sisi efisiensi. Ada dua parameter yang diamati: waktu yang dibutuhkan dan jumlah langkah yang harus dilakukan pembeli maupun penjual untuk menyelesaikan satu transaksi.
QRIS statis memakai satu kode tetap untuk semua transaksi.
QRIS dinamis menghasilkan kode baru dengan nominal yang sudah terisi.

props.caption: Mesin pembayaran menampilkan kode QRIS dinamis. Foto: VulcanSphere, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Apa yang ditemukan

Hasilnya bergantung pada pola transaksi. Untuk transaksi tunggal dengan nominal yang berbeda-beda, QRIS dinamis terbukti mempercepat proses. Penjual tidak perlu lagi menyebutkan atau memverifikasi nominal secara manual sebelum pembeli memindai.

Pada situasi transaksi berulang dengan nominal yang sama, QRIS dinamis juga dinilai mampu meningkatkan efisiensi koreografi proses bisnis. Alurnya menjadi lebih pendek dan lebih sedikit menuntut interaksi antara kedua pihak.
QRIS dinamis disarankan untuk transaksi tunggal yang nominalnya bervariasi.
QRIS dinamis juga direkomendasikan untuk transaksi berulang yang nominalnya sama.

Penulis mencatat satu batasan penting. Penelitian ini mengabaikan penggunaan sumber daya sistem, sehingga hanya menilai sisi pengalaman pengguna dan jumlah langkah transaksi. Pemilihan jenis QRIS yang kurang tepat, menurut mereka, berisiko memperpanjang antrean dan menurunkan kepuasan berbelanja.
Sumber: Pinandito, A., Brilliansyach, R.F. (2024). Efisiensi Penggunaan Qris Dengan Merchant Presented Mode Dalam Transaksi Pembayaran Non-Tunai. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: Which Factors Actually Drive Work From Anywhere Productivity
article.subtitle: Factor analysis and a hierarchy process narrowed eight candidates down to seven and then ranked them.

content.text: Work From Anywhere sounds like a perk until a manager asks a harder question. If nobody shares an office, what actually decides whether the work gets done? A research team took that question seriously and replaced opinion with measurement.

props.caption: Work spreads across homes and shared spaces. Image: helloquence, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The team started with a literature review and pulled out eight factors that could plausibly influence productivity in a distributed setup: gender, marital status, education level, the communication platform in use, work experience, educational background, type of work, and the IT facilities available.
How the factors were tested

Two methods did the work. Factor analysis groups variables that move together and removes the ones that add nothing. The Analytical Hierarchy Process then builds a structure of criteria and weighs them against each other. The data came from a questionnaire of 100 employees who each had at least a year of Work From Anywhere experience, answered on a Likert scale, with a pilot run of 30 respondents to clean up the questions.

props.caption: Focused work at home depends on setup and connection. Image: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What came out of the analysis

Factor analysis extracted seven factors from the original eight and dropped work experience along the way. That is a useful result on its own, because it suggests years on the job say less about remote output than the working conditions around a person.

The hierarchy process then ranked what remained. The communication platform carried the highest weight at 15.11 percent. The type of work sat at the bottom with 12.89 percent. The spread between the top and the bottom is narrow, so no single factor dominates, but the ordering is still informative.

The authors note that not every job suits the model, and roles that depend on physical presence, such as public services and parts of health care, are poor candidates. For the work that does fit, the message is that productivity is shaped by conditions a company can influence rather than by employee traits alone.

Source: Neyla Nuril Fauziyah et al. (2023). Optimizing Work-From-Anywhere Employee Productivity: A Comprehensive Investigation of the Most Influential Factors Using Factor Analysis and Analytical Hierarchy Process Method. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: The Tool You Talk Through Matters More Than You Think
article.subtitle: When work from anywhere factors were ranked, the communication platform came out on top.

content.text: In a shared office, communication happens by accident. You overhear a decision, catch a look across the room, notice that someone has gone quiet. Strip the office away and every one of those signals has to be rebuilt inside a tool. That is why the tool stops being a detail.

props.caption: A home office is a workplace with its own rules. Image: Bob the Wikipedian, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why the platform ranked first

A study of Work From Anywhere productivity collected eight candidate factors and weighed them using factor analysis and the Analytical Hierarchy Process. The communication platform scored the highest weight at 15.11 percent. The type of work scored lowest at 12.89 percent.

The gap is small, so the honest reading is that these factors matter roughly equally. The interesting part is the order. What employees talk through edged out what employees actually do. The tool is not a neutral pipe. It shapes how quickly questions get answered and how much context survives the distance.

props.caption: The remote workspace is only as good as its connection. Image: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What teams can act on
Treat the communication stack as infrastructure, not as an app preference
Check the IT facilities behind each employee, since the survey kept them as a separate factor
Accept that some roles do not fit the model, particularly work tied to physical presence

One result deserves attention for a different reason. Work experience dropped out during factor analysis entirely. Twelve months of experience was the entry bar for the survey, and beyond that the variable did not hold up as a distinct influence.

Put together, the findings point somewhere practical. Companies that want output from distributed teams should spend less time screening for seniority and more time making sure the channel between people works.

Source: Neyla Nuril Fauziyah et al. (2023). Optimizing Work-From-Anywhere Employee Productivity: A Comprehensive Investigation of the Most Influential Factors Using Factor Analysis and Analytical Hierarchy Process Method. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Widget Choice Is a Usability Decision
article.subtitle: In a culinary app study, users stalled on controls they did not recognise, not on features they did not want.

content.text: Interface kits make it easy to reach for a distinctive control. A slider instead of a field, a carousel instead of a list. The result may look memorable. A usability study on a culinary recommendation app suggests it also carries a price.

props.caption: Street food stalls in Garut. Image: Jauza01, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The cost of an unfamiliar control

In the study, one version of the app collected input through a flow style widget. Some participants did not realise the control could be scrolled, so the options below the fold stayed invisible to them. Nothing was broken. The interface simply did not announce what it could do.
The other version used a plain list and a standard numerical field. Every participant finished that task. The feature sitting behind both versions was identical.

props.caption: Familiar controls lower the effort of a first attempt. Image: bohed, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why a small study still tells you something

Five participants is a small sample, and the authors present it that way. It follows a long standing practice of testing early with a handful of users, on the reasoning that the worst problems surface fast. For catching a widget nobody understands, five is often enough.
Errors were grouped into input, navigation and comprehension, which separates a broken control from a confusing label.
Comparing first and second attempts turned errors into a rough measure of learnability.
Think Aloud recordings located the moment of hesitation, not only the failure.

The practical takeaway for anyone shipping an app is unglamorous. Standard controls carry learned expectations, and that is most of their value. A novel widget has to earn its place by being clearer than the standard option, not merely different.
Source: Az-zahra, Pinandito, and Tolle (2015). Usability evaluation of mobile application in culinary recommendation system. 2015 IEEE Asia Pacific Conference on Wireless and Mobile (APWiMob). DOI:

article.title: Why the Same Algorithm Took 237 Lines in Python
article.subtitle: Line count, file size, and runtime each pointed at a different language, and only one of them matters at run time.

content.text: Write the same algorithm three times and you get three different programs. Not different in behavior, but in shape: how many lines it takes, how much space it occupies, and how fast it runs.

The trio in this study was Python, PHP, and Ruby, all implementing one genetic algorithm for the Travelling Salesperson Problem, all passing the same unit tests so that the comparison was between languages and not between programs.
Lines are not the same as size

Python won on line count at 237, ahead of PHP at 280 and Ruby at 302. The advantage comes from grammar rather than brevity. Python does not require closing tags on functions or loops, so a routine that spans several lines elsewhere can be written more compactly.

File size reverses the ranking. The Python implementation came to 7771 bytes, more than PHP at 6786 and well above Ruby at 5703. The authors credit Ruby's style, which expresses more per statement, so the shortest program by bytes is the longest by lines.

props.caption: Code open on a computer monitor. Image: Markus Spiske, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Runtime decides
Neither of those numbers matters if the program is slow. Ruby came out fastest, ahead of Python by 6.5 to 9.99 percent, while PHP trailed Python by 0.22 to 6.09 percent.

The authors also note that the setting can change the ranking. Their own measurements ran outside a web server, and they cite earlier work that found PHP ahead of Python in a web environment. A benchmark answers the question you actually asked, in the environment you actually ran it in.

props.caption: Highlighted source code on a screen. Image: Martin Vorel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Their recommendation follows from the measurements rather than from preference: Ruby, for a genetic algorithm of this kind. The scope is honestly small, one algorithm on routes of up to ten cities.

The transferable lesson is the method rather than the winner. If language choice matters to your project, write the core routine in each candidate and time it under realistic conditions. It costs a day and settles an argument that otherwise runs for years.
Source: Pinandito et al. (2018). Web-Based Implementation of Travelling Salesperson Problem Using Genetic Algorithm: A Comparative Study of Python, PHP, and Ruby. arXiv preprint. DOI:

article.title: Why Your Map App Quietly Simplifies Every Route
article.subtitle: The shape of the data you feed a routing algorithm matters as much as the algorithm you choose.

content.text: Every map you have scrolled through is a compromise. The road data behind it holds far more detail than the screen can show at that zoom level, and something has to decide which points survive.

The same decision sits inside routing. A search algorithm reads the graph it is handed, so an oversized graph means slow answers. That is the problem a 2023 study on navigation efficiency set out to address. Finding the shortest path is easy. Finding it in a wasteful graph is not.
Simplification is a design decision

The Douglas-Peucker algorithm has thinned out coastlines and borders in cartography for decades. Applied to transit routes it does the same job: keep the points that define the shape of a journey, drop the ones that only add noise.

props.caption: Routes and networks can be modelled as layered graphs. Image: Martin Grandjean, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the study measured
The team compared route computation on public transport data from Malang City, Indonesia, with and without a simplification step applied first.
They tracked computation time and memory use on an Android device, the environment where resources are tightest.
Simplified input produced shorter computation times and lighter memory use than the original graph.

props.caption: A route information board for Malang minivans. Photo: Mujionomaruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: There is a trade-off to respect. Simplify too aggressively and a route line can cut a corner it should not, which matters when that line is what the user follows on the map. The useful property of Douglas-Peucker is that it is parameterised. You choose how much deviation you are willing to accept.

props.caption: Minivans waiting at Arjosari terminal, Malang. Photo: Mujiono Ma'ruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That is the real lesson for anyone building location features. Performance work does not have to mean a faster algorithm or a bigger server. Sometimes it means looking at the shape of the data you are feeding in, and deciding that half of it was never load bearing.

Source: Muhammad Yasir Anshari Haq, Riswan Septriayadi Sianturi, and Aryo Pinandito (2023). Enhancing the Efficiency of Navigation Systems: Dijkstra Algorithm Optimization Through Integration of Douglas-Peucker Line Simplification Technique. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Why Price and Distance Outweigh Star Ratings
article.subtitle: The weights a culinary recommender learned say more about diners than about restaurants.

content.text: Every recommendation screen hides a set of numbers that decide what a person sees. A 2015 paper on a mobile culinary recommendation system published those numbers, and they are worth reading as a statement about how people actually choose a meal.
The three criteria and their weights
The system compares three criteria: distance, price, and rating. After the pairwise comparisons were processed, the resulting eigenvector gave each criterion the following share of influence.
Price: 0.5556, well over half the decision.
Distance: 0.3333, roughly a third.
Rating: 0.1111, about a ninth.

props.caption: Nasi bungkus, an inexpensive meal that suits a tight budget filter. Image: Midori, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What those numbers imply

The ranking is blunt. Reputation, the signal most food applications put at the centre of the screen, carries the least weight of the three. Two practical constraints, what a meal costs and how far it is, carry the rest. That matches how the input flow is built: the user supplies a budget and a travel radius first, and the candidate list is trimmed before quality is even considered.

Distance here comes from the Haversine formula, which measures the straight line between two points on a sphere. It ignores roads, one way streets, and rivers. For a five kilometre radius, that approximation is acceptable, but it quietly assumes that a place is equally reachable in every direction.

props.caption: A neighbourhood warung, the low cost option price weighting favours. Image: Indonesiagood, CC BY 4.0.

content.text: A caution about who set the weights

The weights come from comparisons made by the people who configured the system, not from observing a population of diners. A budget conscious student and a diner entertaining guests would not produce the same matrix. The useful lesson for anyone building a recommender is structural rather than numeric: keep the weights as an explicit input that can differ per user, because a single fixed matrix encodes one person's priorities for everyone.
Source: Pinandito et al. (2015). Alternatives Weighting in Analytic Hierarchy Process of Mobile Culinary Recommendation System Using Fuzzy. ARPN Journal of Engineering and Applied Sciences.

article.title: Why a Group Recommendation Never Fits Everyone
article.subtitle: Correlation results from a Malang tourism study show how far a shared ranking drifts from individual taste.

content.text: A group recommendation is a compromise by design. Someone agrees fully, someone agrees partly, and someone usually wanted a different place entirely. The interesting question for anyone building a recommendation feature is how large that gap tends to be.
Where the gap showed up

In the Malang souvenir recommendation study, the group ranking tracked three of four users closely: 0.97, 0.99, and 0.88. The fourth sat at 0.69. Averaged out, the group result correlated 0.88 with individual preferences. That number sounds strong until it is read as what it is, an average that hides a member who was not well served.

props.caption: A street corner in Malang, where the study was run. Image: Nurhadi Cahyono, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Weights are the real negotiation

Each traveller sets their own criteria weights before the ranking runs. In the worked example one user treated distance, price, and shop age as equally important, while the other leaned heavily on distance and price. Those two weightings pull the same list of options in different directions, and the Borda count is what settles the argument.
Let every member set weights separately. A single shared weighting hides whose preference is being ignored.
Show the reasoning behind a top result. Users accept a compromise more readily when they can see what drove it.
Expect one member to be least aligned, and consider a second option that suits them.

props.caption: Comparing options around a table. Image: US Fish and Wildlife Service, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the study leaves open

The demonstration used fifteen alternatives, three criteria, and a small set of decision makers in one Indonesian city. Correlation testing shows that two rankings move together, not that users were happy with the outcome. Satisfaction was not measured here.

Even with those limits, the study supports a useful design habit: treat a group ranking as a starting point for discussion rather than a verdict, and give every member a way to see and adjust their own weights.

Source: Ratih Kartika Dewi, Eriq Muhammad Adams Jonemaro, Agi Putra Kharisma, Najla Alia Farah, and Mury Fajar Dewantoro (2021). TOPSIS for mobile based group and personal decision support system. Register: Jurnal Ilmiah Teknologi Sistem Informasi. DOI:

article.title: Why Extending a Concept Map Differs from Building One
article.subtitle: The Extended Kit Build method starts from what a learner already knows instead of a blank canvas.

content.text: Most mapping exercises hand the learner a blank canvas. That is also where many of them stall. Deciding which pieces belong on the page is a different skill from arranging them once they are there.
The Extended Kit Build method separates those two jobs. A learner starts from the map built earlier in the course, and that existing structure becomes the ground on which new material is placed.
What the kit supplies

In a Kit Build exercise the teacher takes a map apart into its components, the concepts and the linking phrases between them, and hands that kit to the learner. Reassembling it turns attention to the relationships rather than to the drawing.

props.caption: A finished concept map with labelled links between ideas. Image: Komila Olimova, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The extended version adds a second step. Once the new structure is assembled, it is attached to the map the learner already holds, so unfamiliar material lands on top of something familiar.
Why the sequence matters
Three design decisions carry most of the weight.
Starting from existing work cuts the number of decisions in front of the learner at any one moment.
Supplying the components removes guesswork about vocabulary, which is often the hardest part for a beginner in a new subject.
Extending rather than replacing means earlier study is reused instead of discarded.

props.caption: A hand drawn map of linked ideas. Photo: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Learners in the study responded well to that arrangement, judging it easy to use and useful, and saying they intended to keep using it. The wider lesson is about where difficulty sits. When a method feels effortless, it is often because someone moved the hard part somewhere the learner does not have to face it alone.

props.caption: A student working through study material. Photo: Heidy Garcia, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Prasetya et al. (2021). The Effect of Extended Kit-Build Concept Mapping on Students' Perceptions. 2021 7th International Conference on Education and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Why Cheap Phones Are Slow at Finding Routes
article.subtitle: A study of Dijkstra's algorithm across device classes found that memory, not raw speed, decides how long a route search takes.

content.text: A transit app promises the same answer on every phone. The route from A to B does not depend on how much you paid for your device. The time it takes to work that route out very much does.

A 2023 study from Brawijaya University looked at what happens when Dijkstra's algorithm has to run across a range of smartphones, in a public transit system where the phone and the server both take part.
The bottleneck is memory

The headline finding is blunt. Memory capacity is what most strongly shapes how long Dijkstra takes. Devices with more memory finish their calculations faster, and lower-end devices take noticeably longer on the same graph.

That is awkward for navigation apps, which are expected to behave identically on a flagship and on a budget handset. Waze and Google Maps both lean on shortest path search, and the authors point out that the amount of data being processed changes how that search performs.

props.caption: A phone running a map navigation app. Image: Santeri Viinamaki, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the server can absorb

The proposed answer is dynamic load distribution. Instead of fixing in advance which part of the work runs where, the system watches the complexity of the calculation and the capability of the device, then reallocates as conditions change.

When a low quality device is struggling, load balancing can move work to the server. The paper reports that this transfer effectively mitigates the performance loss, at the cost of depending on the network. The server needs protection too: the mechanism adjusts in real time so that many clients asking at once do not overload it.

props.caption: A city bus in Jakarta. Image: Exynoss78739, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The design target stated in the paper is a waiting time that does not exceed one second. That number matters more than any single benchmark result, because it is a budget the whole architecture has to fit inside.

The practical takeaway: treat route finding as a shared job. Give the phone the part it can handle, hand the rest to the server when the device is weak, and measure against a waiting time the user can feel.

Source: Justico et al. (2023). Dynamic Load Distribution of Shortest-Path Finding in Client-Server Public Transit System. 2023 International Conference on Modeling and E-Information Research, Artificial Learning and Digital Applications (ICMERALDA). DOI:

article.title: When Social Media Stops Being a Study Tool
article.subtitle: A survey of 100 students traces how overload turns into exhaustion and lower learning productivity.

content.text: Social media can be genuinely useful for students. It is where they ask about assignments, trade notes, find explanations, and keep in touch with classmates. The same channels, used without pause, also wear people down. A study presented at SIET 2023 set out to trace that trade-off with a model rather than a hunch.
The chain the authors tested

The team used the Stressor-Strain-Outcome model, a framework that separates the pressure people face, the internal strain it produces, and the outcome that follows. Each part was measured with a survey of 100 undergraduate students and analysed with a Generalized Linear Model.
Stressors: information overload, communication overload, and social overload.
Strains: technostress and exhaustion.
Outcome: learning productivity.

props.caption: Influencers at work, the content that keeps feeds busy. Image: Syced, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the data showed
Not every link in the chain behaved the same way. The analysis found a set of significant paths rather than one single cause.
Social overload and communication overload both push students toward technostress, the feeling of being overwhelmed by the technology itself.
Technostress, communication overload, and information overload each contribute to exhaustion.
Exhaustion, in turn, affects learning productivity.

props.caption: Scrolling is easy to start and hard to stop. Image: Leanne Walker, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The practical reading is that the problem is cumulative. Constant notifications and endless feeds do not damage learning in one step. They build strain, strain builds fatigue, and fatigue finally shows up in how much work a student gets done.

Source: Shandra Elvyra Sudarsono Putri, Mochamad Chandra Saputra, and Aryo Pinandito (2023). The Effect of Social Media Overload, Exhaustion, and Technostress on Student's Learning Productivity Using Stressor-Strain-Outcome Model. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology (SIET 2023). DOI:

article.title: When compressing your JSON API actually pays off
article.subtitle: A study measured how much bandwidth application-level Zlib and Base64 save, and the payload size where the savings stop.

content.text: REST APIs usually ship JSON over HTTP with no compression at all. For a desktop client on a wired connection that is fine. For a mobile app running on a metered data plan, every extra byte carries a price.

A 2023 study in the Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science put numbers on that tradeoff. The team built a PHP server and a browser client, then measured 1500 different JSON payload sizes to find out what a Zlib plus Base64 pipeline really buys.

props.caption: JSON has become the default payload format for REST APIs. Diagram: Diego Mariano, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Where the compression lives

The design choice that matters is placement. Instead of leaning on the web server Accept-Encoding and gzip layer, the team compressed at the application level. The server runs Zlib through the PHP gzencode function, then Base64 encodes the binary result so the payload stays string safe. The client reverses both steps, decompressing with the Pako library in JavaScript.
That approach keeps working even when the web server cannot be reconfigured for compression. It also lets the API decide, payload by payload, whether compressing is worth the effort.

props.caption: A short JSON response. Payloads this small are where compression loses rather than wins. Image: Dcbma, CC BY 4.0.

content.text: What the measurements showed

Large payloads compress well. For JSON between roughly 12.5 and 101 kilobytes, the compressed and encoded output settled at about 33 percent of the original size. That is a bandwidth saving of up to 66 percent, which is the headline claim the authors set out to test.
Server CPU cost rose from 0.064 milliseconds on a 68 byte payload to 3.269 milliseconds on a 101 kilobyte payload.
Memory overhead stayed under 2.62 percent, which the authors describe as negligible.

Small payloads are where intuition breaks. A 68 byte response grew to 112 bytes after compression and encoding. A 135 byte response grew to 144 bytes. Base64 expands the binary that Zlib produces, and below roughly 150 bytes that expansion costs more than the compression saves.

A Mann-Whitney U test on memory usage returned a p value of 0.0000022, so the overhead is statistically real but minor. The practical rule fits in a sentence: compress the big responses, leave the tiny ones alone.

Source: Pinandito, A., Kharisma, A.P., Jonemaro, E.M.A. (2023). Architectural Design of Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interface with Application-Level Base64-Encoding and Zlib Data Compression. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: What Happens to Your Layout on a Small Screen
article.subtitle: A study measured how much content delivery suffers when a desktop page meets a tablet or a phone, and whether design work can close the gap.

content.text: Most visits to a website now arrive on a screen smaller than the one the site was designed for. A tablet or a phone shows a fraction of the width, and the layout has to decide what to do about it.

Responsive Web Design answers that by letting a single page render differently depending on screen size. The study behind this article takes that as given and looks at what the change costs. When a layout reflows, the amount of information visible at once changes, and so does how effectively a visitor can get through it.
The comparison

The authors measured effectiveness and efficiency of content delivery on three screens: a computer display, a tablet, and a smartphone. Effectiveness is about whether content can be found and used at all. Efficiency is about how much effort that takes.
They also recorded how each page was built. Every site in the study followed one of three common layouts: a single column, two columns, or three. That detail turns out to matter for the result.

props.caption: A responsive layout shown across device sizes. Image: Muhammad Rafizeldi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the screens showed

Delivery got worse on smaller screens. That is not surprising, but it is worth stating plainly, because it is the baseline that design work has to beat. A desktop page placed on a phone loses effectiveness and efficiency along with the screen width.
What the authors tested next was whether the design process could change that. They applied two established approaches and measured the outcome on the same screens.

props.caption: A user interacting with a touchscreen device. Image: Intel Free Press, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Both approaches improved content delivery on the tablet and the smartphone. The gains were not limited to one screen size or one layout style, which is the more useful part of the finding: the improvement came from the process, not from a single trick.
The three column layouts showed the largest gap between the two approaches, and that is where the companion article picks up.

Source: Pinandito et al. (2017). Analysis of web content delivery effectiveness and efficiency in responsive web design using material design guidelines and User Centered Design. 2017 International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology (SIET). DOI:

article.title: When a 360 Degree Tour Beats a Campus Video
article.subtitle: A study compared a YouTube walkthrough with a WebVR tour of the same faculty building.

content.text: Universities struggle to reach prospective students who live far away. Videos help, but a video only shows what its creator chose to film. If a student wants to see the laboratory benches or the walk from the gate to the lecture hall, a fixed edit rarely answers the question.

A study from Universitas Brawijaya put two media head to head for exactly this job: a two dimensional YouTube video and a 360 degree WebVR tour, both describing the Faculty of Public Health at Universitas Airlangga in Surabaya.
How the two versions were built

The video team shot with digital cameras and edited in Wondershare Filmora, mixing panoramic, tracking and aerial shots with a presenter walking viewers through each spot. The WebVR version used a dual lens camera to capture photo spheres, then stitched them into seamless panoramas in PTGui. Both covered four areas of the faculty, with two to five spots in each.

props.caption: A phone based VR viewer. Credit: Bert Niehaus, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Respondents were smartphone users aged 18 to 35 who had never visited the campus but were interested in studying in Surabaya. The comparison ran in Google Chrome.
What the team found

The WebVR tour gave users more control over what they looked at, and that control translated into access to more detailed information. A video viewer follows the camera. A WebVR viewer decides where to look, and keeps looking until the question is answered.

props.caption: A stitched panorama, the raw material of a WebVR scene. Credit: Alexandre Duret-Lutz, CC BY-SA 2.0.

content.text: The authors frame this as the core difference between the two media. Video is efficient at delivering a scripted message. WebVR is better at answering questions the script did not anticipate, because the viewer sets the order.
The limits

The finding is qualitative: more control over what is seen, and more detail available to the viewer. It is also tied to a single campus tour. A WebVR build costs more to produce, since photo spheres need stitching, and the result depends on a browser that renders them smoothly.

Source: Pratama et al. (2023). Improving Information Delivery Effectiveness and Efficiency Using WebVR Technology. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology, 657-663. DOI:

article.title: A web tool that drafts the concept map for the teacher
article.subtitle: Rather than generating a finished diagram, the system suggests keywords and propositions a teacher can accept, edit, or ignore.

content.text: The Kit-Build method asks students to rebuild a concept map from a set of ready made pieces. It works well in classrooms, but it leans on one heavy prerequisite. A teacher has to prepare a solid concept map for every reading before the lesson can happen.

That preparation is slow. Doing it well for a set of English reading texts can take hours per text, and teachers who are short on time simply skip the method. Automatic generation looks like an obvious fix, until you read the output. Maps produced automatically tend to come out too general for a specific lesson.

props.caption: A concept map built around learner centred pedagogy. Image: Dr. Mahesh Koltame, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: What the team built
