The researchers took the middle path. Their web based authoring tool mines a reading text and offers suggestions instead of finished diagrams. A teacher selects a sentence, reviews what the system proposes for it, and places the useful parts onto their own canvas.
Stanford CoreNLP parses the text, tagging parts of speech and mapping dependencies between words.
TF-IDF and RAKE rank candidate keywords by how much they matter to the text.
Two extraction methods propose propositions: verb based patterns and open domain triples.

props.caption: A concept map linking ideas with labelled arrows. Image: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: What the evaluation found

Three expert teachers tested the tool across 15 English reading texts, each around 719 words and 34 sentences long. For every text the system suggested roughly 157 keywords, 85 verb based propositions, and 62 open domain propositions. The suggestions arrive grouped in three sections inside a support panel.

The accuracy picture was mixed, and the authors report it plainly. Keyword suggestions had high recall at 0.953 but low precision at 0.405 when borderline suggestions were judged strictly. Proposition triples scored lower on both counts.
When potentially useful suggestions counted as correct, keyword precision climbed to 0.926.
The authors conclude the tool is best used to refine a concept map in more detail, not to create one from scratch.

Source: Pinandito, A., Prasetya, D.D., Hayashi, Y., et al. (2021). Semi-Automatic Concept Map Generation Approach of Web-Based Kit-Build Concept Map Authoring Tool. International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies. DOI:

article.title: Moving Transit Directions from Your Phone to Your Wrist
article.subtitle: A smartwatch companion app can guide passengers step by step without them reaching for a phone.

content.text: Standing in a packed minivan, one hand on a rail, the other holding a phone to check the next stop. Anyone who rides public transport knows the problem. The moment you most need directions is the moment your hands are least free.

The study starts from a practical observation about coverage. Google Maps can provide public transit navigation on Android devices, but its availability is limited to certain cities and regions. That gap leaves room for local developers to build their own transit apps, which then have to solve the interaction problem on their own.
What the team designed

The researchers proposed an input interaction method built around Android Wear devices. The system splits the work between a smartwatch and a phone: the watch handles the input and the glanceable guidance, while the phone does the heavier route calculation and sends the itinerary back.

props.caption: An Android Wear smartwatch, the kind this study targeted. Photo: Maurizio Pesce, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The interaction is organised into three phases that follow how a passenger actually travels.
Entering the origin and the destination on the watch itself.
Reviewing the itinerary that the phone sends back to the watch.
Following the step by step guidance during the trip, with the watch alerting the rider when a stop or an interchange is coming up.

props.caption: Public minivans at a terminal in Malang. Photo: Mujiono Ma'ruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What they found

The evaluation suggests that simplifying a step by step directions app down to a wearable device is feasible for future implementation. The researchers also note a caveat: a watch interface may reach a different usability level than a traditional mobile map application. Moving directions to the wrist is not simply a matter of shrinking the screen.

props.caption: A route information board for Malang minivans. Photo: Mujionomaruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: For transit apps, the takeaway is that a second screen can carry the parts of navigation that do not need a map. A stop name, a countdown, and a vibration at the right moment may be enough to get someone off at the right place.
Source: Brata et al. (2017). Design of public transportation navigation system on android wear device. 2017 International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: What Wrist Sized Directions Get Right and Wrong
article.subtitle: A watch is good at narrow, timely prompts and bad at exploration. Transit interfaces should treat it that way.

content.text: A smartwatch screen is roughly the size of a postage stamp. That constraint forces a designer to decide what a person truly needs in the moment, and what can wait until later.

A 2017 study of public transport navigation on Android Wear devices explored what happens when step by step directions leave the phone and move to a watch. The findings point to something more useful than plain feasibility.
Designing for a glance

Passengers on a bus or a minivan cannot stare at a screen. They need an answer they can absorb in a second, then look away. The study organised the wearable experience into three phases: choosing a destination, reviewing the itinerary, and following guidance while in motion.

props.caption: An Android Wear smartwatch with its companion pairing screen. Photo: Maurizio Pesce, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Each phase has a different tempo, and that tempo shapes what the interface should show.
Input has to be quick and forgiving. Typing an address while standing in a moving vehicle is not realistic, so origin and destination need another way in.
The itinerary view has to work at a glance, because the rider is comparing options rather than reading a document.
Guidance has to be proactive. A wrist that buzzes before the stop arrives solves a problem that a map on a phone screen cannot.

props.caption: A close view of the hardware the study targeted. Photo: Jobu0101, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The study is careful about one point. Simplifying a phone interface onto a wearable is feasible, but it may reach a different usability level than a traditional mobile map application. Smaller is not automatically worse or better. It is a different interaction, with its own strengths.

props.caption: Riders waiting for minivans in Malang, Indonesia. Photo: Mujiono Ma'ruf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That nuance matters for anyone designing for wearables. The wrist is good at narrow and timely prompts, and poor at exploration. Treating it as a second screen for the phone, rather than a replacement for the map, is where the design starts to make sense.
Source: Brata et al. (2017). Design of public transportation navigation system on android wear device. 2017 International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: How Two Concept Map Tools Felt to the People Using Them
article.subtitle: A short user experience questionnaire split the verdict into two very different halves.

content.text: Concept mapping software has an awkward job. It has to let a student build something structured while staying out of the way, and how that feels decides whether the tool survives a semester. A 2019 study measured that feeling for two versions of one tool.

props.caption: A concept map of a system of ideas. Image: Komila Olimova, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Both versions supported Kit Build mapping, where students assemble a map from provided concepts and links. One was the basic tool. The other suggested keywords and propositions while the student worked through an English reading.
How the evaluation worked
The team used the short form of the User Experience Questionnaire. It is a compact instrument: a few opposing word pairs, rated by the user, which roll up into a pragmatic score and a hedonic score.
Pragmatic quality covers usefulness, efficiency, and control.
Hedonic quality covers stimulation and originality.

props.caption: A user testing session in progress. Image: Samuel Mann, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What users reported

Both tools scored positively, which is the baseline any team would want. The difference showed up in the split. The version with suggestions came out hedonically better, so users found it more stimulating to work with.
On the pragmatic side the story was more mixed. Suggestions do not automatically make a tool faster or clearer to run, and the supported version was not always ahead on that half of the scale.
That split matters for anyone building an editor. Help can make an interface more interesting to use without making it more efficient, which is why the two are scored separately.
The study does not crown a winner. It gives a sharper reading of what the added features changed, and that is the part a design team can act on.

Source: Pinandito et al. (2019). User Experience Evaluation on Computer-Supported Concept Map Authoring Tool of Kit-Build Concept Map Framework. 2019 International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology (SIET). DOI:

article.title: Two Designs, One Culinary App, and the Widgets That Decided It
article.subtitle: A lab study compared two versions of the same recommendation app. The features matched. The interface did not.

content.text: A team at Universitas Brawijaya built an Android app that recommends food. Then they built it a second time with a deliberately different interface, and put both versions in front of users to see which one held up.

props.caption: The app recommended dishes like this one. Image: Serenity, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The two versions were named GoEat and LetsEat. They offered the same recommendation feature, but each solved the input problem differently.
GoEat used a flow style for entering alternatives and criteria, a numerical up-down control, and a red colour scheme.
LetsEat used a list for input, a standard numerical field, and a green colour scheme.

props.caption: A warung, the kind of place the app finds. Image: Olivier Van Aken, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How they measured it

Testing ran in a controlled lab with five participants, following the common recommendation for early usability work. They were undergraduate students aged 20 to 26 and regular Android users. A smartphone was mirrored to a PC, while audio and video recording captured faces, fingers and voices at work.

Two methods ran together. Concurrent Think Aloud asked participants to speak their thoughts while using the app, which shows where confusion starts. The System Usability Scale questionnaire collected a score afterwards.
What went wrong

Almost everyone finished the tasks, so the app was not broken. Trouble concentrated on the second task, choosing food alternatives. Some participants never realised the control in front of them could be scrolled, so they stopped looking.

That fault hit GoEat harder. Its flow based input had a lower completion rate on the second task, 80 percent against 100 percent for LetsEat. The team sorted errors into input errors, navigation errors and comprehension errors, then used first and second attempts to gauge learnability.
The conclusion is narrow and practical. Reaching for an uncommon widget to collect user input costs usability, even when the feature underneath works exactly as intended.
Source: Az-zahra, Pinandito, and Tolle (2015). Usability evaluation of mobile application in culinary recommendation system. 2015 IEEE Asia Pacific Conference on Wireless and Mobile (APWiMob). DOI:

article.title: Two Design Approaches, Tested on Real Screens
article.subtitle: User Centered Design and Material Design Guidelines both helped on tablets and phones, but they did not help the same layouts equally.

content.text: Two teams can both say they improved a website, and both be right, while producing very different results. The difference usually comes from the process they followed rather than from the changes they made.

This study put two design approaches through the same measurement. The first was User Centered Design, which builds decisions around what users say and do. The second was Material Design Guidelines, a published set of interface rules covering layout, depth, motion, and typography.
Two different sources of guidance

User Centered Design starts from evidence about the people using the site. You observe, you test, you revise, and the layout follows from what you find. The strength is fit. The cost is that every decision has to be earned through research.

props.caption: The same content arranged for a narrow screen. Image: User:tfinc, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Material Design Guidelines start from a shared specification instead. The strength is consistency and speed, since the rules already answer most layout questions. The risk is that a specification knows nothing about your particular users.
Where each one won
On tablet and smartphone, both approaches improved the effectiveness and efficiency of content delivery. Neither was wasted effort.

The split appeared in one place. For pages built in a three column layout, Material Design Guidelines delivered a better usability improvement than User Centered Design on the smartphone, specifically for content delivery efficiency.

props.caption: A touchscreen device used for reading web content. Image: Intel Free Press, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That is a narrow result, and the authors present it as such. It does not say that guidelines beat user research in general. It says that for one layout style, on one class of device, a published specification closed more of the gap than a research led process did.
The practical use is not to pick a winner. It is to notice that a three column page on a phone is a hard case, and that a codified set of layout rules handles that particular case well.

Source: Pinandito et al. (2017). Analysis of web content delivery effectiveness and efficiency in responsive web design using material design guidelines and User Centered Design. 2017 International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology (SIET). DOI:

article.title: Likes and Retweets as Extra Signal for Sentiment Analysis
article.subtitle: Adding engagement data to a text classifier pushed the F1 score to 0.838.

content.text: Sentiment analysis reads opinion out of text. On Twitter that job is harder than it looks, because posts are short, informal, and full of sarcasm. A study from Universitas Brawijaya asked a simple question: if the text is not enough on its own, what else on the platform can help?

props.caption: Opinions now arrive in short bursts on a phone. Image: Rawpixel, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Two kinds of signal

The team split the problem in two. Text was classified with Naive Bayes, a long standing workhorse for this kind of task. People also react to a post in ways the words do not capture, so the researchers treated likes and retweets as a second set of features, measured rather than read.

Not every count is worth keeping. Fisher Score was used to test which of those engagement features actually carried information about sentiment, so that weak signals could be filtered out before they added noise.
How the two were merged

Text and engagement were combined with weights named alpha and beta. Choosing those weights is the whole design decision, because they set how much the model trusts the words and how much it trusts the crowd's reaction.

props.caption: A town hall audience posts questions in real time. Image: Pete Souza, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The best configuration put slightly more weight on the text than on the engagement features, and the combined model reached an F1 score of 0.838. The result is a useful reminder that engagement data is a supplement, not a replacement. Words still carry most of the meaning, and reactions sharpen the picture around the edges.
Text classified with Naive Bayes, engagement handled as separate numeric features
Fisher Score used to select which like and retweet features to keep
Best result at alpha 0.6 and beta 0.4, with F1 at 0.838

For teams building anything on social data, the takeaway is that a platform gives you more than the sentences it stores. The surrounding behaviour is cheap to collect and, with the right weighting, it earns its place in the model.

Source: Rizal Setya Perdana and Aryo Pinandito (2018). Combining Likes-Retweet Analysis and Naive Bayes Classifier within Twitter for Sentiment Analysis. Journal of Telecommunication, Electronic and Computer Engineering.

article.title: Why a Like Carries Less Weight Than a Sentence
article.subtitle: Engagement counts help sentiment models only after they are filtered and weighted.

content.text: Numeric engagement data is tempting precisely because it is easy to collect. A like is a number, a retweet is a number, and both arrive without any parsing. The trouble is that a number is not an opinion, and a model that leans on it too hard will learn the wrong thing.

props.caption: The platform supplies the reaction, not just the text. Image: MainlyTwelve, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Filter, then weight

The approach in this study does the two steps in that order. Fisher Score first ranks which engagement features are worth keeping, cutting the ones that say little about sentiment. Only then does the model decide how much each family of features should count.

That second decision takes the form of two weights, alpha for the text side and beta for the engagement side. Rather than guessing, the team ran the experiment across combinations and read the F1 score at each setting.

props.caption: Reactions are cheap to count but hard to interpret. Image: Rawpixel, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the tuning showed

The winning setting kept the larger share on the text, at 0.6 against 0.4, and produced an F1 score of 0.838. The gap between the two weights is not dramatic, and that is the interesting part. Engagement data adds something real, but it does not take over the decision.
Screen non textual features before adding them, not after
Treat text and engagement as separate families with separate weights
Report the score at each setting so the tradeoff stays visible

Anyone working with social data can carry one habit out of this. A reaction metric measures the audience as much as the message, so it belongs in the model beside the words rather than in place of them.

Source: Rizal Setya Perdana and Aryo Pinandito (2018). Combining Likes-Retweet Analysis and Naive Bayes Classifier within Twitter for Sentiment Analysis. Journal of Telecommunication, Electronic and Computer Engineering.

article.title: The Hard Part of Chat Privacy Is the Key
article.subtitle: Ciphers are standard and fast. Key handling is where a private messaging design is won or lost.

content.text: Encryption algorithms are rarely the weak point in a private messaging system. They are the part that has been studied, attacked and standardised for decades. The weak point is almost always the key.

A 2018 study on protecting chat content shows this by where it spends its design effort. AES handles the message itself. Almost everything else in the proposal is about making sure the right person, and only the right person, can unlock it.
Key handling is the real design surface

The proposed system generates a key from sixteen random numbers, then disguises that key with several layers of MD5 hashing tied to private values that live inside the application. Sending a message means sending both the encrypted content and enough information for the recipient to rebuild the key.

props.caption: Key exchange is the step where most messaging designs are decided. Image: MarcT0K, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That structure raises questions every messaging product has to answer.
Where does the secret live? If the values needed to derive the key are stored inside the app, an attacker who extracts them from one device gains something real.
How is the key transported? Any shortcut that sends the key in a recoverable form cancels out the encryption protecting the message.
What happens when a device is lost? A design that binds the key to one installation has to say what happens when that installation disappears.

props.caption: Layered protection, as used in the study prototype. Photo: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The performance results are reassuring on this front. On a low spec Android handset, encryption and decryption stayed between a few milliseconds and a few tens of milliseconds for messages up to a thousand characters, well inside what users perceive as instant.

props.caption: Protected data is only as strong as the key that unlocks it. Photo: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That is the useful takeaway for teams building private communication features. Fast cryptography is available off the shelf. The work that decides whether a feature is genuinely private happens in the design of the key, its storage, and the recovery path.
Source: Wardhono et al. (2018). End-to-End Privacy Protection for Facebook Mobile Chat based on AES with Multi-Layered MD5. International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies. DOI:

article.title: The 150 byte rule for compressing API responses
article.subtitle: Moving compression from the web server into the application changes who pays for it, and makes one small payload size the deciding factor.

content.text: There is a version of API performance work that consists of adding a header and moving on. Turn on gzip at the web server, set Accept-Encoding, and let the infrastructure handle the rest. That works until it does not: a shared host you cannot configure, a proxy that strips the header, or an endpoint where you want compression on one route but not another.

The team behind a 2023 study in the Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science took the other path. They moved compression into the application itself, so the API code decides what happens to each response before it leaves the server.

props.caption: Cabling in a data centre. Compression shifts load between server and network. Photo: Derrick Coetzee, CC0.

content.text: Why application level instead of gzip

Compressing inside the application trades flexibility in one direction for flexibility in another. The server does more work, and the client has to decode the result on its own. In exchange, the behaviour travels with the code instead of depending on an environment somebody else controls.
The pipeline runs Zlib on the server through the PHP gzencode function, then Base64 encodes the output.
The browser client decodes the Base64 and decompresses with the Pako library in JavaScript.

props.caption: JSON and XML, the two markup styles most REST payloads use. Diagram: Diego Mariano, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: The threshold that matters

The most portable finding is a number. Below about 150 bytes of JSON, compressing makes a response larger rather than smaller. A 68 byte payload arrived as 112 bytes. A 135 byte payload arrived as 144 bytes. The cause is Base64, which encodes every three bytes of Zlib output as four characters.
Above that line the picture flips. Payloads from roughly 12.5 kilobytes upward came back at about a third of their original size, saving up to 66 percent of the transfer volume.
Server CPU cost scaled with payload size, reaching 3.269 milliseconds for a 101 kilobyte response.
Client side decompression added 0.30 to 8.10 milliseconds, which the authors consider acceptable on modern hardware.

The authors are careful about scope. They measured a single API function from a transport navigation service, applied no caching or pagination, and did not benchmark against native HTTP compression. Those gaps are the obvious next study. For now the takeaway is a habit: pick a size threshold, compress above it, and leave the small responses alone.

Source: Pinandito, A., Kharisma, A.P., Jonemaro, E.M.A. (2023). Architectural Design of Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interface with Application-Level Base64-Encoding and Zlib Data Compression. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Does Having the Text Open While Mapping Help You Learn?
article.subtitle: Making the reading material available lifted short-term scores but not what stuck two weeks later.

content.text: Reading comprehension is where a lot of students quietly fall behind. Concept mapping is one of the tools that helps, and the kit-build variant adds a wrinkle. Learners do not draw a map from scratch. They rebuild a fixed set of concepts and links taken from an expert map.

props.caption: The reading text described the Komodo dragon. Image: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That raises a design question. If students are rebuilding a map, should they keep the reading material open? One view says yes, the text lets them check details. Another says no, because forcing them to rely on memory turns the activity into retrieval practice, which is good for retention.
Three groups, one text

The team tested this with 101 participants recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Everyone read a 2,701 word text about the Komodo dragon and took a comprehension test. Then they were split into three conditions.
Map and Text: rebuild the concept map with the text available.
Map only: rebuild the map with the text taken away.
Double Text: read the text a second time instead of mapping.

props.caption: Comprehension support is a recurring classroom concern. Image: Harrison Keely, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Right after the activity, the Map and Text group did better than the Map only group, with a median normalized change of 0.45 against 0. That difference was significant. Two weeks later it had disappeared. On delayed retention, the two groups were not significantly different.
Where the real signal was

Reading time mattered more than access. Participants who spent longer with the text while building the map did better on both tests, and beat both control groups. The catch is that most participants barely read at all. Making the text available was not enough, on its own, to change the outcome for the group as a whole.

props.caption: Students checking source material during an activity. Image: Onwuka Glory, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Furtado et al. (2021). Influence of Access to Reading Material during Concept Map Recomposition in Reading Comprehension and Retention. IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems. DOI:

article.title: Splitting Dijkstra Between the Phone and the Server
article.subtitle: Dynamic load distribution turns where a route is computed into a runtime decision, and that changes what you have to protect.

content.text: Every navigation feature hides a decision: where does the computation run? Put all of it on the phone and weak devices suffer. Put all of it on the server and the network becomes the bottleneck, along with the bill.
The client-server approach in this study treats that decision as something to make continuously, rather than once at build time.
Two signals drive the decision
The first signal is calculation complexity. A short route across a small graph is cheap. A long one across a dense network is not, and the cost shifts as the graph changes.

The second signal is device capability. Because memory capacity turned out to be the strongest influence on Dijkstra's calculation time, the client's hardware profile is worth measuring rather than assuming.

props.caption: Cabling at the rear of a data center rack. Image: Derrick Coetzee, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The trade you are making

Moving work to the server buys consistent performance on cheap hardware. It also buys a dependency. The route search now needs a working connection, and the server takes on load from every client that cannot cope on its own.

The paper is careful about that second half. Adjusting the Dijkstra calculations in real time is what keeps the arrangement from collapsing when demand spikes. Prevent the server from overloading, and the experience stays steady for everyone.
Design for a waiting time, not a benchmark

The stated goal is a waiting time that never exceeds one second. Working backwards from that is more useful than optimizing an average. If the target is a wait no user notices, the interesting question is not which device is fastest. It is which devices miss the target, and what the system does about them.

props.caption: A Transjakarta bus on corridor 2. Image: Sulthan Naufal, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That framing travels well. Any feature that pairs a phone with a backend has a class of devices that will be too slow for it, and a decision to make about whether to help them or leave them behind.

Source: Justico et al. (2023). Dynamic Load Distribution of Shortest-Path Finding in Client-Server Public Transit System. 2023 International Conference on Modeling and E-Information Research, Artificial Learning and Digital Applications (ICMERALDA). DOI:

article.title: Filtering Spam Out of a Twitter Timeline on Android
article.subtitle: A reusable classifier module scored 82 percent accuracy on Indonesian tweets.

content.text: Twitter timelines fill up with more than conversation. Promotions, duplicate posts, and links to nothing useful arrive alongside the posts a user actually wants. A 2017 project built a way for Android developers to filter that noise out of their own apps.

props.caption: A sample spam message. Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The idea is a reusable framework rather than one finished app. A developer drops the classifier in as a module, and the app can label each incoming tweet as spam or legitimate before it reaches the timeline. The heavy work sits behind that interface.
Training it on real tweets

The team collected tweets through the Twitter search API around trending topics in Indonesia, all written in Indonesian. One hundred tweets were labelled by hand for training, and another hundred were held back for testing.
Training sets ran from 10 tweets up to 100, in steps of ten.
Text was cleaned, tokenised, and reduced to word stems first.

props.caption: An Android handset. Image: Acabashi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the classifiers scored

Naive Bayes reached 82 percent accuracy on the test set. A nearest neighbour classifier, weighted with a term frequency measure, came in at 71 percent. Both beat guessing, and the simpler of the two was clearly ahead.
The value of the work is in that packaging. A small classifier that runs on the phone, trained on a hundred labelled examples, is a far easier thing for an app team to adopt than a research pipeline.

The honest limits are the dataset size and the language. Two hundred tweets from one country is a narrow base, and spam patterns shift quickly. The authors present the framework as a starting point developers can retrain on their own data.

Source: Pinandito et al. (2017). Spam Detection Framework for Android Twitter Application Using Naive Bayes and K-Nearest Neighbor Classifiers. Proceedings of the 2017 International Conference on Software and Computer Applications. DOI:

article.title: Measuring Your Own Eyeglass Prescription With a Phone Camera
article.subtitle: An offline app uses the blur line and the front camera to estimate diopter level, landing within a quarter diopter of the optometrist.

content.text: Checking whether your eyesight has changed usually means booking a full eye examination. The equipment is precise but heavy, and a trained optometrist has to operate it. A team at Brawijaya University asked a narrower question: could a phone estimate a myopia patient's diopter level between visits?

props.caption: Reading a Snellen chart, the standard check. Image: Beendy234, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The method rests on a simple observation. Hold a phone close and the text stays readable. Move it away and at some point the letters blur. That threshold is the blur line distance, and it differs for each eye. The app measures that distance with the front camera and built in sensors, then converts it to a diopter value.
How it was tested
Ten participants measured their own eyes with the app, then had the same eyes measured by a doctor using a phoropter and a Snellen chart. Comparing the two sets of numbers turns a demo into evidence.
The average gap between the app and the doctor was 0.256 diopter, with a standard deviation of 0.08.
That is well under half a diopter, the range the authors treat as an acceptable error.
The System Usability Scale came out at 80.50 with a deviation of 4.11, which places it in the accepted range.

props.caption: A phoropter, the instrument the app is compared against. Image: Frank C. Mueller, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The small standard deviation matters as much as the average: the app was consistently close, not occasionally lucky. Participants also said the immediate result made them more willing to monitor their own condition.

Two limits are worth stating plainly. The app runs entirely offline, which is how it reaches users with poor connectivity, but that also means no clinical record leaves the phone. More importantly, it cannot measure a normal eye accurately, where the error climbed above one diopter. Anyone with a chronic condition still needs the standard test.
As a screening aid, the case is reasonable. A quarter diopter of average error, from hardware already in a patient's pocket, is a cheap way to notice a change before the next appointment.
Source: Brata et al. (2020). A new perspective of refractive error calculation with mobile application. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering (IJECE). DOI:

article.title: A Chat Assistant That Walks Novices Through IoT Setup
article.subtitle: The SEMAR platform gained a conversational guide, tested on three smart systems and a university class.

content.text: Setting up an Internet of Things project is rarely as simple as plugging a sensor into a board. You have to pick the right pins, choose a protocol, and get the network settings right before the device can talk to a server. SEMAR, an integrated server for collecting and visualizing IoT data, was built to make that last part easier. Its authors found that the first part still stops novices cold.

Their answer is an assistant that runs in a browser and holds a conversation. A user describes the project, the hardware on hand, and where it will run. The service replies with step by step instructions for wiring sensors, configuring the board, setting up the network, and choosing a protocol.
How the assistant is built

The service has three parts: a setup guidance function, a response function, and a conversational interface. It runs on GPT-4o, and it grounds answers with retrieval augmented generation over the SEMAR setup guide.

The authors narrowed the requirement scope to four domains: processing boards (Raspberry Pi or Arduino), sensor connectivity (UART, GPIO, I2C), network connectivity (WiFi, cellular, LAN), and communication protocols (MQTT, HTTP, WebSocket).

props.caption: Raspberry Pi 5, one of the supported boards. Image: SimonWaldherr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the tests showed

The team ran two evaluations. First they used the service on three real systems: a smart light, a smart water heater, and a room temperature monitor. It produced working configurations for each, including one where the user swapped boards mid conversation.

Second, they handed it to 22 undergraduates at Institut Bisnis dan Teknologi in Indonesia, working in five groups. Of the 19 students with no IoT experience, 16 finished the assignment, and all three experienced students did too. Usability scores were high for ease of use, usefulness, learning curve, efficiency, and error handling.

props.caption: An ESP8266 development board used in the tests. Image: Ogidya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The assistant was not flawless. It once generated a pin constant that would not compile, and it recommended a package that fails on the newest Raspberry Pi. Students fixed both problems by asking follow up questions, and several asked for the ability to edit messages they had already sent.
Source: Kotama et al. (2025). Implementation of Sensor Input Setup Assistance Service Using Generative AI for SEMAR IoT Application Server Platform. Information. DOI:

article.title: What Changes When Patients Measure Their Own Diopters
article.subtitle: A usability study shows the habit is learnable, while the accuracy question stays open.

content.text: Between eye appointments, most people with myopia have no idea whether their vision has changed. The prescription in their glasses is either right or it is not, and the only way to find out has been to book another visit. A TELKOMNIKA paper explored what happens when that check becomes something a phone can attempt.
Why patients lose track

The standard tools for measuring refractive error are a phoropter used with a Snellen chart, and retinoscopy. Both are accurate and both require an operator with training. That combination keeps measurement inside the clinic and out of daily life, which delays the point at which someone notices their myopia is progressing.
The prototype targets the blur line, the distance at which text stops being sharp for the reader.
It works within a 19 to 89 centimetre window, which maps to roughly minus 1.12 up to minus 5.26 diopters.

props.caption: A Snellen chart on a clinic wall. Image: Creative magnet, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the study showed about the habit

Five participants with normal vision, myopia without glasses, and myopia with glasses used the Android prototype. Everyone completed the sequence of seven tasks, with a success rate of 100 percent and an average time of 2.03 minutes. The usability score of 80.5 places the app in the usable band. Measuring at home, in other words, is something people can be taught to do quickly.

props.caption: Corrective lenses and their case. Image: Evan-Amos, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The number is not a prescription

The item that scored lowest in the questionnaire, at 2.20 out of 5, asked whether the app's result matched the participant's actual condition. Some participants saw a different value than their real prescription. The authors are direct that accuracy was out of scope, describing the work as an early stage usability evaluation rather than a validation study.
Treat a reading as a trend line, not a diagnosis. Repeated measurements over months say more than a single value.
Readings outside the supported range, or a sudden change, still belong with an optometrist.
The value of the idea is the direction it points at: cheap, frequent, self directed tracking that tells someone when it is time to book a real examination.

Source: Komang Candra Brata and Mukhammad Sharif Hidayatulloh (2019). An idea of intuitive mobile diopter calculator for myopia patient. TELKOMNIKA (Telecommunication Computing Electronics and Control). DOI:

article.title: Scoring Hijaiyah Pronunciation with Pitch, Volume, and Rhythm
article.subtitle: A mobile learning prototype rates Quran reading practice from 0 to 100 instead of true or false.

content.text: Learning to read Hijaiyah letters, the first step toward reading the Quran, usually depends on a mentor. The Iqro method works well, but it needs an Ustaz or Ustazah sitting beside the learner to judge whether a letter was pronounced correctly. Time and availability make that hard to arrange every day.
Why true or false is not enough

Most Hijaiyah apps on the market lean on vocabulary, writing, and reading drills. When they do score pronunciation, they hand the audio to a general speech recogniser and return a simple correct or incorrect verdict. The authors argue that this hides progress, because a learner cannot see whether they are getting closer.
The skill being tested is Makhraj, the correct articulation point of each letter.
A binary score gives no sense of improvement between attempts.

props.caption: Reading the Quran, the skill the scoring system targets. Image: Rezasfllh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Three acoustic features

The prototype extracts pitch, volume, and rhythm from the learner's voice and folds them into a single score between 0 and 100. The approach borrows from automatic singing evaluation, where pitch contours are aligned with dynamic time warping before rhythm is measured. A field study with five early participants shaped the design, and two requests stood out: a real number instead of a verdict, and a flow where the learner simply speaks to the app.

props.caption: Reading practice at home, the setting the app supports. Image: Bisajunisa, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: How close the scores came

Ten respondents read a set of letters aloud. Each attempt was scored twice, once by an Ustaz and once by the application. Comparing the two sets of results gave a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.51 for Iqro level 1 material.

That is a moderate agreement, not a match. In the table the app consistently scored higher than the human judge, which suggests the feature weights still need tuning. The authors describe the work as a feasibility study and plan to test timbre as a fourth feature, collect more data, and extend the method to higher Iqro levels.

Source: Komang Candra Brata, Mohamad Handy Nugraha, and Adam Hendra Brata (2022). An alternative m-learning scoring approach to automatically evaluate Iqro's pronunciation based on pitch, volume, and rhythm features. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering. DOI:

article.title: Scoring the Concept Map Process, Not Just the Result
article.subtitle: A new scoring method looks at how students build a concept map, not only at the map they end up with.

content.text: A concept map shows what a student understands by connecting concepts with labelled links. The kit-build framework turns that into a hands-on exercise. Learners receive the concepts and links taken apart from a teacher's map and put them back together. The system then compares the rebuilt map with the original, quickly and without a human scorer.

props.caption: A hand drawn concept map linking ideas around a central topic. Image: Chabre, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The catch is that the check only looks at the final map. Two students can arrive at the same map by very different routes. One builds it steadily, cluster by cluster. Another jumps around and fills gaps at random. The product looks identical, but the thinking behind it is not.
How sub-map scoring works

The team treated a concept map as a set of sub-maps. Each sub-map is a small cluster of propositions that share one meaning. The assumption is simple. If a learner really understands a cluster, they will build it in one continuous run rather than scattering it across the session.
Every sub-map is scored by how many of its propositions were connected in one unbroken sequence.
All sub-maps carry equal weight, so the overall score is their average.
If a learner returns to a sub-map later, the longest connected run counts.

props.caption: Concept maps group related propositions into clusters. Image: Dr. Mahesh Koltame, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The evaluation ran with 60 second-year students in an Object-Oriented Programming course. The goal map held 15 propositions across five sub-maps. Students took a pre-test, worked through the activity, took a post-test, and sat a delayed test a week later.
What the numbers showed

Sub-map scoring correlated with learning gain at 0.711, a strong relationship. Full-map scoring came in at 0.674, which counts as moderate. In a regression model with both measures plus the pre-test score, only sub-map scoring stayed significant, at a p-value of 0.00959.

props.caption: A concept map about concept maps. Image: Wikibooks user Dvitalo12, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The practical takeaway is about feedback. A teacher who sees only the finished map reads a correct answer and moves on. A teacher who can see the process spots the learner who assembled the right map without ever holding the whole idea together.
Source: Rismanto et al. (2024). Evaluating the kit-build concept mapping process using sub-map scoring. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning. DOI:

article.title: Why the Same Concept Map Can Mean Two Different Things
article.subtitle: Two students can hand in identical maps and still walk away with different levels of understanding.

content.text: Imagine two students in the same class. Both rebuild the teacher's concept map perfectly. Both score the same. One of them actually understood the material. The other got there by trial and error, sliding pieces around until the picture finally looked right.

props.caption: A concept map made of linked clusters. Image: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That gap is what the kit-build framework could not see. Its automatic scoring compares the learner's map with the teacher's map and counts matching, missing, and extra links. Everything about the journey between the first piece and the last one gets thrown away.
The process leaves a trace

The sub-map scoring method reads that trace. It splits a map into clusters of related propositions and watches the order in which a learner connects them. Someone who works through a cluster from start to finish is treated as having grasped it. Someone who keeps breaking away is not.
A clean run through a sub-map earns full marks for that cluster.
Scattered connections score lower, even when the finished map is correct.

props.caption: Related ideas tend to cluster together in a map. Image: Alexopoulou and Markopoulos, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Across 60 students the measure held up. Process scores tracked learning gain more closely than final-map scores did, and they stayed significant in a regression that also controlled for the pre-test result.
What it changes in the classroom

For teachers, the value is diagnostic speed. Knowing that a learner's map is correct tells you very little. Knowing that a correct map was assembled in fragments tells you where to step in, and it tells you before the next exam rather than after it.

props.caption: Students working through a mapping exercise in class. Image: Onwuka Glory, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: For students, the message is subtler. A tidy finished map can hide shaky ground. This method gives that shaky ground a number, which is roughly what formative assessment is meant to do in the first place.
Source: Rismanto et al. (2024). Evaluating the kit-build concept mapping process using sub-map scoring. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning. DOI:

article.title: The Case for Throwing Away Most of Your Route Points
article.subtitle: A line simplification step made a map search far faster while keeping useful accuracy.

content.text: Storage is cheap, so the instinct with location data is to keep everything. A phone can log a coordinate every second and nobody complains. The complaint arrives later, when some downstream routine has to chew through all of it on a device with a small battery.

props.caption: Turn by turn apps hide the geometry underneath. Image: DirtyPotatoEditor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Simplify before you compute

The study applies a classic answer to a modern mobile problem. Before the RouteBoxer grid search runs, the path passes through Douglas-Peucker simplification, which keeps the endpoints and the points that genuinely bend the line, and drops the rest. The surviving points describe the same road with far less detail.
The numbers from the experiment are worth remembering as a benchmark for this class of work.
Point count reduced by up to 99 percent
Calculation ran up to 87.8 times faster
Precision held above 92.6 percent

props.caption: The search area only needs the broad shape of the route. Image: SatGuide, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Choosing how much to drop

Simplification is not free of judgement. Push it hard and the path cuts corners, which shifts the search area away from the real road. Hold back and the performance gain shrinks. That knob is the whole design decision, and the reported precision figure is what makes the trade visible instead of a guess.

For developers working with GPS traces, the habit worth stealing is to treat raw points as one representation of a route rather than the only one. A simplified version is often the right input for a search, while the full trace stays available for playback or analysis. The same path can be served two ways, and each consumer gets what it actually needs.

Source: Aryo Pinandito and Chandrawati Putri Wulandari (2021). Integrating Douglas-Peucker Line Simplification into Routeboxer Algorithm on a Map-Based Android Application. Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Membuat Skybox 3D Tampil Cepat di Peramban
article.subtitle: Panorama 360 derajat yang dipotong menjadi enam sisi kubus cukup untuk membangun ruang virtual yang ringan.

content.text: Bayangkan calon mahasiswa mengunjungi kampus tanpa harus datang. Mereka membuka peramban, memutar pandangan 360 derajat, dan melihat gedung dari segala arah. Idenya terdengar sederhana, tetapi menuntut proses render yang cepat.

Tim peneliti dari FILKOM Universitas Brawijaya membangun prototipe objek skybox 3D berbasis WebGL. Skybox adalah latar berbentuk kubus yang membungkus sebuah pemandangan, sehingga pengguna merasa berada di dalam lokasi tersebut.
Cara kerjanya

Panorama 360 derajat dipotong menjadi enam sisi kubus: posx, posy, posz, negx, negy, dan negz. Keenam sisi itu menjadi dinding ruang virtual. Ke dalamnya ditambahkan objek dasar seperti bola, kubus, torus, dan silinder sebagai elemen augmented reality, lengkap dengan pemetaan tekstur, efek cermin, gradasi warna, dan animasi gerakan.

props.caption: Panorama 360 derajat menjadi bahan dasar skybox. Foto: Wilfredor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: WebGL dipilih karena berjalan langsung di peramban tanpa plugin tambahan. Tim memakai dua pendekatan sekaligus, yaitu shader dan non shader. Shader ditulis dengan GLSL untuk mengatur posisi verteks dan warna fragmen, sementara jalur non shader dipakai sebagai pembanding.

props.caption: Perbandingan hasil render waktu nyata dan pra render. Gambar: Adamgmz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Hasil pengujian

Pengujian dilakukan di lima titik lokasi kampus, masing-masing sepuluh kali percobaan. Rata rata waktu render yang tercatat adalah 0,12668 detik. Nilai itu menunjukkan bahwa adegan tiga dimensi berisi skybox dan beberapa objek tambahan masih nyaman dibuka dari peramban.

props.caption: Teknik rasterisasi yang dipakai aplikasi waktu nyata. Gambar: KaiaVintr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Bagi pengembang aplikasi wisata virtual, hasil ini menegaskan satu hal. Kunci kenyamanan bukan pada perangkat keras pengguna, melainkan pada seberapa rapi adegan disusun. Memotong panorama menjadi enam sisi dan mengendalikan shader dengan tepat sudah cukup untuk membuat pengalaman berjalan mulus.

Sumber: Cholissodin et al. (2022). Pengembangan Fast Render Objek Grafis Menggunakan Shader dan Non-Shader Berbasis WebGL dari Primitive Object untuk Membuat Raw Metaverse Material Objek Skybox 3D di Filkom UB. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer.

article.title: Why Real-Time Middleware Decides Collaborative Learning
article.subtitle: A shared map is only as good as the layer that keeps two screens in sync.

content.text: Collaborative software lives or dies on a boring question. When one person moves something, how long until the other person sees it? On a shared concept map, that delay is the whole experience. Push it too high and two learners end up fighting over a map that no longer exists.

props.caption: A concept map is a set of linked nodes. Image: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The kit-build platform faced a harder version of that problem than most. A concept map is not a document. Every learner's map gets compared against a teacher's map for automatic diagnosis, so sync errors do not merely look bad. They corrupt the assessment.
Why Socket.IO was the useful choice

Socket.IO gives a server a persistent channel to every connected client, so it can push changes instead of waiting for a client to ask. For a shared map, that is the difference between a live session and a refresh button.
Updates reach every participant without polling.
The existing diagnosis logic stays untouched underneath.
The platform gains a usable basis for distance learning.

props.caption: Shared maps need every edit to land in the right order. Image: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: There is a broader lesson in the choice. The team did not rebuild the learning model to go online. They kept the part that produced the learning results and replaced only the transport. When a method already works, that is usually the cheaper and safer path.
What a prototype can claim

The paper is careful about this. Its evaluation covers potential usability, not measured learning. A prototype that runs smoothly is not evidence that students learn more through it. The authors present it as a foundation for practical use, which is the right level of confidence for the evidence available.

props.caption: Devices ready for a class. Image: U.S. Army, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Pinandito et al. (2021). Design and Development of Online Collaborative Learning Platform of Kit-Build Concept Map. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Reading the Warning Signs Before Burnout Hits Study Time
article.subtitle: What the stressor-strain-outcome model suggests for students and the people who teach them.

content.text: Most advice about social media and studying jumps straight to cutting screen time. The SIET 2023 study on student learning productivity suggests a more careful route. It separates the pressure students feel into distinct types, which means the response can be specific instead of a blanket rule.
Three kinds of overload
The model names three stressors. Each one points at a different part of daily life, so each one calls for a different habit.
Information overload: too much material arriving, so nothing gets processed properly. The fix is closer to filtering than to quitting.
Communication overload: too many messages that all seem to expect a reply. Group chats around coursework are the usual source.
Social overload: too much social demand and comparison. This one feeds technostress directly in the results.

props.caption: A dozen apps, each asking for attention. Image: mikemacmarketing, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Technostress as a signal

Technostress sits in the middle of the chain rather than at the end. It is the point where the pressure of the platform starts to feel like pressure on the person. In the study it leads into exhaustion, and exhaustion is what finally touches learning productivity.
That ordering matters for anyone designing a course or a study routine. A tired student who cannot concentrate may not need more discipline. They may need fewer channels demanding attention at once.

props.caption: A phone in the hand is a standing invitation to interruption. Image: Leanne Walker, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the study does not claim

The results come from 100 undergraduate respondents answering one survey, analysed with a Generalized Linear Model. That design can show which factors move together, but it cannot prove that one causes another. It also cannot say how long exhaustion takes to build or to fade.
Even so, the chain the authors describe is a useful checklist. When study time starts shrinking, it is worth asking which link is under strain rather than blaming the phone as a whole.

Source: Shandra Elvyra Sudarsono Putri, Mochamad Chandra Saputra, and Aryo Pinandito (2023). The Effect of Social Media Overload, Exhaustion, and Technostress on Student's Learning Productivity Using Stressor-Strain-Outcome Model. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology (SIET 2023). DOI:

article.title: Adding One Criterion Can Flip Your Whole Ranking
article.subtitle: The Malang culinary study is most useful as a catalogue of the ways a recommendation algorithm can quietly misbehave.

content.text: Recommendation apps look like a solved problem. Collect a few criteria, weight them, sort the list, ship it. The study from Brawijaya University shows where that plan breaks down.

The team ran three multi criteria methods over 30 real cases from Malang, all scored against the same three criteria: distance, price, and rating. The interesting material is not which method won. It is the failure mode each one carries.
Watch out for rank reversal

AHP builds its ranking from pairwise comparisons. When you add a restaurant to the database, or drop a criterion you no longer care about, the relative order of the alternatives can change even though none of them changed. The literature calls this rank reversal, and the authors list it among the known weaknesses of the method.
For an app that updates its database constantly, that is a real problem. A user who sees a restaurant at the top of the list today may find it third tomorrow, for no reason they can observe.

props.caption: A food court with many competing options. Image: Stephan van Helden, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The nine item ceiling

AHP also caps how much you can compare at once. The paper notes that the number of criteria or alternatives is limited to nine. Past that point, the consistency of human judgments falls away, and the derived weights get worse.

TOPSIS carries the opposite weakness. It ranks alternatives well, but its attribute weighting is highly subjective, because whoever configures the system hands out the weights directly, with no check that they are consistent with one another.
The pattern worth copying

The hybrid method in this study covers both gaps. AHP sets the criteria weights, which enforces consistency through pairwise comparison, and TOPSIS does the ranking, where its normalization and weighting step costs only quadratic order. That split is why AHP TOPSIS came out fastest in the simulation while still beating plain AHP on accuracy.
The lesson for anyone building a ranked list: pick your weighting method for consistency and your ranking method for cost. Do not expect a single algorithm to do both jobs well.

props.caption: Fritters for sale in Jakarta. Image: Sakurai Midori, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Dewi et al. (2018). A Comparison Between AHP and Hybrid AHP for Mobile Based Culinary Recommendation System. International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies. DOI:

article.title: Wisatawan Menerima Aplikasi Kuliner Halal di Malang
article.subtitle: Survei terhadap 64 responden menunjukkan aplikasi pelacak kuliner halal dinilai mudah dan bermanfaat.

content.text: Kabupaten Malang punya banyak pilihan kuliner, tetapi wisatawan yang datang dari luar kota sering kesulitan memastikan mana yang sudah tersertifikasi halal. Informasi itu biasanya tersebar dari mulut ke mulut atau tidak ada sama sekali. Dari masalah itu, sebuah tim mengembangkan aplikasi pelacak kuliner halal berbasis Android.

props.caption: Nasi tempong, salah satu kuliner khas Malang. Foto: Gunawan Kartapranata, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Cara kerja aplikasi

Aplikasi ini menggabungkan perangkat Android dengan layanan Google Maps dan GPS. Pengguna memilih kota tujuan pada menu All Area, lalu memilih kategori menu yang ingin dikunjungi. Peta navigasi akan menunjukkan lokasi kuliner bersertifikat halal beserta informasi menu yang disajikan.

Sebelum sistem ini diperluas ke lebih banyak daerah, tim perlu tahu apakah masyarakat benar-benar mau memakainya. Mereka memakai Technology Acceptance Model dengan dua faktor utama: persepsi kemudahan dan persepsi kemanfaatan. Data dari 64 responden diolah memakai metode Partial Least Square.

props.caption: Penanda halal membantu wisatawan memilih tempat makan. Foto: Emna Mizouni, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Yang ditemukan

Responden datang dari luar Kabupaten Malang. Pasuruan menyumbang 22 persen, Surabaya 20 persen, Sidoarjo 16 persen, dan sisanya dari kota yang lebih jauh seperti Banjarmasin, Indramayu, dan Magelang. Kelompok inilah yang paling membutuhkan informasi kuliner halal di Malang.
Persepsi kemudahan memperoleh nilai rata-rata 3,742
Kemanfaatan 4,05, minat menggunakan 4,07, dan penggunaan nyata 4,04
Semua nilai berada di atas skala setuju, jadi responden menerima aplikasi ini

Uji hipotesis memakai t tabel 1,669. Pengaruh kemudahan terhadap kemanfaatan punya t hitung 6,820. Kemudahan terhadap minat 2,037. Kemanfaatan terhadap minat 5,389. Minat terhadap penggunaan nyata 10,517. Semua berada di atas t tabel, jadi setiap jalur dalam model terbukti nyata.

props.caption: Kuliner lokal jadi alasan wisatawan mencari rekomendasi. Foto: Evan Ilham Pasha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Nilai predictive relevance sebesar 0,885 menandakan model ini baik dalam menggambarkan keadaan sebenarnya di lapangan. Sebaliknya, jalur kemudahan menuju minat adalah yang paling lemah, dengan 72,3 persen variasi minat dijelaskan oleh indikator lain.

Bagi tim pengembang, hasil ini memberi arah yang jelas. Memastikan aplikasi terasa mudah dipakai bukan sekadar urusan tampilan, karena kemudahan itulah yang menumbuhkan keyakinan akan manfaat dan minat untuk memakainya.
Sumber: Sucipto Sucipto dkk. (2019). Analisis Penerimaan Aplikasi Tracking Kuliner Halal oleh Wisatawan di Kabupaten Malang. Jurnal Sosioteknologi. DOI:

article.title: Mencari Citra Mirip dengan Haar Wavelet dan K-Means
article.subtitle: Ekstraksi ciri wavelet dipadukan pengelompokan gambar, dan hasilnya presisi naik sekitar 40 persen.

content.text: Mencari gambar di komputer tidak bisa dilakukan dengan mencocokkan nama berkas. Dua foto kuda bisa punya nama yang sama sekali berbeda, dan foto pantai dari dua fotografer tidak akan berbagi kata kunci apa pun. Pendekatan yang dipakai adalah temu kembali citra berbasis konten, yaitu mencari gambar berdasarkan isi gambarnya sendiri.

props.caption: Alur kerja temu kembali citra. Gambar: Seda Nur Yazici, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Sebuah penelitian membangun sistem seperti itu dengan dua komponen utama. Haar wavelet transform dipakai untuk mengekstrak ciri gambar, lalu ukuran jarak F-Norm menghitung seberapa mirip dua citra. Hasil ekstraksi itu kemudian dikelompokkan dengan algoritma K-Means sebelum pencarian dijalankan.
Pengujian pada 500 gambar

Basis data ujinya berisi 500 gambar yang tersebar di lima kategori: dinosaurus, bus, pantai, kuda, dan bunga. Jumlah klaster ditetapkan lima, satu untuk tiap kategori. Dua parameter diuji, yaitu persentase fitur yang dipakai dan ambang batas kemiripan yang menentukan kapan proses pencarian berhenti.
Presisi temu kembali naik sekitar 40 persen dibandingkan skenario tanpa pengelompokan.
Waktu pencarian menjadi 1,6 sampai 2,7 kali lebih cepat.
Pada kategori dinosaurus, recall 1,00 dengan presisi 0,25 di 3,80 detik berubah menjadi presisi 0,99 di 1,48 detik.

props.caption: Representasi transformasi wavelet kontinu. Gambar: DaBler, domain publik, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Angka terakhir itu menunjukkan dua hal sekaligus. Presisi naik karena hasil pencarian jadi lebih tepat, dan waktu turun karena sistem tidak lagi memeriksa seluruh isi basis data satu per satu. Kualitas dan kecepatan membaik bersamaan, bukan saling menukar.

Pengaruh pengelompokan juga terlihat pada kategori kuda, di mana presisi meningkat hingga 51 persen dibandingkan skenario tanpa klaster pada ambang kemiripan 0,5. Artinya, keuntungan terbesar muncul justru ketika gambar di dalam satu kategori cukup beragam, karena di situlah pencarian menyeluruh paling banyak membuang waktu.

Perlu dicatat bahwa uji ini memakai basis data kecil, 500 gambar dengan lima kategori yang sudah jelas batasnya. Keadaan sebenarnya jauh lebih ramai, dan jumlah klaster yang tepat belum tentu tetap lima. Meski begitu, alur berpikirnya tetap berguna: pilih metode ekstraksi ciri yang ringan, lalu susun data agar pencarian tidak perlu menyentuh semuanya.
Sumber: Jonemaro dan Rusdianto (2016). Sistem Temu Kembali Citra Berbasis Konten Menggunakan Haar Wavelet Transform Dan K-Means Clustering. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: An Offline Diopter App for Places Without an Optometrist
article.subtitle: Eye care access in Indonesia is uneven, and that gap shaped the design of a myopia measurement app.

content.text: Access to eye care is not evenly distributed. In parts of Indonesia, patients who need their refractive error checked face a shortage of standard equipment and of the professionals who can operate it. A phoropter paired with a Snellen chart is accurate, but expensive, stationary and tied to a trained optometrist.

props.caption: A standard eye examination session. Image: Dresden Vision, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Clinic measurements remain the reference standard, and nothing here changes that. What a research team from Brawijaya University proposed is a stopgap patients can carry. The app estimates diopter level from the distance at which the phone screen starts to blur, using only the front camera and built in sensors.
Design choices that followed from the context

Earlier phone based eye measurement attempts existed, but most required an internet connection and manual steps patients found complicated. Both problems hit hardest where the need is greatest, so the team designed against them.
The measurement runs offline, so a poor connection is not a barrier to using it.
The steps are guided, with instructions to close one eye and move the phone to find the blur line.
No extra hardware is needed, which keeps the cost of monitoring close to zero.

props.caption: Clinic equipment that a phone cannot replace. Image: Frank C. Mueller, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The study began with interviews about how often participants visited professional eye care and how they coped day to day. Twenty people took part, and ten went on to test the measurement itself, compared against readings taken by a doctor with a phoropter and a Snellen chart.

The average difference between the two methods was 0.256 diopter, comfortably inside the half diopter margin the authors set, and usability scored 80.50 on the System Usability Scale. The app also fails in one place, which the authors report: for normal vision the error rose above one diopter.

That honesty makes the work useful as a model. A tool aimed at underserved users is judged on availability first and accuracy second, and this one is explicit about both. It does not replace the optometrist, but it makes the wait less blind.
Source: Brata et al. (2020). A new perspective of refractive error calculation with mobile application. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering (IJECE). DOI:

article.title: Pelajaran dari Membangun Tur Virtual Kampus
article.subtitle: Kecepatan adegan tiga dimensi lebih ditentukan oleh kerapian susunannya daripada oleh perangkat pengguna.

content.text: Tur virtual kampus sering gagal bukan karena idenya buruk, melainkan karena pemandangannya tersendat saat diputar. Pengguna menutup tab sebelum sempat melihat gedung utamanya.
Sebuah studi tentang render cepat objek grafis berbasis WebGL menawarkan catatan praktis untuk siapa pun yang ingin membangun pengalaman serupa, mulai dari tur kampus sampai pameran virtual.
Tiga keputusan yang menentukan
Tim peneliti menyusun adegan dari sebuah panorama 360 derajat yang dipotong menjadi enam bidang kubus. Pilihan pilihan teknis di baliknya layak ditiru oleh tim yang baru memulai.

props.caption: Adegan tiga dimensi yang dirender secara waktu nyata. Gambar: KaiaVintr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Pilih WebGL karena berjalan langsung di peramban. Tidak ada plugin yang perlu dipasang, sehingga pengguna bisa langsung masuk.
Siapkan jalur shader dan non shader. Pendekatan non shader berguna sebagai pembanding untuk melihat apakah penulisan shader benar-benar memberi dampak pada kecepatan.
Uji di beberapa lokasi, bukan hanya satu titik. Pengujian di lima lokasi kampus memperlihatkan bahwa waktu render bisa berbeda tergantung kerumitan pemandangan.

props.caption: Panorama 360 derajat sebagai bahan dasar skybox. Foto: Wilfredor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Hasil pengujian mereka mencatat rata rata waktu render 0,12668 detik dari lima puluh percobaan. Uji coba di dalam gedung tercatat jauh lebih cepat daripada di area terbuka, karena jumlah objek yang harus digambar lebih sedikit.

props.caption: Contoh hasil render objek tiga dimensi. Gambar: Adamgmz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Pelajaran utamanya sederhana. Kecepatan adegan tiga dimensi tidak hanya ditentukan oleh perangkat pengguna, tetapi oleh seberapa banyak yang harus digambar. Mengurangi jumlah objek dan memilih sudut pandang dengan bijak sering kali lebih efektif daripada menambah daya komputasi.

Sumber: Cholissodin et al. (2022). Pengembangan Fast Render Objek Grafis Menggunakan Shader dan Non-Shader Berbasis WebGL dari Primitive Object untuk Membuat Raw Metaverse Material Objek Skybox 3D di Filkom UB. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer.

article.title: Porting a web algorithm into a reusable Android module
article.subtitle: The RouteBoxer port shows what changes when browser code has to become a library that other projects can pick up.

content.text: Reuse in software is often accidental. A helper written for one project gets copied into the next one, and then into the one after that. It keeps working until the platform changes, at which point every copy has to be fixed separately.

RouteBoxer is a small library for covering the area around a route with bounding boxes. It began life as a helper for maps in the browser. The Android version was not copied from anywhere. It was written as a library from the first commit, which changed several decisions along the way.

props.caption: Everyday roads and signage. Route data drives the rectangles the library returns. Photo: LondekaT, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: What changes when code becomes a library
The public surface has to stay small enough to document: a route and a distance go in, boxes come out.
It has to sit on the platform's own map stack, in this case the Google Maps Android API.
It should ship in more than one form: a compiled library file to drop in, or a source module to import and adapt.
Development stays inside the toolchain the target developers already use, here Android Studio.

Offering both a compiled artifact and an importable source module is the part teams skip most often. It costs little and it removes the main reason developers abandon a small library, which is not being able to change the one line they disagree with.
Document how the parameters scale

props.caption: Navigation on a long trip. A wider corridor means far more boxes to query. Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0.

content.text: The most useful line in the paper is not about code structure. The authors report that the number of boxes grows exponentially as the requested distance increases. A caller who doubles the corridor width does not get twice the work, and without that fact written down they will find out in production.

The general lesson for anyone porting an algorithm across platforms is that the algorithm is usually the easy part. The platform API, the packaging, and an honest note about how the inputs scale are what determine whether the port gets used. A library that hides those costs is a library that gets ripped out later.
Source: Pinandito, A., Saputra, M.C., Perdana, R.S. (2016). RouteBoxer library for Google Android platform. 2016 IEEE Asia Pacific Conference on Wireless and Mobile (APWiMob). DOI:

article.title: The Real Cost of Putting AR Labels in the Right Place
article.subtitle: Accuracy in outdoor augmented reality is a budget decision, and this study lays out the numbers.

content.text: A seven metre error is the difference between a marker sitting on a shop door and a marker floating over the middle of the road. That is roughly the gap between a conventional outdoor AR setup and the combined VSLAM and Street View approach tested here.

Outdoor AR has quietly become ordinary. Campus tours, transit stops, heritage trails and retail promotions all lean on it. When the anchor is wrong, users do not read it as a sensor limit. They read it as a broken app.
Why the three layers fit together

Sensor fusion gives an absolute position, but a soft one: the GPS fix wobbles and the compass follows magnetic noise. Visual SLAM is excellent at relative motion and poor at holding an absolute frame, because small errors accumulate as the user walks. Street View matching is the opposite: slow and sparse, but it lands on a fixed coordinate.

props.caption: A Street View car at work in Barcelona. Credit: Jove, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Used together, each layer covers the weakness of the others. That lesson generalises beyond AR. If two weak signals fail in different ways, combining them costs less than making either one strong.
What the accuracy bill looks like
CPU load: 29 percent on the proposed method against 13 percent on the conventional one.
Memory: 294 MB against 152 MB, roughly double the footprint.
Coverage: matching only works where Street View imagery of the area exists.

props.caption: Malang, where the campus tests took place. Credit: Uliyanti, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: For a phone two or three years old, doubling the memory footprint of a camera screen is a real constraint. It shows up as heat, battery drain and dropped frames. The authors are direct: accuracy costs load, and the right choice depends on the app.
What this changes for builders

Check Street View coverage for your target streets before designing around it. Keep the sensor fusion path as a fallback. And decide early whether you need a marker on a doorway or just a marker in the right block, because that sets the resource budget.
Source: Brata et al. (2024). An enhancement of outdoor location-based augmented reality anchor precision through VSLAM and Google Street View. Sensors, 24(4), 1161. DOI:

article.title: Building an Online Collaborative Kit-Build Platform
article.subtitle: The kit-build method worked in classrooms. Making it work across a network took a real-time layer.

content.text: Kit-build concept mapping asks learners to rebuild a teacher's concept map from its pieces. It has a good track record. Learners who do it tend to understand the material better and remember it longer than learners who map freely or study in the usual way.

props.caption: A concept map assembled from linked propositions. Image: Dr. Mahesh Koltame, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Group work on top of that has done well too. Pairs and small groups using kit-build have outperformed conventional collaborative learning in earlier studies. The problem here was practical rather than pedagogical. The kit-build system was built for a room, not a network. Learners in different places could not work on the same map at the same time.
What the team built

The paper describes the design and development of an online collaborative platform for kit-build concept mapping. A prototype was built and then evaluated to see whether it had legs for real classroom use, including use at a distance.
Real-time communication runs on Socket.IO, middleware that pushes updates to connected clients.
Learners share a map and see each other's changes as they happen.
The prototype was assessed for potential usability rather than for learning outcomes.

props.caption: Students working together on a mapping task. Image: Onwuka Glory, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The evaluation pointed to the middleware choice as the effective part. Socket.IO gave the platform collaborative features without forcing a rebuild of the kit-build assessment machinery underneath. That matters, because automatic diagnosis is the reason kit-build is worth using in the first place.
What comes next

The authors describe the result as preliminary. The system showed enough potential to justify real use in distant collaborative learning, which is a modest claim to make for a prototype. The obvious next step is classroom trials that measure learning, not just whether the system runs.

props.caption: The original kit-build activities ran in shared classrooms. Image: Harrison Keely, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Pinandito et al. (2021). Design and Development of Online Collaborative Learning Platform of Kit-Build Concept Map. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Mapping the Journey Before Redesigning a Transit App
article.subtitle: Mental models and user journey maps turned passenger frustration into a short list of requirements.

content.text: Teams that redesign a transit app usually start with the screen. The researchers here started with what passengers believe happens during a trip. That belief is the mental model, and the gap between it and the real service is where most frustration lives.

props.caption: Transit stops are where plans meet reality. Image: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The study, run in Malang, combined two elicitation tools. The mental model captured how each participant pictured their journey: which stops they remembered, which lines they trusted, when they expected to transfer. The user journey map organised those expectations stage by stage, from planning at home to arrival.
Where the journey breaks

Twenty participants took part in the field study. Mapping their accounts surfaced recurring pain points, and most were not about missing data. They were about attention. Passengers divided themselves between the vehicle, the stop and the phone screen, and that division produced the mistakes.
Checking the remaining time to an interchange point while the vehicle is moving.
Repeatedly monitoring the screen, because nothing announces the next checkpoint by itself.
Recovering after a wrong stop, which is harder when the route is unfamiliar.

props.caption: The prototype put guidance on a wearable screen. Image: Maurizio Pesce, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Those findings pointed away from a better map and toward a different interaction. The team prototyped a wearable app that announces checkpoints with a vibration and shows the itinerary on a small screen, so the phone can stay in a pocket.
