They did both twice, once per interface, with different destinations of equal distance to head off any learning effect.

The authors measured completion time and success rate, then asked each participant to fill in the short form of the User Experience Questionnaire, which splits experience into pragmatic quality and hedonic quality.

props.caption: A phone showing a map navigation view. Image: Santeri Viinamaki, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the numbers showed

Both interfaces got everyone to the destination, so success rate was a tie at 100 percent. Time separated them. The digital map was quicker in both scenarios: about 4.99 minutes against 5.45 for blind search, and 4.91 against 5.20 for directed search. The gaps are small but consistent.

The questionnaire told a different story. Pragmatic quality scored higher for the digital map, 1.90 against 1.53. Hedonic quality flipped the other way, 1.48 for AR against 0.53 for the map, and the overall score also favored AR, 1.50 against 1.21.

props.caption: An augmented reality view layered over a camera feed. Image: Mimzy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The authors read this as a familiarity effect. People already know how to read a map, so the map wins on task performance. But the AR view, with real street scenes annotated in place, was more engaging and more memorable. They describe the two as close on usability overall and suggest combining their strengths rather than choosing one.

Source: Brata and Liang (2020). Comparative study of user experience on mobile pedestrian navigation between digital map interface and location-based augmented reality. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering. DOI:

article.title: Desktop, Mobile or Web: Timing the Same Accounting Task Three Ways
article.subtitle: The same accounting system, built for three platforms, put seven employees on a stopwatch.

content.text: Accounting systems sit at the centre of how a business runs. When they work, nobody notices. When they are slow, every invoice takes longer and the effect compounds across a month of transactions.

A study from Universitas Brawijaya asked a question that most buyers never test: does the platform you run the system on change how long the work takes? The team built the same accounting system three times, for desktop, mobile and web, and timed employees doing real tasks on each.
How the experiment ran

The tests took place at a motor spare parts distributor in Surabaya with seven employees who already used an accounting system in their daily work. Everyone got 15 minutes of training on each platform first, so unfamiliarity would not distort the numbers. Each task was repeated five times. The timer started when the participant was ready and stopped when the task was done.

props.caption: Desktop accounting work, the baseline in the comparison. Image: CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Business processes, participants, hardware and network conditions were held constant. Platform was the only variable that changed, which is what makes the comparison meaningful.
What the team found
Time to complete the same tasks differed by platform. The authors conclude that organisations should target mobile or web development rather than a traditional desktop build.

The result is not a clean sweep for either new platform. Web applications came out ahead in certain usage scenarios, while mobile looked stronger in many others. Which one wins depends on what the task involves.

props.caption: A spare parts shop, the setting for the timed tasks. Credit: Visitor7, CC BY-SA 3.0.

content.text: Why it matters

Platform choice is usually settled by habit, or by whatever the vendor already sells. This study suggests it deserves an actual test, and that a desktop first assumption can cost time every working day.

Source: Diana et al. (2023). The Impact of Platform Differences on System Use in Accounting Information System. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology, 439-445. DOI:

article.title: Design Thinking untuk Layanan Home Care Rumah Sakit
article.subtitle: Lima tahap kerja yang mengubah keluhan pasien dan perawat menjadi dua prototipe aplikasi.

content.text: Merancang aplikasi kesehatan sering gagal di tahap yang sama: tim melompat ke solusi sebelum memahami masalahnya. Sebuah penelitian di Rumah Sakit Semen Gresik mencoba urutan yang sebaliknya. Tim memulai dari pengguna, bukan dari fitur.

props.caption: Sesi kerja Design Thinking. Foto: Corinna Schuster, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Konteksnya nyata. Layanan home care pasien di rumah menjadi tumpuan ketika kunjungan langsung ke rumah sakit turun tajam pada masa pandemi, dari lebih dari 600 menjadi sekitar 200 kunjungan per hari. Pertanyaannya bukan bagaimana membuat aplikasi, melainkan bagaimana membuat perawatan di rumah berjalan lebih rapi.
Lima tahap yang dijalankan
Empathize: tim menggali keluhan dan kebiasaan pasien maupun tenaga kesehatan.
Define: temuan itu dirumuskan menjadi masalah yang jelas dan terbatas.
Ideate: solusi dikumpulkan sebelum dipilih yang paling masuk akal.
Prototype: rancangan diwujudkan menjadi aplikasi HomeCare dan HomeCare Giver.
Test: prototipe diuji ke pengguna dengan User Experience Questionnaire.

props.caption: Alur tahapan Design Thinking. Gambar: PowerlockeDurim, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Tahap empati menghasilkan satu keputusan penting: pengguna tidak tunggal. Pasien dan tenaga kesehatan menghadapi masalah yang berbeda, sehingga keduanya memerlukan aplikasi sendiri. Keputusan itu bukan hasil brainstorming, melainkan hasil pengamatan.

Pada tahap uji, tanggapannya positif. Aplikasi untuk pasien mendapat nilai baik di hampir semua skala pengalaman pengguna, dengan ketepatan sebagai skala terkuat. Aplikasi untuk tenaga kesehatan juga positif, dengan daya tarik dan kebaruan menonjol. Artinya, versi sederhana dari app yang berjalan sudah layak dikembangkan lebih jauh.

Yang bisa dipelajari dari studi ini bukan hanya hasilnya, tetapi langkah-langkahnya. Lima tahap itu memberi jalan yang dapat diikuti tim lain, sekaligus menjaga agar keputusan desain tetap bisa dipertanggungjawabkan di depan pemangku kepentingan rumah sakit. Catatan pentingnya, penilaian hanya melibatkan satu rumah sakit, jadi temuan ini sebaiknya diperlakukan sebagai titik awal, bukan patokan akhir.

Sumber: Isadora, Hanggara, dan Mursityo (2021). Perancangan User Experience pada Aplikasi Mobile HomeCare Rumah Sakit Semen Gresik Menggunakan Metode Design Thinking. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: Merancang Aplikasi Home Care dari Sisi Pasien
article.subtitle: Penilaian pengalaman pengguna pada dua aplikasi layanan rumah menunjukkan di mana penggunanya paling puas.

content.text: Rumah Sakit Semen Gresik memiliki layanan home care, yaitu perawatan pasien yang dilakukan di rumah. Selama pandemi COVID-19, kunjungan pasien ke rumah sakit turun dari lebih dari 600 orang per hari menjadi sekitar 200 orang. Layanan di rumah pun menjadi semakin penting.

props.caption: Perawatan pasien oleh tenaga kesehatan. Sumber: National Library of New Zealand, tanpa batasan, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Untuk mendukung layanan itu, sebuah penelitian merancang pengalaman pengguna aplikasi mobile home care dengan pendekatan Design Thinking. Prosesnya melewati lima tahap: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, dan test. Hasilnya dua aplikasi, yaitu HomeCare untuk pasien dan HomeCare Giver untuk tenaga kesehatan.
Cara penggunaannya dinilai

Setelah prototipe selesai, penilaian dilakukan memakai User Experience Questionnaire. Alat ukur ini membagi pengalaman pengguna ke enam skala: daya tarik, kejelasan, efisiensi, ketepatan, stimulasi, dan kebaruan. Kedua aplikasi dinilai secara terpisah oleh penggunanya masing-masing.
Aplikasi HomeCare untuk pasien mendapat nilai positif di seluruh skala.
Hampir semua skalanya dinilai baik, dengan ketepatan atau dependability berada di tingkat sangat baik.
Aplikasi HomeCare Giver untuk tenaga kesehatan juga positif, dengan daya tarik dan kebaruan sebagai skala terkuat.

props.caption: Tahapan Design Thinking. Gambar: PowerlockeDurim, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Bagi pasien, aplikasi seperti ini mengubah cara mengakses perawatan. Alih-alih menunggu di ruang tunggu, pasien dapat melihat jadwal kunjungan perawat, memantau kondisi, dan berkomunikasi dengan tenaga kesehatan dari rumah. Bagi perawat, aplikasi terpisah membantu mencatat kunjungan dan riwayat pasien tanpa bergantung pada berkas kertas.

Yang menarik, pendekatan yang dipakai menempatkan kebutuhan pengguna di awal, bukan daftar fitur. Tim lebih dulu memahami rutinitas pasien dan tenaga kesehatan, lalu menentukan masalah yang layak diselesaikan. Cara berpikir inilah yang menjelaskan mengapa dua aplikasi perlu dibuat, bukan satu aplikasi untuk semua peran.

Hasil penelitian ini juga punya batas. Penilaiannya memakai kuesioner di satu rumah sakit, sehingga angkanya menggambarkan persepsi responden di sana. Meski begitu, polanya berguna bagi tim yang sedang membangun layanan kesehatan digital: pisahkan kebutuhan pasien dan tenaga kesehatan, lalu uji dengan pengguna sungguhan sebelum menambah fitur.

Sumber: Isadora, Hanggara, dan Mursityo (2021). Perancangan User Experience pada Aplikasi Mobile HomeCare Rumah Sakit Semen Gresik Menggunakan Metode Design Thinking. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: Why Depth-First Search Was the Right Call Here
article.subtitle: The planner behind a mikrolet route service traded optimal paths for rules that were easy to change.

content.text: Depth-first search has a mixed reputation in routing. It does not guarantee the shortest path, and on a dense network it can wander down long branches before finding anything useful. When a team picks it anyway for a public transport trip planner, the reason is worth understanding.

props.caption: A schematic route map for a proposed rail scheme. Image: Sagredo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: In the Malang mikrolet study, the authors are upfront about the trade. They chose depth-first search because it is relatively simple to modify, and the routing rules for paratransit were still being worked out. Producing correct plans mattered more, at that stage, than shaving milliseconds.
Wrapping it as a service

The other half of the design is where the plans live. Rather than baking routing into a phone app, the team exposed it as a REST web service in a location-based style. A request carries an origin and a destination. A response carries candidate journeys.
REST keeps routing logic in one place instead of shipping it in every client.
A request is only coordinates, so an app, a web page, or a kiosk can share one endpoint.
The client can change without touching the planner.

props.caption: Mikrolet routes are informal and hard to look up. Image: Annidafattiya, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Functional testing confirmed the plans came out as expected. That is a modest but real milestone, because a route planner that returns plausible but wrong itineraries is worse than no planner at all.
The honest limitation

The same choice that made the planner easy to modify makes it expensive to scale. As routes and possible plans multiply, the search slows down, and the authors flag optimization as the next step. Depth-first search was a fair call for a prototype. The paper does not pretend it will carry the system forever.

For anyone sitting on legacy transport data, the order of operations is the lesson. Ship something correct on a simple foundation, learn what riders actually need, and optimize once you know which problem you are solving.

Source: Kharisma and Pinandito (2019). Prototype of REST Location-based Service for Trip Planning by Paratransit (Mikrolet) in Malang City. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: The Test Two Weeks Later Tells the Real Story
article.subtitle: Immediate scores flatter almost everyone. Retention is where teaching methods separate.

content.text: An immediate post-test is a generous instrument. Students have just finished the activity, the material is still warm in memory, and almost any method looks effective. A delayed test does not have that luxury. It asks what actually survived.

props.caption: A mind map, a close relative of the concept map. Image: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: That is why the design of this study is worth noting. Both groups were tested right after the mapping activity and then again 14 days later, with the same questions shuffled into a different order. The shuffle matters. It stops students who memorized the sequence from looking better than students who understood the content.
Both groups forgot. One stayed ahead.

Neither group held its immediate score. The control group fell from 81.02 to 69.91. The experimental group fell from 87.50 to 78.57. Both declines were statistically significant, which is the ordinary shape of forgetting.
Control group, open ended mapping: 81.02 immediate, 69.91 delayed.
Experimental group, kit-build mapping: 87.50 immediate, 78.57 delayed.

props.caption: Concept maps group related propositions into clusters. Image: Dr. Mahesh Koltame, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The interesting part is not that scores fell. It is that the ranking did not change. Whatever the kit-build group gained during the activity, they kept relative to the other group. That is a stronger claim than a single post-test can support.
What this means for teaching

If you are choosing a learning activity, an immediate quiz will rarely help you choose well, because most activities pass it. A delayed quiz costs one extra session and tells you whether the activity built something durable. The gains here also concentrated on content students had to reconstruct rather than read.

props.caption: Students reviewing notes after an activity. Image: Onwuka Glory, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The honest caveat is scale. Fifty-five students in one course is a single data point, and the paper notes that retention has been under examined for extension mapping. This is a good argument for running delayed tests more often, not a final answer.
Source: Prasetya et al. (2022). Investigating the memory retention in extension concept mapping. Improving Assessment and Evaluation Strategies on Online Learning. DOI:

article.title: When a Bigger Concept Map Is Not a Better One
article.subtitle: Counting nodes is easy to grade and easy to game. Proposition quality is harder and more useful.

content.text: Ask a teacher to rank two concept maps and the instinct is to count. More nodes, more links, more visible work. The study behind this article suggests that instinct is unreliable.

The team compared two extension concept mapping methods with 55 students. One let students build freely. The other had them recompose a teacher's map from a fixed kit of components, then extend it. The second produced higher quality propositions even though students wrote fewer of them.
Why size misleads

A map can be large and still be wrong. Propositions can be scientifically meaningless, or can link two ideas that do not belong together. Counting treats every statement as equal, and the authors argue that the quality of the interrelationships between concepts is what carries the learning signal.

props.caption: A colorful map, but is it right? Credit: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: There is a practical consequence. If size is the metric in a rubric, students learn to pad the map, and the padding looks like progress right up until they are asked to explain it.
What the recomposition step appears to do

In the kit-build condition, students first rebuild the teacher's map from provided parts. That step forces attention onto how an expert connects ideas, before the student adds anything of their own. It is a rehearsal of structure, not just a task.

props.caption: Concept mapping is usually a classroom activity. Credit: Kambai Akau, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: The perceptions data supports that reading. Students rated the kit-build tool higher on ease of use and usefulness, and reported a stronger intention to keep using it. The authors single out the recomposition step as the part that makes the activity feel workable.
What this changes in a classroom

Grade the quality of the propositions, not the number. Give students an expert structure to rebuild before asking them to extend anything. And expect a good map to look smaller than a free-form attempt, because a clear structure does not need filler.
Source: Prasetya et al. (2022). Analysis of quality of knowledge structure and students' perceptions in extension concept mapping. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 17(14). DOI:

article.title: A Tool That Suggests Concepts While Teachers Build a Map
article.subtitle: Semi-automatic concept mapping left teachers with bigger maps and no loss of quality in a trial with 47 English teachers.

content.text: In a Kit-Build classroom the teacher's concept map is the lesson plan. Students rebuild it from a set of parts, and the gap between their map and the teacher's shows what they missed. That makes the teacher's map important, and expensive to produce.

A team at Hiroshima University and Universitas Brawijaya built a support tool to reduce that cost. Instead of asking teachers to write every concept and link by hand, the tool reads the English passage and proposes candidates.
How the suggestions are made

The tool runs the passage through the Stanford CoreNLP toolkit, which splits sentences, tags parts of speech and extracts open information triples. A rule based step on the part-of-speech sequence pulls out verb and verb-noun phrases as candidate relationships. The teacher keeps the useful ones and discards the rest.

props.caption: The tool works from a reading passage of about 300 words. Credit: Knowledge and philosophy, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: The word semi-automatic is doing real work here. Nothing is decided for the teacher, and no map is generated from start to finish. The tool offers material, and a person who knows the class decides what belongs in the lesson.

props.caption: A map is a judgement about what matters, not a word list. Credit: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: What the trial showed

Forty-seven English teachers and tutors in Malang, East Java, mapped two intermediate reading passages twice, once with the plain tool and once with the supported one. Statistical analysis found that the tool had a significant effect on how many propositions ended up in the map.

Maps grew. Quality did not shrink. Independent tests on map scores came out slightly in favour of the supported tool, and the difference reached significance in three of four conditions. The authors sum it up as better efficiency at a similar level of quality.
Source: Pinandito et al. (2021). Design and development of semi-automatic concept map authoring support tool. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 16(8). DOI:

article.title: Concept Map Recomposition and Higher Order Thinking
article.subtitle: Fifty four students, two ways of building a map, and one clear difference.

content.text: A concept map is only useful if it makes the learner think. Draw one from scratch with the textbook open and it is easy to copy a diagram without processing it. The Kit Build method removes that shortcut. Students assemble a map from a fixed set of concepts and linking phrases, so the result reflects what they actually understand.

props.caption: A concept map of water patterns on Earth. Image: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A study of 54 undergraduates compared that approach against ordinary scratch mapping. Both groups studied the same material and both sat a test before and after, so the comparison came down to how students built the map rather than what they were taught.
Two ways to build a map

In scratch mapping, students draw freely. The map can be excellent, but nothing forces them to connect every idea, and quiet gaps are hard to spot. In Kit Build mapping, the concepts and linking phrases arrive as separate pieces. Students decide which pieces belong together, and the result can be checked against an expert map automatically.
Scratch mapping: free form, familiar, and hard to grade consistently.
Kit Build mapping: constrained, comparable, and checkable by software.

props.caption: Nodes and phrases forming a single map. Image: Zulayho Matjanova, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the numbers showed

On higher order thinking, the Kit Build group finished ahead. The gap was moderate in size but statistically significant, so it is unlikely to be noise from the sample. On the lower order questions, the two groups ended close together.

Both groups improved between the first test and the second, which is what any teacher would hope for. The difference sits in where the improvement landed. Kit Build students gained more on questions that ask them to reason with the material, not simply recall it.

The authors also checked the maps themselves. Recomposition scores tracked the later test results, so a well built map was a decent signal of how well a student had grasped the topic. That link is what makes automatic scoring worth anything.
One topic and one cohort of 54 students is a modest base, so treat the size of the effect as a hint rather than a fixed number. The direction is the useful part.
Source: Nurmaya et al. (2023). Promoting Students' Higher Order Thinking with Concept Map Recomposition. IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems. DOI:

article.title: Collaborative Concept Mapping Across Two Screens
article.subtitle: Pairs of graduate students built maps together from separate rooms, and the arrangement held up.

content.text: Distance learning has a habit of turning group work into a shared document with three names on it. Building a concept map together is harder, because the point of the exercise is the argument a pair has about how ideas connect.

A 2020 study tested whether that argument survives when the two people are not in the same room. Forty international graduate students worked in pairs, each partner at a separate computer in a separate room, to imitate a real distance course.
How the session ran

The study used a tool that fuses collaborative learning into the Kit Build concept map framework, letting two learners work on the same map in real time from a distance. The sequence of the session was deliberately simple.

props.caption: A concept map with labelled links between ideas. Image: Komila Olimova, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A pre-test recorded what each pair already understood about the reading material.
The pair then mapped the material together, with one condition drawing freely and the other reassembling components supplied by the teacher.
A post-test followed immediately, and a delayed test came ten days later to see what remained.

props.caption: A hand drawn map of connected ideas. Photo: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the pairs showed

A Wilcoxon paired test on the results showed that learning collaboratively with the Kit Build map significantly improved the students' understanding of the material, with the effect holding at a strong level of significance. The team concluded that the online collaborative approach is effective for learning, whether a pair maps freely or rebuilds a supplied structure.

props.caption: Students working together on study material. Photo: KalvinKalvin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: For anyone running a distance course, the useful part is the setup rather than the software. The partners never shared a room, and the collaboration still produced a measurable gain, which suggests that the social part of group work travels over a network better than it is usually given credit for.
Source: Pinandito, Hayashi and Hirashima (2020). Online Collaborative Kit-Build Concept Map. Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2020).

article.title: Choosing a Platform for an Outdoor AR Navigation App
article.subtitle: What a running load comparison between Unity and native Android means for a build decision.

content.text: Every team building a walking navigation app with augmented reality hits the same fork early. Build directly on ARCore in native Android, or work through Unity and lean on the engine tooling. Both routes ship an app. The question is what each costs the device.

props.caption: Augmented signage on a city street. Image: Bernd Schwabe, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A research team answered that with a controlled comparison. They implemented one location based AR navigation prototype for outdoor pedestrians, then built it again on the other stack. Both versions used ARCore and handled the same navigation job, so the measured difference came from the platform rather than the feature set.
The trade in plain terms

The native build won on running load. It kept the AR view alive while drawing less from the phone, which is the difference between an app you can use on a twenty minute walk and one you have to close early. The engine build carried extra weight, since an engine is a general purpose runtime sitting between the app and the hardware.
Pick native Android for long sessions on everyday phones.
Pick Unity when the same content has to reach several platforms with rich 3D assets.

props.caption: A phone measuring a room with AR. Image: Fmalka, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How to use a result like this

Treat it as a direction, not a verdict. The comparison used one prototype and one generation of ARCore, and running load shifts with every phone model and OS update. If the audience carries mid range handsets, benchmark both stacks on those exact devices before committing.
Measure on the weakest device you intend to support.
Test outdoors, under real light and motion, not on a desk.

There is also a middle path. A team can prototype in Unity to iterate quickly on look and feel, then move the parts that matter to a native build once the design settles. The study does not test that route, but it explains why the final step is worth taking.

The headline finding is simple enough to act on. For an outdoor AR walking app, the platform choice shows up directly in how much the phone has to work, and that cost lands on the user every minute the camera is on.

Source: Komang Candra Brata et al. (2023). An investigation of running load comparisons of ARCore on native Android and Unity for outdoor navigation system using smartphone. 2023 Sixth International Conference on Vocational Education and Electrical Engineering (ICVEE). DOI:

article.title: Catatan Puskesmas dan Masa Depan Skrining Kehamilan
article.subtitle: Pelajaran praktis dari model KNN yang dibangun di atas 16 atribut pemeriksaan.

content.text: Setiap ibu hamil yang datang memeriksakan diri meninggalkan jejak berupa catatan. Selama ini catatan itu hanya dibaca satu per satu oleh tenaga kesehatan. Penelitian tentang deteksi risiko diabetes melitus pada kehamilan menunjukkan bahwa tumpukan catatan tersebut bisa diolah lebih jauh menjadi peringatan dini.
Kekuatan ada pada datanya

Tim memakai 248 catatan pemeriksaan dari Puskesmas Lawang dan menyaring 16 atribut yang dianggap paling berpengaruh. Sebagian besar atribut itu sudah rutin dicatat, seperti usia ibu, usia kehamilan, indeks massa tubuh, dan hasil skrining penyakit menular.
Data yang dipakai bukan data baru. Semuanya berasal dari pemeriksaan yang memang sudah berjalan.
Kelengkapan pengisian menentukan hasil. Satu kolom yang kosong bisa mengubah posisi sebuah data di ruang atribut.

props.caption: Alat ukur glukosa sederhana yang dipakai di layanan primer. Foto: Christidy, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: KNN sebagai pilihan yang ringan

K-Nearest Neighbor dipilih karena sederhana. Model ini tidak perlu proses pelatihan yang berat, cukup menyimpan data dan menghitung jarak ke tetangga terdekat saat ada data baru masuk. Untuk fasilitas kesehatan dengan perangkat terbatas, pendekatan seperti ini lebih realistis daripada model yang menuntut komputasi besar.
Akurasi terbaik yang dicapai adalah 78,38 persen pada k=4 dengan rasio data latih dan uji 7:3.
Nilai k yang terlalu kecil membuat model sensitif terhadap data pencilan, sedangkan k yang terlalu besar membuat batas antar kelas kabur.

props.caption: Pemeriksaan gula darah di layanan kesehatan komunitas. Foto: Roy Zuo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Yang belum selesai

Angka 78,38 persen berasal dari 248 data dan satu lokasi. Jumlah sebesar itu cukup untuk membuktikan konsep, tetapi belum cukup untuk dijadikan alat bantu keputusan resmi. Diperlukan data dari lebih banyak puskesmas, penanganan data kosong yang baku, dan pengujian ulang pada populasi yang berbeda.

Yang menarik, riset ini memperlihatkan bahwa nilai tambah terbesar bukan pada algoritmanya, melainkan pada disiplin pencatatan. Selama tenaga kesehatan mengisi data dengan rapi, model sederhana pun bisa memberi manfaat.

Sumber: Aryo Pinandito, Satrio Agung Wicaksono, dan Satrio Hadi Wijoyo (2023). Implementasi Machine Learning Dalam Deteksi Risiko Tinggi Diabetes Melitus Pada Kehamilan. Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Ilmu Komputer. DOI:

article.title: Bounding boxes along a route, now as an Android library
article.subtitle: RouteBoxer takes a route and a distance and returns a small set of rectangles that cover everything nearby.

content.text: A navigation app spends a lot of time answering questions about proximity. Which restaurants sit near this route? Which drivers are close to the path? Testing every candidate against a long polyline is slow, and most spatial indexes cannot help with a line shape.

RouteBoxer turns that line problem into a rectangle problem. Hand it a route and a distance, and it returns a set of bounding boxes that cover the area within that distance of the route. From there a database can filter on boxes before anything precise runs.

props.caption: A route sign at dawn. A route becomes a set of rectangles for spatial queries. Photo: ZeLonewolf, CC0.

content.text: How the boxes are built
Take the bounding box of the whole route and extend it by one grid cell in every direction.
Overlay a grid of square cells across that area, where the cell size follows the distance you asked for.
Mark every cell that intersects a vertex of the route, along with the eight cells surrounding it.
Merge the marked cells into as few non overlapping rectangles as the shape allows.
The merge step is where the practical value sits. Fewer rectangles means fewer lookups later, so the output is a compact cover of the corridor rather than a raw pile of grid squares.

props.caption: A road network from map data. Route corridors drive spatial queries. Map data: OpenStreetMap, CC BY-SA 2.0.

content.text: Why it was ported to Android

RouteBoxer was originally a helper for maps in the browser. The authors ported it to Android because mobile developers had no equivalent, building the work on the Google Maps Android API inside Android Studio and shipping it as a library. It can be added to a project either as a compiled library file or as a source module.

One property of the algorithm deserves attention before use. The authors report that the number of generated boxes grows exponentially as the distance increases. A wider corridor is not a little more expensive, it is a lot more, so the distance parameter and the grid resolution are the two knobs to watch.

props.caption: A phone showing a route on a map. Boxes are what the app queries against. Photo: Santeri Viinamaki, CC BY-SA 4.0.

content.text: Source: Pinandito, A., Saputra, M.C., Perdana, R.S. (2016). RouteBoxer library for Google Android platform. 2016 IEEE Asia Pacific Conference on Wireless and Mobile (APWiMob). DOI:

article.title: When the Standard Design Pattern Stops Fitting
article.subtitle: MVC assumes one application and one set of users. A framework design study shows what to add when neither holds.

content.text: There is a moment in every framework project when the team realises the standard pattern does not cover what the business actually does. The instinct is to start over. A study from Universitas Brawijaya argues for a smaller move.

Their starting point is ordinary. Web applications are the practical answer when units inside an organisation keep changing how they work. Information systems sit at the centre of that, supporting processes that shift as the organisation does.
Where the standard pattern runs out

Model-View-Controller is popular for good reasons. Splitting an application into model, view and controller makes the parts reusable and maintainable, and it keeps a change in one place from rippling into the others.

props.caption: Processes cross desks, and so must software. Image: Tyne and Wear Archives and Museums, no known restrictions.

content.text: Two things are missing. One is business process choreography, the coordination of steps that span more than one system. The other is integration between applications. Neither is a display problem, so neither belongs neatly in the view or the controller.
What the team changed
Add a role rather than remove one. The CollectionService carries inter-application data exchange, a job MVC never assigned to anyone.
Split responsibility in the controller. A Presenter absorbs part of the work so the controller is not doing two jobs at once.
Keep the known parts recognisable. Developers who already understand MVC should be able to read the new pattern without starting from zero.

props.caption: One foundation, several applications sharing it. Credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/T. Slovinsky, CC BY 4.0.

content.text: The wider lesson is about how to touch a design pattern at all. Changing how objects of a class interact is exactly the kind of edit that breaks assumptions across a codebase, so the team's proposed pattern is a derivation, not a rewrite.

Source: Aryo Pinandito, Ferdika Bagus Pristiawan Permana and Rizal Setya Perdana (2017). Framework Design for Modular Web-based Application Using Model-CollectionService-Controller-Presenter (MCCP) Pattern. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science, 2(1), 41-65. DOI:

article.title: Can Software Grade a Concept Map as Well as a Teacher
article.subtitle: Automatic scoring removes the slowest part of using concept maps in class.

content.text: Marking concept maps by hand is slow, subjective, and the reason plenty of teachers quietly stop assigning them. The Kit Build approach sidesteps part of that. Because students rebuild a map from a fixed set of concepts and links, software can compare the result against the expert map and score it without a person reading every proposition.

props.caption: A mind map of related topics. Image: Supriyabah, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A 2023 study put that automatic scoring to the test. The authors asked two things: whether better maps, as the software measures them, go together with stronger higher order thinking, and whether machine scores agree with the scores a human assessor produces.
Why manual scoring is the bottleneck

Assessing a concept map means judging structure, accuracy, and completeness at once. It is defensible work, but it does not scale. A stack of thirty maps can eat an evening, and by the time the marks come back the class has moved to another topic.
Feedback arrives too late to change how students revise.
Different markers can read the same map differently.

props.caption: Ideas arranged around one central topic. Image: Tanjatod, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the comparison showed

The automatic scores held up against manual assessment closely enough that the authors describe the method as promising. Better map quality also went hand in hand with better answers on higher order questions, which is the outcome the assessment is meant to predict.

That combination is what makes the result useful. Scoring a map the moment it is finished gives students a signal while the material is still fresh, and it returns to teachers the hours that marking would have taken.

The study does not claim software should replace a teacher's judgement, and it does not try to score the ideas a student brings that were never in the expert map. What it shows is narrower and more practical: for this kind of closed mapping task, the automatic score is good enough to act on.

Source: Nurmaya et al. (2023). Investigation of the Relationship Between Map Quality and Higher-Order Thinking in Kit-Build Concept Map. Human Interface and the Management of Information, Lecture Notes in Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Putting Bus Stops Directly on the Phone Camera
article.subtitle: An Android app that answers the only question a lost passenger has.

content.text: Standing at an unfamiliar bus stop, the hard part is often working out where you are and which service to take. A 2015 project put that answer onto the phone camera, so nearby stops appear as labels over the street.

props.caption: A bus shelter on a city street. Image: Lapot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The app is called BusAR, an Android application for bus route planning built around augmented reality. Instead of asking a passenger to read a list of stops, it overlays the nearby ones onto the live camera view and guides the walk to the stop they need.
What runs under the interface

Position comes from the phone sensors: GPS for location, plus the magnetometer, accelerometer, and gyroscope for direction and orientation. Route data arrives from bus and directions services over a standard web interface, and distances are worked out with the great circle formula.
The camera view shows stops, not a map to interpret.
A compass arrow points toward the next waypoint.

props.caption: An augmented reality overlay in use. Image: Kippelboy, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Why it is worth the trouble

The authors point to a practical motivation. Most foreign visitors who need directions end up asking at an information desk, and the paper cites a figure of 65 percent for Taipei. Turning the phone into the guide removes that trip.
It is also light on data. The team measured an average of about 0.25 kilobytes per second, a fraction of what comparable route planning apps used in the same tests.

Testing happened outdoors in real conditions rather than on a desk, which is the right way to judge a walking aid. Uneven light, moving traffic, and drifting sensors are the conditions that break these apps.
Source: Brata, Liang, and Pramono (2015). Location-Based Augmented Reality Information for Bus Route Planning System. International Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering.

article.title: ARCore on Native Android and Unity: Which Runs Lighter Outdoors
article.subtitle: Two builds of the same walking navigation app, measured side by side on a phone.

content.text: Outdoor augmented reality navigation is a tough test for a phone. The camera runs constantly, sensors feed the orientation, and anchors have to stay stuck to real places while the user walks. Developers building these apps face an early decision: use ARCore directly in native Android, or work through a game engine such as Unity.

props.caption: A location based AR view running on a phone. Image: Mimzy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A group of researchers put both approaches on the same footing. They built a location based AR prototype for outdoor pedestrian navigation twice, once in Unity and once as a native Android app, both powered by ARCore. Then they ran the two builds through the same outdoor scenarios and watched how hard each one worked the device.
What they measured

The comparison focused on running load, the cost of keeping a live AR view alive while the phone also handles tracking and rendering. That load is what a user feels as heat, battery drain, and slowdowns when the camera pans across a busy street.
Same ARCore features, same navigation task, two development stacks.
Evaluated outdoors, where tracking and lighting are unpredictable.

props.caption: An Android handset and its case. Image: Acabashi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How the two stacks compared

The native Android build came out ahead. It delivered the same augmented walking experience while asking less of the hardware, which is exactly the property that decides whether an app survives a long walk in the sun. The Unity build still worked, and it brought its own advantages.
Native Android: better performance and more efficient use of device resources.
Unity: multi platform reach and an easier path to complex 3D content.

The authors frame the result as a trade rather than a winner. The engine layer that makes Unity pleasant for 3D work also sits between the app and the device, and that shows up in running load once ARCore is tracking continuously outdoors.

The practical reading for teams is to pick by priority. If the navigation app is the product and it must run long sessions on modest phones, native Android is the safer base. If the project needs to ship widely and leans on heavy 3D assets, Unity earns its overhead.

Source: Komang Candra Brata et al. (2023). An investigation of running load comparisons of ARCore on native Android and Unity for outdoor navigation system using smartphone. 2023 Sixth International Conference on Vocational Education and Electrical Engineering (ICVEE). DOI:

article.title: Ants Versus Dijkstra: Which One Finds the Bus Route?
article.subtitle: A comparison of two routing methods shows that speed and memory pull in different directions.

content.text: Finding a bus route sounds like a solved problem. You know where you are, you know where you want to go, and you want the shortest combination of lines in between. It turns out there is more than one way to compute that answer.

Dijkstra is the classic choice. It expands outward from the starting point until it reaches the destination. Routing software has relied on it for decades because it is reliable and its results are predictable.

Ant colony optimization takes a different path entirely. It borrows the behaviour of real ants, which find short routes by laying down pheromone trails that later ants follow. In software, simulated ants explore a graph repeatedly and the best paths accumulate artificial pheromone.

props.caption: Ant colony optimization borrows the trail behaviour of real ants. Photo: Rajani Gairshail, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How the comparison worked

The study asked a specific question: can ant colony optimization produce recommendations as good as Dijkstra when both get the same resources? The team ran Dijkstra first to establish the best route, then let the ant based method try to match it.
Both algorithms were evaluated on computation time and memory consumption, including the memory allocated at the start and at the end of each run.
Measurements were repeated rather than taken once, so that results could not be distorted by a single unlucky run of the JavaScript garbage collector.

props.caption: Real ants converge on short paths over time. Photo: DEEPAN RAJA .M, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What they found

The ant based approach was more efficient in execution time and in the number of pathways it traversed. The trade-off was memory. The findings suggest that ant colony optimization may need a larger memory budget to deliver the outcomes the researchers were looking for.

props.caption: A network graph of the kind both algorithms search. Image: Logan Essex, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The honest reading is that neither method wins outright. Dijkstra gives a predictable answer with a modest footprint. Ant colony optimization can move faster across a large search space, but it asks for more memory to get there. Which one fits depends on the device and the shape of the network.

Source: Abdul Jabbar and Aryo Pinandito (2023). Recommending Public Transit Route: Ant-Colony Optimization or Dijkstra? 2023 International Conference on Modeling and E-Information Research, Artificial Learning and Digital Applications. DOI:

article.title: MVVM Renders Faster Than MVC in Android Apps
article.subtitle: Two design patterns, one app, the same data. One of them put interface elements on screen faster.

content.text: Design patterns usually get discussed as a matter of code hygiene. Cleaner structure, easier testing, fewer surprises later. A study from Universitas Brawijaya adds a harder number to that conversation. The pattern you pick also changes how quickly your interface appears on screen.

props.caption: An Android development environment. Image: Google LLC, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The team built the same Android application twice, once with MVC and once with MVVM, and measured how long each version took to render its interface. The app was a public transport route navigation tool for Malang, drawing routes from a starting point to a destination using latitude and longitude coordinates.
Keeping the comparison honest

Both versions were tested under identical conditions: the same testing technique, the same three scenarios, and the same point data. That matters, because rendering time is easy to skew if one build is asked to draw more than the other.
MVC and MVVM share one core idea: separating the interface layer from the business logic layer.
MVVM adds data binding, so the view refreshes itself as data arrives.
With MVC, code has to tell the view to refresh, which adds a step.

props.caption: An Android phone with an app on screen. Image: Acabashi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The result favoured MVVM. Its interface rendered faster across the scenarios. The authors credit how well MVVM isolates business logic, which cuts down the delays that appear while a screen waits for data to be ready.
What rendering time means in practice

Rendering time is what users actually feel. A screen that appears a moment later than it should feels heavy, especially on the mid-range devices most people carry. The paper does not argue that MVVM is universally better. It argues that the choice carries a measurable cost, and that it belongs on the list of things worth testing.

props.caption: A phone in use. Responsiveness shapes how heavy an app feels. Image: bohed, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Source: Paramadani, Akbar, and Pinandito (2023). User Interface Rendering Time in Android Applications: Revealing the Effects of Design Patterns. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Learning Java on a Phone: A Mobile Learning Prototype
article.subtitle: An Android app brings guided Java practice to the device students already carry.

content.text: Java is one of the hardest courses in a computer science program, and most tools that help students practice it live on websites and laptops. Practice stops the moment a student walks away from a desk. A team of researchers asked a simple question: can the phone in every pocket carry that practice instead?

props.caption: A smartphone is the device students already carry. Image: Acabashi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Their answer is an Android application built around three parts: learning materials, exercises, and scoring. The app keeps its cloud data in Firebase and mirrors it into a local SQLite database on the device. That mirror is what makes the app useful on a commuter train or in a lecture hall with weak signal, because the material and the quizzes stay reachable without a connection.
How the team designed it
The design did not start from a feature list. The team collected user stories from college students first, then mapped those stories onto screens.
A learning flow that feels obvious from the first tap
Material complete enough to stand on its own
Code exercises paired with worked examples
Self evaluation of code and personal progress tracking

Because a phone screen is small and typing on glass is awkward, the team applied Mayer's multimedia learning principles. Spatial contiguity, modality, and personalization shaped the screens. In practice that means placing a label beside the diagram it explains, narrating instead of crowding the display with text, and writing instructions in a conversational voice.

props.caption: The app focuses on concepts and guided exercises. Image: Martin Vorel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the trial showed

The prototype was tested with students. The team reports that the overall functionality is feasible for future implementation, with a usability score of 84. The authors position the app as an alternative route into Java concepts rather than a replacement for writing code on a desktop.
The claim is modest but practical. Guided practice on a phone can fill the gaps between lab sessions, and the offline copy means those gaps do not have to be spent online.

Source: Komang Candra Brata, Ahmad Afif Supianto, and Fadhyl Farhan Alghifari (2024). Designing an Intuitive Android Based m-Learning to Support Students in Learning Fundamental Java Programming. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: What a Phone Can Teach: Design Lessons from a Java Learning App
article.subtitle: Offline access, small screens, and guided practice shaped a prototype that scored 84 on usability.

content.text: Ask a lecturer why students struggle with Java and the answer rarely involves talent. It usually involves time and access. The desktop lab is open for a few hours, the laptop runs out of battery, and the moment a question appears there is nothing to practice on. An Android learning app studied by a research team takes that gap seriously.

props.caption: The prototype targets the Android platform. Image: Android, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Offline first, cloud second

The most interesting decision in the app is architectural rather than visual. Content lives in Firebase, but a copy is synchronized to SQLite on the handset. The ordering matters. A student on a bus with one bar of signal still opens the material, still answers the quiz, and the app syncs later when the connection returns.

For anyone building learning software for Indonesian campuses, that pattern is worth copying. Connectivity is uneven, data plans are metered, and a tool that fails offline fails exactly when a student has spare time to use it.

props.caption: Small screens force tighter content design. Image: Mictlancihuatl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: A small screen changes how you teach

The team leaned on Mayer's multimedia learning principles to survive the constraints of a handset. Labels sit next to the diagrams they describe. Explanations favor spoken style over dense blocks of text. Instructions address the reader directly. None of these are exotic, but together they turn a cramped screen into something a beginner can follow.

The other design input came from students themselves. Their user stories asked for material that stands alone, examples worth reading, a way to check their own code, and visible progress. Those requests are a useful checklist for any mobile learning project, because they describe what learners reach for when nobody is standing at the whiteboard.
What it changes for students

The prototype earned a usability score of 84 and the team judged the functionality feasible to develop further. The result does not argue that phones should replace labs. It argues that the dead time between sessions is teachable, and that a well designed app can occupy it.

Source: Komang Candra Brata, Ahmad Afif Supianto, and Fadhyl Farhan Alghifari (2024). Designing an Intuitive Android Based m-Learning to Support Students in Learning Fundamental Java Programming. Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science. DOI:

article.title: Design Patterns Are Also a Performance Decision
article.subtitle: Architecture choices usually get argued as matters of taste. On Android, one of them was measured.

content.text: The usual case for design patterns is maintainability. Cleaner separation, easier testing, fewer surprises six months later. A 2023 study on Android interface rendering adds a second ledger to that argument, and it is one teams rarely check.

props.caption: Where the pattern choice gets made. Image: Google LLC, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The team built one Android route navigation app twice, once with MVC and once with MVVM, then timed how long each version took to put its interface on screen. MVVM came out ahead. The reason is mechanical rather than mysterious.
Why data binding pays off

In MVC, the controller has to tell the view to refresh after data arrives. That is an extra hop, and the user waits through it. MVVM binds the view to the data, so the screen redraws itself when the data lands.
MVC keeps interface and logic apart, but refresh stays manual.
MVVM keeps the same separation and makes refresh automatic.
That saved step shows up as rendering time.

props.caption: Rendering time is what the user feels. Image: Acabashi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What to take from it

The study is one comparison, not a verdict. MVVM carries its own costs, including more indirection and a steeper learning curve, and the paper does not claim it wins everywhere. Its claim is narrower and more useful: the pattern is a variable that affects performance, so it should be measured rather than assumed.

That has a practical consequence for how teams benchmark. Fast devices hide rendering delays that mid-range hardware exposes. If you want to know whether your architecture is costing you, test on the phones your users actually carry, running the scenarios they actually run.

Source: Paramadani, Akbar, and Pinandito (2023). User Interface Rendering Time in Android Applications: Revealing the Effects of Design Patterns. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology. DOI:

article.title: Three Ways to Rank a Restaurant List, Compared
article.subtitle: A study in Malang measured accuracy and computation time for AHP, Fuzzy AHP, and AHP TOPSIS on the same recommendation task.

content.text: Picking where to eat sounds trivial until you have to automate it. A recommendation system has to weigh distance, price, and rating at the same time, then produce a ranked list fast enough to be useful on a phone screen.

A study from Brawijaya University compared three multi criteria methods on exactly that task, using 30 real cases from Malang, Indonesia. The methods were plain AHP, Fuzzy AHP, and AHP combined with TOPSIS.
How the three methods differ

AHP breaks a decision into a hierarchy of criteria and alternatives, then derives weights from pairwise comparisons. It is simple and widely used, but its accuracy depends on how consistently those comparisons are filled in.

Fuzzy AHP keeps the same structure but replaces crisp numbers with triangular fuzzy values. Judgments like fairly important or strongly important become ranges rather than single points, which softens the effect of subjective scoring.
AHP TOPSIS splits the job. AHP sets the criteria weights, then TOPSIS ranks the alternatives by their distance from an ideal solution. Its selling point is speed rather than accuracy.

props.caption: An Indonesian rice dish served at a food court. Image: Gunawan Kartapranata, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Accuracy: Fuzzy AHP leads
On the 30 test cases, plain AHP reached 30 percent accuracy. AHP TOPSIS improved that to 40 percent. Fuzzy AHP was clearly ahead at 66.67 percent, more than doubling the baseline.
The authors attribute the gain to the weighting step. Fuzzy values handle vagueness in human judgment better than fixed numbers, so the criteria weights land closer to what users actually mean.
Time complexity: AHP TOPSIS wins

On a phone, computation cost is a first class concern. AHP and Fuzzy AHP both grow on the order of mn squared, where m is the number of criteria and n the number of alternatives. AHP TOPSIS grows quadratically in n, and it came out fastest in a simulation with three criteria and 50 to 150 menu options.

props.caption: A warung, a small Indonesian food stall. Image: Rafidaslam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The authors conclude that all three methods are workable for a mobile culinary app. The choice depends on what you are short of. If accuracy matters most, Fuzzy AHP is the pick. If the device is slow or the list is long, AHP TOPSIS is the safer bet.
Source: Dewi et al. (2018). A Comparison Between AHP and Hybrid AHP for Mobile Based Culinary Recommendation System. International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies. DOI:

article.title: Weighing Up Where to Eat, One Comparison at a Time
article.subtitle: An Android recommendation system applied a decision science method to a problem people solve badly every day.

content.text: Where to eat is a decision with too many inputs. Price matters, but so does distance. A high rating is worth something, until the queue outside makes it worthless. People weigh these factors differently on different days and rarely agree with each other.

A team at Universitas Brawijaya built an Android application to handle that weighing. Their approach rests on the Analytical Hierarchy Process, a method for turning messy multi-criteria decisions into a ranked list.
How the method works

AHP starts by breaking a decision into criteria. Then it asks a simple question over and over: which of these two matters more, and by how much? Answering hundreds of small comparisons is far easier than assigning absolute scores, and the answers combine into a weight for each criterion.

props.caption: Reading a menu is the easy part. Choosing between two places is harder. Image: Jakub Kapusnak, CC0.

content.text: The method also checks itself. Once the comparisons are in, AHP calculates whether the answers contradict each other, and flags a set of judgements that cannot all be true. That consistency check is what separates it from simply averaging a survey.
Why a phone

The decision happens while standing on a street, not at a desk. Building the system on Google Android puts it where the question is asked, and a smartphone already carries one of the criteria that matters most: location.

props.caption: A phone knows where you are, which is half of the decision. Credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0.

content.text: The paper sits at the start of a line of work from the same group on mobile culinary recommendation, which later compared AHP against hybrid variants. Matching what a human expert would pick stayed the difficult part throughout.

Source: Aryo Pinandito, Chandrawati Putri Wulandari and Ratih Kartika Dewi (2015). Culinary Recommendation Systems Using Analytical Hierarchy Process on Google Android Platform. International Conference on Engineering and Information Technology (ICEIT).

article.title: Locking a Chat App with AES and Layered Hashing
article.subtitle: A prototype pairs standard AES encryption with several layers of MD5 hashing to protect the key, not the message.

content.text: When you send a private message, the app carrying it can usually read it. That is the uncomfortable starting point for a 2018 study on chat privacy.

The paper argues that social media platforms sit in a position to share user data with other parties, including governments, through formal legal requests. Protection against an outside attacker is a well studied problem. Protection against the platform itself is harder, because the platform runs the software.
The design the team proposed

The proposed system encrypts chat content with AES and protects the key with several layers of MD5 hashing. The split matters. AES does the heavy lifting on the message, while the hashing protects the secret that makes the message readable.

props.caption: Sending a message from a phone is the everyday case studied here. Photo: StockyPics, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Key generation is deliberately simple. The app draws sixteen random numbers between 10 and 99 to form a 32 digit manipulation key, then converts pairs of digits into characters to produce the real key used for AES. Distribution is where the layering earns its place. The manipulation key is passed through multiple rounds of MD5 using private values that only the application knows, so only the recipient can recover it and decrypt the conversation.

props.caption: Layered protection is the core idea behind the proposed chat design. Photo: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: How it performed

The team tested the prototype on a deliberately modest Android phone with messages growing from 1 to 1000 characters. Encryption ranged from about 1.5 to 12.1 milliseconds, and decryption from 2.1 to 25.3 milliseconds. At the longest message, encryption took 12.1 milliseconds and decryption 25.3 milliseconds.

props.caption: The prototype was benchmarked on low end Android hardware. Photo: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Those numbers sit comfortably under the 100 millisecond threshold usually cited for interface responsiveness. The security work does not make the chat feel slow, even on hardware that was already old when the study was published.

The interesting lesson is structural. The cryptographic primitive is standard and well understood. The design effort went into key handling, because that is where a chat system is most likely to leak.
Source: Wardhono et al. (2018). End-to-End Privacy Protection for Facebook Mobile Chat based on AES with Multi-Layered MD5. International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies. DOI:

article.title: Giving Old Course Material a Second Life on Phones
article.subtitle: A three stage pipeline extracts, transcodes and republishes legacy e-learning content for mobile devices.

content.text: Universities accumulate course material the way attics accumulate boxes. Lecture recordings, slide decks and interactive packages pile up over the years, built for whatever computer was standard at the time.

The problem is that most of that content was authored for a personal computer. A composite package that mixes video, slides and animation may simply not open on a phone, which is the device most students actually carry.
A three stage pipeline
The proposed method takes old composite e-learning content and prepares it for mobile delivery in three stages.

props.caption: Course material built for a desktop computer. Photo: LeanForward lf, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: Extraction. The system reads the original package and pulls out its parts, including presentation slides, images and video.
Transcoding. Media that phones cannot play is converted into a format they can handle.
Regeneration. The pieces are reassembled and served as a web service that a smartphone application can consume.

props.caption: Students in a classroom, the audience the pipeline is built for. Photo: Esthee2010, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: What the test showed

The team ran the pipeline on composite content built with Microsoft Producer. Extraction succeeded on all of the sample content, and the regenerated material was accessible from the mobile application. A usability test returned an acceptance score of 94%.

props.caption: Reusing old material avoids rebuilding courses from scratch. Photo: KalvinKalvin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.text: The appeal of this approach is that it does not ask anyone to rewrite old course material. It treats existing content as an asset and adds a conversion layer in front of it, which is usually far cheaper than starting over.

Source: Herman Toile, Kohei Arai, and Aryo Pinandito (2014). Adaptation of composite E-Learning contents for reusable in smartphone based learning system. 2014 International Conference on Advanced Computer Science and Information Systems. DOI:

article.title: What Platform Choice Costs an Accounting Team
article.subtitle: A three platform experiment points to mobile and web, but the more useful finding is how the team measured it.

content.text: Most companies do not choose a platform for their accounting system. They inherit one. The system arrives on the desktops in the office, people learn it, and the question is never asked again.

A study from Universitas Brawijaya put that question to the test. The team built the same accounting system for desktop, mobile and web, then timed seven employees at a spare parts distributor in Surabaya as they worked through the same tasks on each.
What the timing showed

Time to complete a task, measured in seconds, varied with the platform. The authors recommend building for mobile or web rather than desktop. They are careful not to crown a single winner: web had the edge in some scenarios and mobile in many others.

props.caption: A spare parts counter, where the tasks were timed. Credit: Visitor7, CC BY-SA 3.0.

content.text: That split is the useful part. Typing a long invoice at a desk and checking a stock figure on the warehouse floor are different jobs, and they do not share a best platform.
How to run the same test in house
Train people first. The study gave 15 minutes of training per platform to keep the learning effect out of the numbers.
Repeat the task. Each measurement ran five times, so one slow attempt could not shape the conclusion.
Hold everything else still. Business process, participants, hardware and network stayed constant.
Time the real work. The metric was seconds to finish an actual business process, not a satisfaction score.

props.caption: Accounting work is repeated daily, so seconds add up. Credit: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0.

content.text: The cost of building three versions is real. The team needed about three months to develop all three, which is the strongest argument for testing before committing to a platform strategy rather than after.

Source: Diana et al. (2023). The Impact of Platform Differences on System Use in Accounting Information System. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Sustainable Information Engineering and Technology, 439-445. DOI:
